Ere the last streaks of sunset die And song of thrush and blackb;.rd cease, And whilst from valley streP,„, arise White mists and shadow..-in fresh wreath ; Oh, husbandman, revi:aw again Thy corn stacks Ir:tit up in the sun, That, as freak r;isulage to the bird, Are warmth dud beauty to thine home; Then, thi:uk.who gave the shower and breeze, The e'wening dews and ripening heat, The cheerful reaper a full time To bend the sickle through the fields And lead their treasure to the fold : Oh, husbandman, review again Thy corn stacks built up in the sun; Sing unto God an evening hymn And thankful say, "This He hath done." —E. CULTURE, &c.

A plant of a new species of Aerides was sold last week in London for 235 guineas. The purchaser was Sir Trevor Lewrence, of Dorking, and the price is said to be the highest ever given for an orchid put up for sale at a public auction. THE Cuors.—ln the district lying between Wigan and Preston two days ago about half the grain crop was still unhoused, and seven fields of eatseteeo sef wheat, and two of barley were counted which remain theiee cut. The wind has been more severe here, for most of the haddocks were lying prostrate on the ground. Most of the potatoes are undug, and grass was being fast destroyed from the ground being wet, and cattle trampling it. Between Wigan and Tyldesley there was some grain still out, and housing was going on. There were several fields of clover down, and some of this bears signs of being badly weathered. Upon Chat Moss there is grain both to cut and standing in the haddock. There is also clover down. lam informed that a consider- able part of the second crop has been well housed. There is some disease in the potatoes in that district. A Bovient RACER.—Wabash, the two-year-old calico oalf, says a INTew York paper, that is credited with a mile racing record of 2.20, was taken to Philadelphia recentiy by his owner, Colonel Chas. J. Burns, of Evansville, Ind. Wabash has won seven races off the reel this summer, and was only beaten once. On that occasion he fell down. At Bedford Park, recently', he easily beat J. C. Mason's black gelding, The Major, a mile in 2•20. After the race, Colonel Burns declined to accept an offer of 000 for his fleet-footed bovine. The calf is nearly 131 hands high, his legs are like those of a giraffe, and his horns are tipped with nickel plated knobs. Colonel Burns bought the calf when a year- ling from an Indiana farmer, who was driving the split-hoof trotter to a sulky, and beating all ordinary roadsters with ease. The calf is of plebeian blood, and was bred, raised, and trained by the farmer. Hitched to a light waggon, Wabash trotted to Belmont Park, and was sent around the track several times at a three-minute gait. The calf's wind and limbs are perfectly, sound, and his owner says he has driven him forty miles a day without making him turn a hair. MILLIONAIRE AND BAREFOOT BOY. 'Tis evening, and the round red sun sinks slowly in the west, The flowers fold their petals up, the birds fly to their nest, The crickets chirrup in the grass, the bats flit to and fro, And tinkle-tankle up the lane the lowing cattle go ; And the rich an from his carriage looks out on them as they come— On them and on the BarefootNoy.44t drives the cattle

home. "1 wish," the boy says to hiroself—" I wish that I were he, And yet, upon maturer thought, Ido not—no, sirree ! Not for the gold his coffers hold would I be that duffer there, With a liver pad and a gouty toe, and scarce a single hair ; To have a wife with a Roman nose, and fear lest a panic

come— tr better to be the Barefoot Boy that drives the cattle home." And the rich man murmurs to himself: "Would I give all my pelf To change my lot with yonder boy 9 Not if ?know myself, Over the grass that's full of ants and chill with dew, to go, With a cruel bruise on either heel and a splinter is my toe! Oh, I'd rather sail my yacht a year across the ocean's foam Than be one day the Barefoot Boy that drives the cattle home." —Harper's Monthly.

THE EXAMINER, SATUR DAY, OCTOBER 13 1883.

ENSILAGE IN MORAYSHIRE.—Lord Thurlow, who takes a practical interest in agricultural matters, is making an ex- periment in the preparation of ensilage in the Home Farm, Dunphail. The work of constructing a silo on the most approved method has been completed. The pit is con- structed of concrete, and the necessary provision for drain- ing the moisture from the contents is provided. The ex- periment will be made on a scale of sufficient magnitude to thoroughly test the utility of preserving green crops as winter food for cattle, and the greatest care will be exer- cised in conducting the details of the trial, so as to ensure its complete success. The Earl of Seafield is making a similar experiment on his farm in Tochineal.

THE LOWTON TRAGEDY. INQUEST AND VERDICT. The inquiry concerning the death of Joshua Rigby, farmer, Lowton, who was found dead in his house on the morning of September 18th, was resumed on Wednesday, in the Police Court, Leigh, before Mr. Barker, district coroner. Mr. W. Cobbett was present on behalf of the Treasnry ; and the accased man, Jahn Gibbon, nephew of the deceased. was again represented by Mr. H. M. Richardson. A larg,, crowd witnessed the prisoner's arrival by train from Strange- ways. The court-room was crowded. The first witness called was Elias Boardman, carter, living at Green-lane End, Bedford, who said on the morning of the 18th ult. he left Messrs. Picksley, Sims, and Co.'s works at 3-20 in the morning, on his way to go to Liver- pool. When at Lowton, opposite the house of the de- ceased, at about 4-20, he saw a light in one of the window bottoms.

Dr. Campbell Brown, county analyst, said the grey shirt produced, belonging to the prisoner, had two blood stains on the front of the left sleeve and a spot of blood ox the back near the neck. The stains appeared to be of blood that had been smeared off. On the prisoner's right boot (produced), between the sole and the upper, partly lying in the seam, and partly sticking out of it, the witness picked off a grey hair, about 2iin. long, and very fine. He found that it cor- responded in calibre with grey hairs which he had taken from the deceased's nightcap. The hair was undoubtedly human. The nightcap had manifestly blood upon it, and there was a crushed mark. There was a semi-circular stained mark on the cap of something that had oozed out. There were little holes made in the cap by some hard ma- terial. There was blood upon a great many parts inside the nightcap. On the prisoners trousers (produced) there was a spot of blood on the outside of the right leg, a little below the knee.
By the Coroner: I cannot say whether it is the blood of a man.

By the Jury: There are slight punctured wounds in the nightcap. I could not say whether the blood on the night- cap corresponded as to the time when made with the smear on the trousers. The stain on the trousers is such as I sometimes find on anybody's trousers. I attach no impor- tance to it.

Evidence was given by J. H. Stephenson, reporter ; Joshua Rigby, cabman, nephew of the deceased; and Thomas Bact, Isaac Wilcock, William Richardson, Thomas Boydell, and James Rigby, brother of the deceased. Police-constable Naylor said that on Tuesday, the 18th September, about nine o'clock in the morning, he was sum- moned by William Richardson, whom he accompanied to the deceased's house, where he found the prisoner and Thos. Bent in the front kitchen. Gibbon desired him to go up- stairs, and witness went up, and saw the deceased lying be- tween the bed and the wall. His left arm was by his side against the wall, and his right elbow was against the bed. The back part of his head was against the wall. Witness asked the persons present to lift the body on to the bed. He then noticed blood on the sacking on the floor, and saw that the deceased's throat was cut. A razor was on the bed near the pillow, and a knife about half a yard down the bed. Both were open with the handles towards the deceasefl. The knife had Ilood on it from th@ top of the blade to about half way up. He went down to the kitchen and asked the prisoner what time his uncle came home the night previous, and prisoner said about 10-30 ; and in reply to a further question, he said he did not notice

anything unusual about him. As his uncle, the prisoner added, did not get up at the usual time that morning, he went upstairs about 8-30, and found him lying between the bed and the wall; he then called Thomas Bent, and sent for witness straight away. Witness sent to the house again about eight o'clock at night, and found, on further exami- nation, woands on the arms, head, and body of the deceased. Gibbon was there when he examined the body, but made no remark. Before coming down, witness asked Gibbon for the old man's trousers, and he said, "They are here," and fetched them out of his own bedroom. _

By Mr. Cobbett : When in the morning I saw prisoner, I asked him who slept in the house besides the old man. He said, "There was nobody slept in it only me and him." I saw none of the clothes of the deceased on my first visit. I should have seen them if they had been there. I should have seen them if they had been there. No clothes were on the stair rail.

By Mr. Richardson: I made a report of the case in the morning as one of suicide, but did not mention the clothes. I afterwards reported more full- to Inspector Charnley, who wrote it down last Monday. There is nothing in the report but what is true.
By the Foreman: I left no one in charge when I went to report the case as a suicide. There was a fire in the kitchen.
By the Coroner: There might have been a lamp or can- dlestick in the kitchen.

Inspector Charnley said that, in company with Sergeant Dunn, P.C. Naylor, and Mr. Stephenson, he went to the house of the deceased on the night of the 18th ult., after nine o'clock. The house was locked up, and he went to John Bent's, father-in-law of the prisoner. In about five minutes the prisoner came downstairs. Witness told him he wanted to examine the house and the body of the de- ceased, as the report of the constable was unsatisfactory. Gibbon and his father-in-law went with witness. He found a rough plaister on the neck of deceased. He removed it and examined the wounds, and then asked Gibbon if there were any other wounds about the body. The prisoner replied, "Not that I know of." Witness then examined the head and found two wounds, one near the top and the other down the right side. He saw wounds on the shoulder and arms, and on the left breast, and some slight wounds on the right cheek. Gibbon was present Witness asked where deceased's shirt was, and he said, "It is downstairs in the washtub." In the back kitchen witness found a wash-tub, containing water and linen. He examined the contents, and found the shirt, flannel singlet, and night cap, which he produced. Each art;cle had a quantity of blood upon it. He called Sergeant Dunn and John Gibbon to the door, and asked the prisoner how many persons slept in the house on the pre- vious night, and Gibbon said: "There was no one besides my uncle and me." Further asked Gibbon if he saw any- thing unusual about his uncle, and he said, "No ; be had been to the Jolly Carter having a gill or two. He came in about half-past ten, and went right upstairs." Further questioned, Gibbon said he had heard nothing during the night; that he got up about five o'clock that morning with- out noticing anything unusual, and attended to his work about the buildings until about half-past eight, when he thought it was time for his uncle to be getting up. Then he went upstairs to see what was the matter, and saw his ' uncle " cruddled " down by the side of the bed. He added that be did not go into the room, but called William Richardson, who went for the police, and no one went in the room until Richardson came with a constable. On searching the prisoner at the police station witness found a leather purse containing £lO 12s 6d and two keys, a bag containing 3s 10d, another bag containing a key, and a money bag inside it. He charged Gibbon on suspicion ef having caused the death of the deceased, and the prisoner replied, "No, sir." Witness re- turned to the farm, in company with Sergeant Dunn, and on the rail at the top of the stairs he found a pair of trousers belonging to the deceased, which were wet in front from a little below the waistband to the knee. On the 21st ult, at the house of the prisoner's father-in-law witness found the coat produced. In it there wasa handkerchief, inside which there was the will of the deceased, two bank books, and other papers. • The Coronerolhen summed up. He said there was no testimony that anybody but John Gibbon was on the pre- mises during the night on which the deceased met hie death. He was hound to say that the prisoner's conduct when the discovery was made was not that of a guilty man. Who- ever committed the murder, there had been an attempt, by the placing of the razor and the knife where they were found on the bed, to lead people to the supposition that de- ceased had committed suicide. If the jury had reasonable dr.ubt, they would return a verdict of wilful murder against some persons unknown. The jury, after deliberating fifty minutes, returned a verdict that the deceased had been murdered, and that there was sufficient evidence against the prisoner to send I•im for trial.
The Coroner said that was a verdict of wilful murder against Gibbon? and committed the prisoner for trial at the next astizee.

TIIE COMING K—.—Cammack.—Advt. The height of patience may be considered to be a deaf man listening for the ticking of a sun-dial. The only time when a man is generous in drawing the line between his own and his neighbour's property is when he shovels the snow off the pavement. A green one, who had crossed the Atlantic, told a story. of a storm, when the rain poured down in such torrents that the ocean rose six iuches. "There's no mistake," said he, "because the captain kept a mark on the side of the vessel." " Sire, one word," said a soldier one day to Frederick the Great, when presenting to Lim a request for the brevet of lieutenant. "If you say two," answered the King, "I will have you hanged." "Sign," replied the soldier. The Bing stared, whistled, and signed. No man's spirits were ever hurt by doing his duty. On the contrary, one good action, one temptation resisted and overcome, one sacrifice of desire of interest, purely for con- science sake, will prove a cordial for weak and low spirits beyond what either indulgence or diversion can do for them.

A. little girl, after her first visit to the country, was asked, "What did you like best in the country ?" The child re- plied, "I like the country because there are no corners. When I am at home, mother does not allow me to go farther than the corner of the street; but ill the country there are no corners, so I could go anywhere."

Bing James I. gave all manner of liberty and encourage- ment to the exercise of buffoonery, and he tAok great de- light in it himself. Happening once to bear somewhat hard on one of his Scotch courtiers, "By my saul," returns the Peer, "he that made your Majesty a King spoiled the best fool in Christendom." •

I was showing my watch to my nephew, who was about six years old," says a celebrated writer, "when he pointed to the face of the dial, and said, 'Why, there is another little watch.' I said, •It is called the second-hand.' He tossed his head contemptuously and walked off, saying, / wouldn't own a second-hand watch.'" ARREST OF THE ABSCONDING CATHOLIC PRIEST.—The Rev. John Rinks, a Catholic priest in Liverpool, who dis- appeared about a month ago, in company with a female member of his congregetion, and who is charged with ap- propriating to his use the sum of £BOO belonging to the church, has teen Arrested in Paris. AN ALARMING ACCIDENT occurred on the North-eastern line, near Crossgates station, three miles front Leeds, on IThursday afternoon. Whilst the express which leaves IHull at 12-42 was proceeding at the rate of upwards of 140 miles an hour, and just after passing Crossgates station, lit left the metals, bumping over the sleepers, and eVentually cutting into the soil until the wheels were buried tip to the axles 11`.1.ore the engine cauld be stopped. There was, of Course, great alarm among the passengers, but no serious • • Injury is reported.

fOOR FITCH."—Poor Fitch! He in",rcommon with many others of the day who did and did not give their ideas to the world, was on the right track, but could not put them into practical and practicable shape. He was really a man of remarkable genius. The son of a Connecticut farmer, he had been apprenticed to a watch and clock maker, where doubtless he increased his knowledge of the mechanical arts. During the early part of the Revolution- ary War, he was armourer to the State of New Jersey, and later, became a land surveyor. While acting in that capacity, the idea first suggested itself to him, as it did almost simultaneously to Symington, in Scotland, of pro,- pelling carriages by steam, but he soon abandoned it on account of the roughness of the American roads. After that he turned his attention almost exclusively to the pro- pulsion of vessels by steam, visiting England and France, but obtaining no pecuniary advantage from the experiments he proposed or consummated. In the sketch of his life, which appeared a few years since, the writer describes Fitch's difficulties in raising the money to finish his second steamboat "In a letter to David Roltenhouse, when asking an advance of £5O to' finish the boat, he says, This, sir, whether I bring it to perfection or not, will be the mode of crossing the Atlantic for packets and armed vessels. But everything failed, and the poor/projector loitered about the city for some months, a despised, unfortunate, heart- broken man. 'Often have I seen him,' !aid Thomas P. Cope, many years afterwards, stalking about like a troubled spectre, with downcast eyes and lowering countenance, his coarse soiled linen peeping through the elbows of a tattered garment.' Speaking of a visit he once paid to John Wilson, his boat-builder, and Peter Brown, his blacksmith, in which, as usual, he held forth upon his hobby, Mr. Cope says: ' After indulging himself for some time in his never-failing topic of deep excitement, he concluded with these memorable words: " Well, gentlemen, although I shall not live to see the time, you will, when steamboats will be preferred to all other means of conveyance and especially for passengers; and they will be particularly useful in the navigation of the river Mississippi.' He then retired, on which Brown, turn- ing to Wilson, exclaimed in a tone of deep sympathy, Poor fellow; what a pity he is crazy!'" Fitch, reduced to utter poverty and despair, threw himself into the Alleghany in 1798, and thus terminated his chequered life.—" Th 43 Sea; its Stirring Story of Adventure. Peril, and Heroism." MISCELLANEILTS. A hull provision --ni;i:cha;CN-41-1-0-iiii-see-d—a- short time .E,go with about £lO,OOO has been c iptared in Madrid. Thomas Warden, the absconding secretary of the London and River Plate Bank, was arrested in London, on Monday afternoon. At Glasgow, on Monday, James M‘Culloch was remanded on the charge of haying been concerned in the recent dyna- mite outrage. The foundation stone of new municipal buildings a Glas- gow, which are to cost £250,000, waa laid on Saturday by Lord Provost lire with m tecnic and civic ceremonies. On Monday, at the Birkenhead Police Court, Thomas Green, who is charged with stabbing two youn g women during a Salvation Army riot last we it, was committed for trial. Mr. Astrnp Cariss, a Liverpool accountant, is missing, and a report presented to a buildins . society, of which he Was secretary, says there is due fromi him to the society a , Sum of nearly £1.700. On behalf of Mr. Fitzroy, of St. Jude's Church, Liver- Pool, al appeal against the recent decision of Lord Penzance, sentencing Mr. Fitzroy to three years' suspension, was lodged on Thursday. At Bridport, late on Wednesday night, a lady either acci- dentally fell or sprang over the highest point of East Cliff, about 300 feet high, and her body, dreadfully mangled, was found on the rocks beneath. PENAL SERVITUDE rose ARMY DEsEnTsus.—The Duke of Cambrlige has issued orders that, in all cases of re-enlist- anent after a soldier has been dismissed from the army, he shall be tried by general court martial, in order that sen- tences of penal servitude may be awarded. A STEAMER DESTROYED BY FIRE.—As the steamer E.n- press, of Hull, was entering ,he Humber on Saturday a fire was discovered in the forehold of the vessel. An explosion Shortly afterwards took place, killing four men and injuring two others. The vessel was destroyed by the fire. THE FRAUDS BY A BIRMINGHAM BANK MANAGER.— The directors and shareholders of the Birmingham Midland Bank have decided to take over the whole of the liabilities and assete of the Birmingham Lienitec'., owing to the frauds of Burgan,lfie late manager of the latter.

CHARGE AGAINST A BOROUGH AUDITOR.—At Leeds, 011 Wednesday, Mr. William Strickland, aged 50, a gentleman Of independent mean, and one of the borough auditors, was Corm!tted for trial at the assizs, chargcd with having appro- priated CO his own use railway stocks of the value of £2,000, for which he was a trustee. Bail was refused.

WHOLESALE POISONING IN LIVERPOOL —The Liverpool police are investigating an extraordinary charge of poison- ing made against a woman named Flannigan, who resided in Latimer-street, Scotland-road. It is alleged that she insured the live 3 of her victims and then poisoned them, afterwards drawing the amounts due at their deaths. The accused is Missing. THE SUNDERLAND DISASTER.-011 Saturday evening a meeting of the Memorial Committee of the Sanderland disaster decided to commission Mr. Brooker, sculptor, Sun- .d9rland, to execute the statute, eight feet in hAght, in mar- ble, according to a model submitted and approved, at a cost of five hundred guineas, in cornmemmoration of the Victoria Hall disaster.

TEM ANNUAL CONFERENCE OF Tan POOR-LAW GUAR- DUNS of the north-western district has been held at Manchester. Mr. J. T. Hibbert, M.P., presided, and in his address gave some interesting figures regardinz the diminu- tion of pauperism in the country within the decade from 1812 to 1832. The conference agreed to hold its next /meeting at Macclesfield. AN;T:/-VACCINATORS AT LEICZSTER.—SeveraI months ago the 'Leicester Board at Guardians decided not to prosecute the thousands of anti-vaccinators In the town, but recently, by the casting vote of the chairman only, they resolved to Prosecute delinquents as before. On Wednesday, the first batch of twenty anti-vaccinators were summoned, and tines Of 10a. were inflicted. _ _

THE VAGRANCY ACr NOVEL DECISION.—The Potteries Stipendiary Magistrate has decided that workmen who, during the strike, perambulate the public highway, asking for charitable gifts in behalf of those affected by the strike, are contravening the Vagrancy Act. On Tuesday he fined in small sums a number of North Staffordshire miners who had followed this practice, but granted a case for a superior Court. MURDER IN LITERPOOL.—CharIes Henry Dutton, aged 22 years, boilermaker, was on Monday remanded at the Liverpool Police Court, charged with the wilful murder of Hannah Hampshaw, aged 63, his wife's grandmother, who lived with him in Athol-street, and whom he assaulted in a inoat atrocious manner on Saturday night. At the inquest, held on Tuesday, a verdict of wilful murder was returned against Dutton. SOCIAL SCIENCE CONGRESS —The opening address at the gavial Science Congress at Huddersfield, on Monday, was delivered before a large audience by Mr. Pridgin Teals, President of the Health Department, who emphatically con- demned the existing over-pressure in education, and especially the competitive examination system, as seriously injuring the health and physical development of children, and pupil teachers. Martwoon.—Since the death of Marwood, the late public hangman, hundreds of his photographs have been sold by a photographer at Horncastle. Twenty-one ropes and nine nets of straps have been secured foom the widow and despatched to London. They will be offered for sale to Madame Tussand's exhibition. Applications for reline of the late hangman have been numerous, some having been received from America. ROYAL VitilT TO LEEns —The Duke and Duchess of Albany visited Leeds, on Wednesday, on the occasion of the Music-al Festival. Their Royal Highnesses drove to the Town Hall and were p-esented with an address from the Corporation. The Dale:: suitably responded. Their Royal Highnesses afterwards proceeded to Victoria Hall to hear the opening performance of "Elijah." The Dake and Duchess met with an enthusiastic reception. A FOOLE Tans ACROSS TRE STRAITS OF DOVER. —Captain Dewar started last week in his miniature paddle- boat, to cross the Channel from Dover to Calais. The boat being entirely unfitted for such a voyage and the sea very lumpy, all hopes of his safety have been abandoned at Dover. As soon as he got into the tideway be lost all control over his vessel, an I was drifted eastward—euite the opposite direction to which he wanted to go. Oa Friday night one of the hing., lYnts !ailing out ef Dover picked up the cap- tain and his boat on the Goodwin Sands. He was landed at Dover in a very exhausted state during the night. A TraeniueE DEATH.— The passengers of an express train which was running between Dunblme and Bridge of Allan, one night last week, at a speed of GO miles an hour, were startled by the appearance of a man passing along the footbeard and tapping at the windows of the carriages. When the train came to a stand at Bridgo of Allan a search vras made along the line, and the dead body ef a man, ter- ribly disfigured, was foand near to Dunblane station. A return ticket from Dundee to Glasgow was found upon him It is not known how he left the carriages, as all the doors were fastened when the train reached its destination.

UNSEEMLY PROCEEDINGS AT A LIVERPOOL CEIIaROR. The Rev. E. T. A. Fitzroy, the incumbent of St. Jude's, Liverpool, who was recently suspended for three years by Lord Penzance for drunkenness and gave notice of appeal, eppeared at the church, on Sunday morning, and attempted tie celebrate Holy Communion, bat he was prevented. After Saying " matins " amidst considerable opposition, he an- nouncee that he should take pert in tha eleven o'clock ser- vice. At that hour he appeared in church, but such a tumultuous scene took place that Archdeecen Bardsley an- nounced that. there would be no service, and as soon as the Sacred edifice had been cleared it was locked up for the rest Of the day. Mr. Fitaroves contention is that the inhibition ty the Bishop of Liverpool ceased on the day Lord Penzance Pronounced juegment, welch, it is urged by Mr. Fitzroy, Cannot take effect until his appeal has been heard. Remiss PATENTS. The following patents amongst Others, published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending October 6th, 1883 : Thomas Charles Olney, of Manchester, for improvements in the construction of hot water apparatus for heating build- lege, and In valves to be used therewith, which valves are also applicable to other analagons purposes; Charles Leigh Clarke, Manchester' improvements in galvanic batteries; jehn Vincent Taylor, Warrington, improvements in the manufacture of steam packing; Joseph Hamer, Stalybridge, an improved tool for extracting internal stoppers from bottles; Charles Lexton Jackson and James Westley, Bolton, improvements in the construction of bleaching kiers; Roger Tatham, ftochdale, and Alfred Hollings, Salford, improvements in secondary batteries; Alfred Seale Harlem, berbv, improvements in refrigerative aeparaeus ; • Mark Haslam, Stockport, improvements in silk felt and Other hats, and in machinery or apparatus employed in such Manufacture ; John Maule Sutton, M.D., Manchester, im- Proved apparatus, or-machinery, for drying excreta, urine, and other substances, and for the treatment of the vapour and gases given off during evaporation —List supplied by 'Mr. George Davies, C.E., Fel. Inst. P.A., 4, St. Ann's-square, Manchester. A Pcilliasnc CLERGYIIAN.-0a Monday, at Epsom, the Rev.. Gerald Hay, of Ockley, near Dorking, was summoned for unlawfully assaulting Mr. A. R Jackson, partner in the firm of Jackson and Prince, solicitors, of Cannon-street and Sutton. The defendant did not appear.—Mr. G. W. Dennis, of Croydon, appeared for the prosecution, and said the de- fendant WAS a clergyman of the Established Church, and dot only had he set the Bench at defiance by not putting in an appearance, although the summons was served personally, • but had sent to a relative of the prosecutor a letter in which the following extraordinary paesae e occurred :—I came to Sutton yesterday on purpose to punish the impertinence of that man. I knew I should meet him on the way to the station. I told him I wanted to speak to him, so his friends Went on. I then asked him whether he intended to apolo- gise. He raid No.' 'Then take that,' said I, as I struck him on the face. Then we fought. The only marks I have sustained are the peaking of three knuckles during the pro- eerie of pommelling; but look at his forehead the next time Yen see him. I exp,ct the blustering for' will take me be- Tore a magistrate; hut if I haveto pay £5 it will be a small • ?rice for the satisfaction and equanimity I now express. afterwards went on to West Croydon and heard the etschbishop of Canterbury preach at the consecration of St. Michael and All Angels, and thought 1 might have been Ire of you there." The reading of the letter created loud laughter, in which the Bench joined:—On the application Of Mr. Dennis, the Earl of Egmont granted a warrant for the rev, gentleman's apprehension. ~,F.. miF.A.TING'S COUGH LOZENGES cures Coughs, Asthma, Bron- nts —Medical testimony states that no o'her medicine is so rZtual in the cure of these dangerous maladies. ' Mr. Henry Irving and Miss Ellen Terry left Liverpool on Thursday on board the White star steamer Britannic for New York. Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. John Morley are making an excursion in Touraine, and have arranged to entertain M. Clemenceau at a dejeuner. Mr. Gladstone, who was accompanied by Mrs. Glad- stone and Miss Mary Gladstone' left Hawarden on Monday afternoon, on a visit to Earl Derby at Knowaley. The Duke and Duchess of Connaught left Buckingham Palace on Monday evening for BAlmoral, where they will remain for a few days on a visit to the Queen. It is understood that her Royal Highness the Princess Louise and the Marquis of Lorne will leave Quebec in the Allan Royal mail steamer Sardinian on the 27th inst. for Liverpool. ' The Ray. Thomas M'Cullagh, president of the Wesleyan I Conference, is now considered out of 'danger, but owing to extreme physical prostration he is likely to be unfitted for the discharge of his official duties for some time to come. He is still at Hexhatn. • Mr. Sergeant Simon, M.P. for Dewsbury, who has been ill for many months suffering from a complication of disorders, lies in a very critical condition. It was hoped some time since that the learned member was recovering, but he has had a serious relapse. Colonel Stanley, senior member for North Lancashire. was, on Wednesday, thrown from his trap whilst driving , between Grange and Lancaster. Happily, the gallant mem- ber received no hurt beyond a severe shaking, the effects of which, it is hoped, will soon disappear. The PREMIER, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, Lard and Lady Derby, and several distinguished visitors at Knows- ley, on Thursday, drove to Liverpool, and inspected the works of the Mersey tunnel. Mr. Gladstone expressed great satisfaction at what be saw, stating that he had always been an advocate of the tunnel. The party afterwards visited the Art Gallery. Lord and Lady Wolseley's visit to the Earl and Countess of an.by, at Knowsley, has been given up, owing to the r T Wellaalan UL 140/1.1 • t.n.eiey a I.llW.Hea, .• ••••••-••-•,,, which occurred at Thchmond on Sundae- last. The deceased lady, Fraeces Anne, was a daughter of Mr. William Smith, of Golden Bridge House' county Dublin, and was born in 1801. She married, in 1825, Major Garnet Joseph Wol- seley, of the King's 0 wn Borderers, but was left a widow in 1840.
rafti4p~illli POLITICAL.

Mat. W. S. ALLEN, M.P., speaking at Newcastle-under- Lyme, on Thursday evening, advocated the creation of life peers. The Hon. E. LYULPH STANLEY, M.P., in a letter to the Oldham anti-vaccinators, says that if they consider their question more important than all the rest of the field of politics, and if they could find an uncompromising opponent ef vaccination whom they would have any chance of re- turning, they would be quite right to prevent his (Mr. Stanley's) return to Parliament. Dn. PANKHIIRST ATTACKS MANCHESTER LIBERALS.—On Thursday night Dr. Pankhurst addressed a meeting of the committee who conducted his candidature at the late con- test in Manchester. He again attacked the Liberal Asso- ciation and the Liberal press, and quoted extensively from speeches delivered by him at political gatherings to show that he had been a firm supporter of Mr. Gladstone. THE RIGHT Hose. JAMES LOWTHER, M.P., addressing a meeting on Thursday, at Ampthill, in support of Mr. Bart- telot, Conservative candidate for Bedfordshire, said he be- lieved there was a bad spirit abroad, a restless feeling of hostility against the present possessors of property, and a desire to oust them from it, and that some members of the Cdoinet went nearly to the same extent. In domestic legis- lation the Liberals set class against class, whilst the Con- fferVatiVeS studied the good of all. Mr. W. E. BAXTER, addressing his constituents at Forfar, on Thursday night, said that two bills would pass through the House of Commons soon. One wasthe bill for legalising marriage with a deceased's wife's sister, and the other was a bill to alter the oath administered to members of the House of Commons. He regarded that ceremony simply as a farce. Referring to the Channel tunnel scheme, he said the project should not be hurried on, and that ere long the opponents of the scheme would be converted. Sir RICHARD TEMPLE, addressing the Huddersfield volun- teers on Saturday, said they might thank God that the military despotism of the continent had not been introduced Into this country, and also for the "silver streak" that washed our rocl-beund coast. Though disparaging reports were heard about our navy, he believed England could now put double the number of ships into line of battle than the Havel Power next to her could ehow, and as mrty first- class ironclads as all the other Powers put together. A CONSERVATIVE ESTIMATE OF THE PREMIER.—Mr. E Clarke, Q.C., M.P., speaking at Plymouth on Monday night, under the auspices of the local parliamentary debat- ing society, gave an acconnt af the origin of debating societies. He spoke of Mr. Gladstone as beyond comparison the greatest orator in the House of Commons, and said the Premier always evinced the utmost desire to know what every speaker was saying, however unimportant he might be, and no matter what his party might be. He alluded to this as the distinguishing trait of Mr. Gladstone, and one which characterised him beyond anyone else in the House. The JUDGE ADVOCATE-GENERAL (Mr. Osborne Morgan), speaking on Monday at the opening of the Cefn branch of the Denbigshire Liberal Association, said that without such organisations the Liberal party would rapidly degenerate into an undisciplined mob. The Conservative leaders showed that they hoped more from the dissensions of their opponents than from the strength of their awn party, and his advice to the constituencies was to make up their minds to choose the best man at the next election, and then to close their ranks. But., above all, they must be aware of "independent" candidates. It was al, very well to decry the " Cauceis," but what were these Conservative unions and associations which were being lauded and paraded all over the country but so many caucuses in disguise? Lord E Cavarmisu and Mr. J. F. CHEEFIIAM have ad- dressed their constituents at Hartingtou. Lord Edward Cavendish, adverting to the legislation of the future, said be considered the County Government Bill and the question of local taxation of the greatest importance. He held that those who paid the rates ought to have a voice in the selec- tion of representatives. The extension of the county fran- chise would not limit but extend the circle of political power, for the broader the basis the firmer and better would the foundation be.—Mr. Cheetham referred at some length to the Irish difficulty, and said he thought the thanks of the nation were due to Lord Spencer and the other officials for the prompt way in which they had put in force those repressive measures which were necessary to uphold the law and produce a better feeling of security amongst the people. MR. EDWARD CLARKE, M.P., ON THE MINISTERIAL POLICY.—Mr. Clarke, Q.C., MV., addressing a meeting of the West Cornwall Conservatives at Penzance on Thursday, said if they looked at the history of the past three years they would find that the year 1881 would be marked as the I year of Transvaal, and 1882 as the year of Egypt. The war in Egypt was absolutely unnecessary and unjust, and if we i , withdrew our authority from Egypt there would be anarchy afterwards, and the power of the Khedive would not be I worth 24 hours purchase. He characterised the policy of the Government in relation to the Transvaal as discredit- able, saying they had playel false with the colonists, and ' had abandoned the natives to slavery. With respect to Ire- land, the Government not only bargained with the Irish mem- bers in the House of Commons, but bargained with sedition out of the House. He contended that before reform contro- versy was attended to many practical measures for the good of the people should be dealt with. MR. GIBSON, M.P., IN INvERNESS-SHIRE.—At the an- nual meeting of the Northern Counties Constitutional Asso- clwion, held at Forms, Inverness-shire, on Tuesday. Mr. Gieson, M.P., said that in politics it was necessary to have I pluck and courage, and he knew no period in the public life • of this country when it was more necessary to have courage, or when there was more promise of success. Contrasting Conservative with Liberal finance, he maintained that the former resulted in decreased expenditure with efficiency, whereas the latter resulted in increased expenditure without efficiency. Every person who looked at the great question of the government of the country with intelligence and firm- ness was bound to be nerved by criticism, and the greatest and noblest mission of the Conservatives was to act in re- collection of the truth that they ware representatives of the people, by which he meant all classes and conditions of people. Thus truth would bear criticism' and could not be controverted. Mr. Chaplain, M.P., also addressed the meeting.

Some exceptionally high tides are lookeii forward to by meteorologists between the 18th and 20th instants. A dense black fog visited centre Lowlon on Thursday morning. Gas and electric lights were used in the streets. It is stated that the arming of the metropolitan police has already commenced in one or two districts, and the sys- tem will, it is expected, become general next veer. Elizabeth Hawkins, aged 13, was committed for trial on Thursday, at the Thames Police Court, for burglary. The pr:soner entered the house through the kitchen window. An outburst of land springs is reported to have taken place on the Monmouthshire side of the Severn Tunnel. The men at work fled, and no loss of life is reported, but three horses were drowned. FATAL SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT.—WhiIe three men were re- pairing the sails of a wind mill near Liverpool, on Thursday, the scaffold gave way, and they fell from a great height. One we killed, and the others were terribly injured. , THE CONVICT GOULDSTONE.—The High Sheriff of Essex has received a communication from the Home Office stating that the convict, William Gouldstone, convicted of the murder of his five children at Walthamstow, had been cer- tified to be of unsound mind, and that he wit be removed tq Broadmoor Criminal Lunatic Asylum. . , ACCIDENT TO MR. MACARTHUR, M.P.--421n Wednesday.l _while out shooting with a friend at Plackley, Kent, Mr. Alexander Ma ' Carthur M. was accidentally struck in the eye by a ricochet shot from his carop..nion's gun. The injury is such as to necessitate an operation, and it is feared that the hon. member may lose the sight of the eye. REFUSING TO LEAVE CleoL.—On Thursday morning an im- becile, named Wright, belonging to Soeth Shields; whotad been confined in Durham Gaol for larceny, received ,his discharge. During his incarceration he had been at times very violent, and on reaching the prison gates he reftred to leave the gaol, and had to be ejected by force. Two warders were sent to the railway station with him, and on the road he repeatedly kicked and tried to •bite them, causing an exciting scene in the streets.

FOREIGN INTELLIG .

The Yunj,tub Local Self-Government Bill was passed by the Indian Vice-regal Council on Wednesday. The Democrats of Ohio have returned their candidate for the governorship of the State by a majority of ten thousand.

The son of Prince Mavrocordato, the Hellenic Minister to France, met his death accidentally on Sunday, having shot himself while trying a revolver. The Emperor and Empress of Russia left Copenhagen on Thursday to return home. The Prince and Princess of Wales leave the Danish capital on the 15th inst.

THE KHEDIVE OF EGYPT has issued a decree granting an amnesty for crimes connected with the late insurrection, with the exception of murders and outrazes on women. The budget of the French Minister of War was presented on Thursday to the Budget Committee. The total amount of the estimated expenditure is 593,000,000 franca. The French Commissioner in Tonquiu has, according to reports in Hong Kong, bought off in hard cash the opposi- tion of the Black Flags to the occupation of that territory by French troops. A telegram, dated Rome, Thursday, says that the police havelarrested four of the band of marauders who had formed a plan to rob a special train when entering the tannel near Sassari. Prince Alexander of Bulgaria intends shortly to visit Vienna and Berlin. M. Zankoff, the Bulgarian Premier, has declared his intention to place the laws in harmony with the reStoreci constitution.

CE rEWAYo.—Usibepu has sent a peremptory message to Cetewayo, telling hina he must leave the reserve territory and not again return to Zululand. The British troops are building a strong fort at Ekowe, an the Natal frontier. A REMARKABLE ACCIDENT has just occurred at Pittsburg, , Pennsylvania. The brakes on a street car failed to act, and ' the vehicle ran clown a hill and into a railway train which was standing at the foot. Twenty-five persons were hurt, and three of them are reported to have died. GENERAL TIIRBAUDIN, the French Minister of War, has rtsigned. His resignation is understood to have very ma- terially dissipated the difficulties whin nave arisen oetween the French and Spanish Governments, in consequence of the hestile reception of King Alfonso in Paris. v... . . , Romnicta....--,tvang tinartes, at a iuncneon at asucnarest Monday, following the formal opening of a new royal resi- dence, said he bad erected the place as a sign that his dynasty had taken deep root in Roumania, and to afford his people a proof of his boundless confidence in the country's future.

Nimusu i Russr.t.. A Russian schoolmistress and eight young ladies, her pupils, all inmates of the Marie Institute, at Warsaw, of which the Czar is patron, have been arrested by the police of that city. On a search being made of the premises a large number of Nihilist pamphlets were discovered.

THE DEFENCE OF O'DmiNELL.—Telegrams from New ork state that extensive preparations are being made for the defence of O'Donnell, the man who shot James Carey. Large sums have been collected, and a number of " wit- nesses " are to be sent to London, it would seem, under the mistaken impression that they can be called on his behalf.

THE TEANSVALL.—President Kruger and the two other members of the deputation from the Transv4al embarked at Capetown, on Wednesday, for England. Speaking at a public banquet given in honour of the deputation at Cape- town, on Monday night, President Kruger said he confi- dently hoped to see the establishment of a South African confederation extending from Cape Colony to Zambesi. THE POPE made an important speech on Tuesday to a body of pilgrims whe presented themselves at the Vatican. He denied that the Papacy was the enemy of Italy, but pro- tested strongly against the deprivation of the temporal power. The pilgrims were told that it was one of their chief duties to desire that the Pope should be restored "to that condition of liberty and independence which was his due."

THE SALVATION ARMY IN SWITZERLAND. A Renter's telegram from Neuchatel, Switzerland, says that a public meeting was held there on Sunday at which a resolution was adopted,demanding the expulsion of the English mem- bers of the Salvation Army. A Cauncillor of State who was present declared that the body to which be belonged would do its duty, and close the gates of Switzerland to those who traded on her hospitality. The meeting, which was attended by 2,000 pet sons, passed off in an orderly manner. REVOLT OF WORKMEN IN RUSSIAN POLAND.—According to intelligence from St. Petersburg', several hundred work- men employed in the manufacturing establishments at Gonioudz, near Bjelostok, in the Polish province of Garoduo, revolted against the authorities on the 2nd inst. Lieut.- General Obratscheff, acting for the Minister of War, adopted rigorous measures, and ordered the military authorities of the district to send all the workmen at once under escort to their native places without any inquiry into the cause of the disturbance. Their removal was effected at a cost of 5,000 roubles.

Ifrom the inhabitants of Strabane. In his progless through Ulster, on Tuesday, Sir Stafford Nort tic )te received addresses at Omagh, Newtonstewart, Strabam:, and Lon Jon- derry. At the last-named place be replied at some length, urging the necessity of earnest and ni-ganised co-operati,fli with a view to the maintenance of the Union. Sir Staff ird, on Wednesday, arrived at Coleraine from Downhill, the re- sidence of Sir Hervey Bruce, Bart., and was presented with addresses from the Conservatives of Coleraine. In reply, the right hon. gentleman said his visit to Ulster had been des- cribed as an attempt to stir up strife, but it was not. It was , to rouse up Conservative feeling to support the Conserva- tive cause. They shoeld net allow their cause to become a mere exhibition of facetious feeling, but work zealously to secure electoral victories ir, the great battle which was at hand. Sir Stafford was afterwards presented with addresses by the Orangemen of Coleraine and Limavady. On Thurs- day, Sir Stafford Northcote left Downhill, the residence of Sir Hervey Bruce, and drove to Poitrush, where an address from the inhabitants was presented to him by Mr. M‘Naghten, M.P. After visiting the Giant's Causeway he returned to Downhill, and yesterday proceeded to Larne, en route for England. _

MR. RYLANDS, M.P., ON EDUCA- TIONAL ADVANTAGES. On Wednesday, Mr. Rylands, M.P., distributed the prizes to the successful students at the Burnley Grammar School. After expressing regret that there were only 66 boys in that school, where there was provision for 150, he said there never was a time when the education of this country re- ceived so great an amount of attention, or when such great strides were made in the education of the people as at the present time. Since 1870 there had been a very great in- crease in the educational instrumentality of this country. At present we had 18,280 day schools, with scholars on the register to the number of 4,189,612; actually present at the inspection 3,500,000. In addition we had 1,015 night schools, with 34,492 scholats. Since 1870 there had been provision made for tho accommodation of no fewer than 2,659,736 scholars, and ouriously enough provision for over 1;300,000 had been raiaaa voluntary efforts anti ior 1,295,000 by school boards. Without entering into any controversial matter about board schools and voluntary schools he considered we were deeply indebted to both these niatrun affort We should intitxtrtim . have failed to make the great progress we had done, and that without board schools voluntary effort would have failed to reach the necessities of the population. As this education was going on among the poorer classes, unless those who were in better positions in life, those who had more means or who were more anxious about their chil- dren, took precautions to secure the higher education of their children, they would be thrown behind in the race of life which was likely to be witnessed amongst us. There was no doubt that education was now the matter key to wealth and honour in this country. Formerly, if a man happened to be born with certain advantages belonging to a particular class of society, whatever his stupidity might be he had a fair chance of getting some public employment, of being in some way benefited by the circumstances of his position. But now nearly all the public offices were determined by competitive exam- ination, and dunces, idle or ignorant 'young fellows, were necessarily put on one side. They bad also to consider that the higher education given in the grammar school was not only the key to wealth and honour, but a matter of the greatest enjoyment and benefit to those who possessed it. The hon. member further observed that in his judgment the great competition of the world which we had now to meet would be fought out to a great extent by the higher know- ledge which the rople of the 'different countries possessed. Turning to the question of technical education, Mr. Rylands expressed the hope that greater facilities would be afforded to such schools as that, so that promising pupils would be able to pass on to the universities, and that an opportunity would be given for this-couatry to have the best advantage out of the best brains that she could produce.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.

The lith autumnal meeting of the Congregational Unioa of England and Wales opened at Sheffield on Mondayl evening. The Rev. H. Batchelor, of Newcastle-on-Tyne, delivered an address.—The Rev. Dr. Fairhairn on Tuesday delivered the inaugural address, his subject being "Chris- tianity in the Ninteentla Century." Christianity, he said, was full of unexhausted energies, talent, and undeveloped capabilities, fitted to meet the wants of the day. The de- velopment of these energies and capabilities had been made possible by the progress of the past. Their exercise was made necessary by the needs of the present. Coming to the attitude of the age, he said the religious spirit of the day was earnest, active, philanthropic, missionary. He spoke of the attitude of the cultivated and intellectual classes to the Christian religion, if not disaffected, at least as widely es- tranged. The attitude of the industrial and labouring classes to religion he regardel as the gravest of all reproaches to the churches of England. The modern intellectual class he would frankly and honestly meet face to face, and the working classes he would meet with an exhibition of re- ligion in its truth and power. What was necessary to reach and effect both was a more fully realised Christianity. It was reported that the Jubilee Fund amounted to £250,000. About one thousand delegates are present. At Wednesday's meeting a statement as to the position of Congregationalism in Canada was made by Dr. Archibald Duff. A deputation respresenting the free churches of Sheffield was introduced, and an address of greeting was read on behalf of those churches by the Rev. J. Bailey. The sentiments expressed in the address were supported by the Rev. W. H Dellinger and the Rev. Dr. Cocker.—The Chair- man of the Union replied.—After receiving reports on the subject of college work, and adopting a resolution in favour of consolidating the colleges into groups, the meeting was addressed by the Rev. Dr. Condor, of Leeds, on the subject of recent events in Madagascar.—Dr. CONDER moved a resolution, which was passed, expressive of hearty sympathy with the Rev. G. A. Shaw and the Rev. G. Cousins in the trials they have undergone.—Mr. SHAW, who was receiveel with prolonged cheering, spoke at some length in reply to the resolution. He said it had been reported that be had Came home to claim compensation. Whatever the French might intend to do, and whatever they would be abre to do, they would never be able to componsate him or the Malagasy people for what had taken place. If the word "redress" were put in the place of compensation he should not so much obj ct to it, and redress was looked for because he was not in Tanntave as a missionary only but as an Englishman. He spoke of the Christian spirit of the Malagasy people, and hoped he should soon be able to return to. his mission work in the island. Mr. SHAW, the Madagascar missionary, was present at a meeting in the evening, and in some remarks said it was encouraging to find from facts he had been able to collect that the people of the island "were still worshiping God, although they could net see His hand in what was happening." The session was brought to a close on ihursday. It was announced that the London Missionary Society had decided to grant substantial aid for the next nine years to the Con- gregational Unions of Jamaica and British Guiana to enable them to carry on the work of the churches in those islands, and Congregationalists were asked to assist the society in giving effect to this decision. Papers were read on the duty of Church members, and on tine and false ideas of national religion. In the evening there was a meeting in promotion of the temperance movement and a conversazione ,in the Albert Hall.

THE LIBERATION SOCIETY AND THE ECCLESIASTICAL COURTS COM- MISSION. The Executive Cammittee of the Liberation Society, besides issuing a digest of the report of the Royal Commis- sion on the Ecclesiaatical Courts, have adopted a special minute on the recommendatious of the Commissioners. They admit the necessity for the inquiry, and recognise the care and ability with which it has been conducted, but are of opinion that the Commissioners have failed to trace to their real source the evils complained of ; while they have suggested remedies which are inadequate, or objectionable, and which are not likely to be adopted. It is stated that the report is based mainly on the objections of that section , of the Church of England which has disregarded the deci- sions of the existing legal tribunals, and which is trying to free the clergy from the restraints of an establishment with- out relinquishing its privileges. It is also stated that the report will encourage fresh demands, the conceselon of which would alter the relations between the Church and the State. It is pointed oat that if the final Court of Appeal continues to be a lay tribunal appointed by the crewn the O2Sistif."' issati- faction will not be removed; while it is insisted that, so !oiig A; th‘. Church ia eetabliehed, its clergy should be tried by tribunals presided over by lay judges. The committee protest against the requirement that only members of the Church of England shall be judges as being inconsistent with the nationality of the Church. They farther object to the Bishop's veto on all proceedings against clergymen; and to the proposal that the judges of the Court of Appeal shall Rot be bound to give the reaaptes for their decisions, a dangerous departure, as they contend, from the existing legal practice. They also call attention to the fact that the replies to the ibquiries of the Commissioners show that the non-established churches connected with the Church of Eagle:id in Ireland, Scotland, America, and elsewhere maintain diecipline without any coercive jurisdiction and by means of veluntaey compact. The committee would eppose any attempt to give legialative effect to the Commis- sioners' recommendetions, the time of the Legislature being already too over-taxed to •be devoted to attempts at re- organieing the Establishment. In conclusion, they state that they are convinced that no re-coelstruotion of the Eccle- siastical Courts will remove the existing dissatisfaction; that " centinued reliance on legislation and litigation, as means of securing spiritual results, will end in failure in the future, as it has done in the pat, and that changes of a more decisive character than those proposed by the Commissioners are essential for the Chutch's prosperity and the Church's peace. Those changes, to be satisfactory, must be effected by the Church itself, and, therefore, cannot be effected until it has ceased to be established, and has been placed in the same legal position as that occupied by the other religious communities of the country."
It s been resolv,l to take steps for placing a monument to the memory of the late Hr. Hugh Birley, MX., in the Manclie6ter Cathedral.

. _ • The Bishop of Glouor.ster on Thursday consecrated a new parish church, erected in Gloucester is a memorial to Robert Raikes, founder of Sunday school. The Mayor of Birmingham and the Mayoress, for 47 years teetotallers, were on Thursby, at a special lodge sis- Bien, made members of the Good`Templar Order.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Cardinal M'Cabe has iesued a long pastoral in which he deals mainly with the question of education. During a demonstration at the laying of the foundation stones of a nes Orange Hall at Belfast, on Saturday, a stand gave way and several persons were severely injured. ADULTERATING TOBACCO. On Thursday, at Dublin Police Court, Mr. Metcalf, tobacco manufacturer, was fined £75 for adulterating his goods with gum arabic. The full penalty was £1,600. THE AMERICAN EVANGELISTS, Messrs. Moody and San- key, arrived from New York on Tuesday by the Graion steamer Alaska on a seven days' mission to Limerick, to be succeeded by a ten days' mission to Cork. At a meeting of the National League in Dublin, on Wednesday, Mr. Healy, M.P., announced that as a result of Nationalist efforts in the revision courts they would be able at the general election to carry Dublin city and county. CHARGE or MURDER.—Michael Tanguey, in custody for the murder of a lad named Sullivan, near Mulgrave, Kerry, was again brought up on Thursday at Kilarney Court-house, when there was a further private :investigation. Tanguey was afterwaids remanded for a week. At Dublin Police Court, on Thursday, William Li-nie, one of the murder conspiracy informers charged under a warrant with intent to abscond from the United Kingdom after having been bound over to give evidence, was com- mitted to jail until the next commission. Sri:dons CHARGE AGAINST WOMEN.—Three women, named Louisa Langan, Sophia Toole, and Margaret Hamp- ton, were remanded at Belfast, on Monday, on a charge of having adfninistered poison to a man named Wm. O'Neill, causing his death on Sunday night. Mr. W. DAWSON, Lord Mayor of Dublin, addressed his constituents at Carlow on Monday night, unfolding the programme of the Irish party. A vote of confilence in the honourble member, and recognising the dignity, indepen- dence, and patriotism displayed by him as Lord Mayor of Dublin, was carried. • THE MURDER CONSPIRACY.—On Tuesday, in the Irish High Court of Justice, an order was made admitting to bail Dr. Thomas Connolly, who is awaiting his trial for being, as alleged, engaged in the conspiracy to murder John Carroll, at Bruff, County Limerick. An application to have Michael Dileen, who is charged with murdering Constable Linton, at Loughrea, admitted to bail, was refused. AFFRAY WITH THE CONSTABULARY AT Lot:mamma.— M'Carthy, who has been admitted to bail after being in gaol since February last, charged with the murder of Con- stable Linton, arrived in Loughrea on Tuesday night, and was welcomed by a crowd of sympathisers. M`Cartby ad- dressed the people, and denounced the English Government. The police interfered and sought to disperse the crowd, and disorder ensued. Seale arrests were made. AN ORANGE PROCLAMATION.—The follcwing startling placard was issued at Enniskillen, on Wednesday morning : —"No surrender.—To the Orangemen of Fermanagh.—The , rebel association for murder and outrage having been de- feated in Tyrone, has invaded Fermanagh. Came in your thousands to Rosslee, on Tuesday, to protest against repeal, Home Rule, universal suffrage, and the disruption of the British Empire by the defenders of the dynamite and dagger conspiracy. God save the Queen." THE MURDER OF LORD MOI7NTMORRES.—A &Away cor- respondent is informed that one of the principal actors in the murder of Lord Mountmorres has turned informer. An ' investigation has been opened at Galway police station, the court being composed of County-inspector Murphy, Mr. Brady, magistrate, and the district inspector. The informer is a tinker who was present at the murder, saw the shots fired at his lordship, and saw a little boy sitting on the side of a car. He knows the parties, but some have left the , country. He gave the Pules Of those concerned? but the authorities will nat disclose thee'. AN EXTRAORDINARY SI'EECH was delivered by Mr. Healey, M.P., at a National League meeting held at Dun- drum, county Dublin, on Sunday. He said that if the me- tropolitan county had elected as their parliamentary repre- sentative a less impudent, lying, offensive, and insincere man than Colonel King-Harman, who was the bully and corner boy of the Tory Party, the National party would probably not have awakened to their duties. lie urged the meeting to carefully register, so that when the occasion arose they would be able to put out Colonel King-Harman and Mr. lon Trent Hamilton, and place men of the character of Par-. nell and Sexton in their stead. THB PA.RNBLL TRIBUTE.—The treasurers of the Parnell National Tribute have received a letter from Denis O'Connor, Chicago, enclosing a draft for £1 632. The total amount of the Parnell tribute is now £26,980. It is in- tended to close the fund this year. An analysis of the tribute shows that the four Irish provinces have subscribed as follows :—Leinster, £10,398 ; Munster, £9378; Ulster, £2,251; and Connaught, £1,058. Atnerica has contributed £2,379; England, £773; and Scotland, £179. Subscrip- tions from Australia and India amount to £615. The American subscriptions, will be increased, it is expected, before the fund closes on December 1. At the banquet given to Mr. Parnell on the 10th of that month, an address and a cheque will be prssented to the Irish leader. SIR S. NORTHCOTE IN IRELAND.—Sir Stafford Northcote was present on Saturday at a large meeting in the Botanic Gardens at Belfast, which was presided over by the Doke of Abercorn. The tight hon gentleman discuseed the question of the position which Uister holds and which Ulster ought to hold in the councils of the empire. A .;.:(,Iction was passed declaring unswerving attachment to the Crown and the Constitution of the United Kingdom, and a &termina- tion to resist eyery attempt: to weaken the union between Great Britain and Ireland. After the meetiog the Orange- men in procession were met by a Catholic mob, and a lain I to hand fight took place. Stones and sticks were freely used, and several persons, in- cluding policemen, received serious injuries. On Monday, Sir S. Northcote was presented with an address

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ALTRINCHAM.

SINGULAR CASE OF TRESPASS AT ALTRINCIIVI. A curious case ot trespass was heard by the county court judge at Altrincham, on Wednesday, in whic:i the Lhurch- wardens of St. John the Divine, Brooklands, were sued by Mr. Richards, solicitor, of Manchester, for ,ZlO damages for trespass. It was alleged the defendants had without reasonable cause taken possession of his pew, and let it to another person. On behalf of the defendants, it was con- tended that they had acted within their right, the rent of the pew being in arrear two consecutive half-years. The judge held there was nothing to go to the jury, and non- suited plaintiff with costs.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

CAPTURE OF A GANG OF POACHERS.-011 Monday morn- ing, Sergeant Johnson, stationed at Frodsham, assisted by five men of the Cheshire Constabulary, was successful in giving meeting to seven poachers near Frodsham, and identifying them. A. very extensive and complete s,it of netting, lines, pegs, &c., used for taking game, were found upon the men and taken charge of by the police. The men will be summoned for the next Eddisbury Petty Sessions. LOCAL LAW CASE: ACTION FOR ILLEGAL DISTRAINT.— At the Liverpool County Court, on Thursday, an action was brought by Mr. William Armstrong, of Runcorn, against Mr. William Statham, builder, Runcorn, for illegal distraint. —On the case being called, 'it was stated by pliintiff's counsel, Mr. Segar (ins!ructed by Mr. W. IL Linaker, of Runcorn), that the defendant bad agreed to pay the plaintiff £2O on the action being withdrawn.—Mr. Walton, counsel for defendant (instructed by Messrs. R. Davies and Co,, of Warrington), confirmed Mr Segar's s'atement, alai expressed regret thr. the d;stress-warrant bad been executed. 11A.11VEST THANKSGIVING SERVICE AT THE PARISH Cuuncn.—A harvest thanksgiving service was held in the Frodsham Parish Church, on Thursday evening, when every available seat was occupied: Rods large number of persoLs stood in the aiAip. rrne service commenced" with the

Cjrfly thaaiitui people cane. Raise the song of harvest honlo, and this was given by the choir as a processional hymti in which the congregation heartily joined. The prayer were read by the Vicar (Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A ), and the lessons by Rev. A, Grier and Roy. A. P. It Imolds. Dr Stainer's harvest anthem, "Ye shall dwell in the Land,' was carefully rendered by the choir, and was tastefully ac- companied on the organ by Mr. Tho:nas Riley, the organist. The preacher on the occasi.n was the Rev. Canon Greenall, Rector of Grappenhall, Nv ho took for his text part of the third verse of the 9th chapter of Isaiah, "They joy before thee according to the joy in harvest." In the decoration of the church a very considerable amount of labour had been bestowed, and reflected the highest credit um& the skilful and busy hands that had carried out the ornate designs of tastefully arranged corn, fruit, and flovrs which met the eye on every side, and also gave evidence of the abundant supply of materials which had been freely given by the gentry and farmers in the neighbourhood. The work had been carried out by the following ladies and gentlemen of the congregation, viz :--Mesdames A. Thomas, C. E. Linaker, J. Ashton, R. Holland, A. Reynolds, Bolder- stone, Dunsford, H. Reynolds, J. Rigby, Misses Cros6eld, Thomas, Linaker, Hazlehurst, Hutchens, Head, Edwards, Astons, Holland, Clarke Davies, Revs. A. P. Reynolds, A. Grier, and Messrs. R. Holland, A. Thomas, T. Ashton, and others. A collection was made at the close of the service in aid of the funds of the Chester Infirmary, and amounted to upwards of £l4.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GOLDORNE WESLEYAN CHAPEL ANNIVERSARY SERVICES. —The annual sermons in aid of the Trust funds were Preached in the Golborne Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, on Sunday morning and evening Jan by the Rev. J. M. Fair- bourne, of E trlestown. In the afternoon of the same day Mr. Fairbourne also gave an instructive address to the teachers, scholars, and friends. At each of the services there was a good attendance, and the collections realised about £4. TEA MEETING AT GOLBORNE.—A social tea party in aid of the school funds, was held in the Congregational school, High-street, Golborne, on Monday evening. A goodly number of persons sat down to an excellent tea, which was much enjoyed, and at the subsequent proceedings the chair was occupied by Mr. R. Yates.—ln his opening address, the Chairman explained that the object of the gathering was to raise funds towards the liquidation of the debt of £9O at present resting upon the school. The debt troubled the minds of the committee, and they had decided to make an effort to liquidate it. He presumed they would raise about £lO by that tea party, inasmuch as the receipts were clear profit; the provisions having been kindly given by members of the cmgregation and friends. They hoped by Christmas to entirely clear off the debt, and then start the new year with a clear book. (Applause.) An excellent programme of songs, recitations, and dialogues was after- wards gone through; Mr. Johnson presiding with his accus- tomed ability at the pianoforte. THE VIOLENT ASSAULT ON THE GOLBORNE POLICE.— At the Occasional Court-house, Warrington, on Monday, before Mr. J. Mama, James Charles, of Golborne, was charged with having inflicted grievous bodily harm upon P.C. Ratcliffe whilst acting in the execution of his duty, and also with assaulting and resisting the same constable, together with P.C. Whiting. From the evidence given it appeared that the two officers had a warrant for the appre- hension of the prisoner, and they went to a house in James- street, Golborne, where they had ascertained the prisoner was staving. Tney heard the voice of the prisoner inside to the effect that no two policemen could take him in cus- tody, and having some knowledge of his previous character they returned and then entered the house in the company of a priest. Prisoner was advised to go with the officers quietly, but he declined, and pulling off his belt he "slashed" at the head of P.C. Ratcliffe, and caused rather serious injuries around his left eye and ear. Eventually he was taken to the police-station.—He was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. HALE.

CAUGHT UP A TREE AT HALE.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, George Peacock pleaded guilty to stealing a, quantity of apples worth 5s 63, the property of Levi Hitch- mough, of Halewood Farm.—P.C. Worthington said on Tuesday night, about a quarter to ten, he saw the prisoner with a bag over his shoulders. He followed him, and soon afterwards he heard shaking a tree in Mr. Hitchmough's orchard. Witness got through the hedge, and found the prisoner up the tree. He asked him what he was doing there. The prisoner replied that he was going to sleep there that night. The apples p7oducec4 were picked up from the foot of the tree.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

• HUTTON CHURCH —At the Consistory Court, held in St. Nicholas Parish Church, Liverpool, on Tuesday last, the vicar of Huyton (the Rev. CAnon Penrhyn) and his war- dens made application to the court for a faculty to put a stained-glass window in south wall of the aisle of the church, representing the rising of Lazarus. The cost, which wa's estimated at about £lOO, is to be defrayed by Mr. Ihler. The application was granted. THE HUTTON COMPANY OF THE 2ND LANCASHIRE ENGINEER VOLUNTEERS.—The abovo company moved into their new headquarters, Whitfield House, on Thursday evening, the 4th inst. They paraded in full dress, without arms, in charge of Lieutenant Higgins. Ninety men mus- tered to the roll, and were inspected hy the adjutant. The premises have been acquired from Lord Derby, on most generous terms. The house standing in its own grounds, besides containing large rooms and abundant accommoda- tion, has-in addition a large room over the stables and out- building capable of accommodating a large body of men at indoor drill, or for lecture purposes. It is intended to fur- nish the house with two billiard and bagatelle tables, and also to fit up a canteen, &c.. to provide all the advantages for the recreation and amusement of the large body of men ad officers, now numbering 160. There have joined re- cently about 30 recruits from the neighbourhood of Knbtty Ash and the Old Swan, so that the new headquarters will be centrally situated in t e large district from which the mem- bers are drawn, comprising Huvton, Eiuyton-Quarry, Tar- bock, Roby, and Broidgreen ; in addition to those already I mentioned.

:SAD ACCIDENT.-At the Neadon Bank works, a workman, nano a S. asttes, who bad been long with Mr. Falk, and was valued by the firm, was unfortunately killed white tboti-fieg a shaft last Friday. It seems the piece of tia;tae sliip.,l Item its holding when being let down int, the shaft in whieb Astles was waiting to receive and fix it. it fell on his bead and killed him instantaneously. Ho has 1, ft a large family to mourn his loss. At the inquest a verdict was returned of "Accidental death." He was buried on Sunday amid much show of sympathy. HARVEST THANKSGIVING.—The first harvest thanksgiving at the United Free Methodist Chapel, High-street, Wins. ford, WAS held on Sunday and Monday last. During the preceding week the ladies of the congregation, aided by as many gentlemen as had tendencies that way, decorated the chapel most tastefully with corn, fruits, flowers, ferns, &c., which had been assiduously collected and as generously , given by kind donors. Foremost amongst the latter may be named Lord Lelamere through Mr. Milne, Thomas Knowles, Esq , M.P., through Mr. Errington, Mr. Robert Verdin, Mr. Joseph Slater, Mr. Norburv, &a The sermons on Sunday were preached by the Rev. N. Fysh, of Northwieh, and were very appropriate and telling. It was markedly so at the evening service, when the chapel was crowded. There w, a large gathering at the children's service in the afternoon. c ;nducted by Mr. Jabez Hulse, Mr. Hough, and Rev. W. Fish; and a most a,,preciative congregation on Monday evening at the public meeting, when Mr. John Buckley, F.R CI.S., took the chair, and was supported by the Revs. E. Murphy (Wesleyan), F. Fysh (Northwich), James Wright (Sandhach). ME,ssrs. Joseph Slater, and R. Hatton, all of whom spoke in praise of the movement and of various aspects ef the generous impulses called forth by a good harvest. After the meeting had passed votes of thanks to the decorators, choir and organist, speakers and donors of fruit, &c., the service closed with hymn and benedicllon, and the sale of fruit commenced. The proceeds of collec- tions and sale came to the nice stern of 73 lOi, whith will be devoted to circuit anti biller Purposes.
