At Chester Castle, on Saturday, Charles -14addocks and Edward Wainwright, two Chester butchers, were committed for trial on a charge of sheepstealing on an extensive scale.

SUDDEN DEATH AT Sr. HELENS.-,—A man named Peter Crogan, a pensioner 46 years of age, died very suddenly at St. Helens, on Wednesday evening. Shortly after six o'clock he went into the Eagle Vaults, Liverpool-street, and there had a glass of whiskey, after drinking which he went into the back yard, and was later on in the evening found lying there by a person named Julia Tickle. Dr. McNicoll's assistantwas sent for, and declared Crogan to be dead. Heart disease is supposed to have been the cause of death.

THE CHESHIRE BRINE SUPPLY.—A Chester correspondent states that there was such an enormous demand for Che- shire salt during last month that the brine springs of the Winsford district failed, and hundreds of furnaces had to be stopped. The failure continues, and will probably last for some time to come. Prices have consequently risen, and a material advance is probable under the limited conditions of the supply. The total amount of white and rock salt shipped for September was 108 591 tons, against 91,568 for the corresponding month of last year. The United States took no fewer than 24,932 tons against 14,517, and India 32,958 tons against 23,726 for the corresponding month of last year.

MAN UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.—At Chester Police Court, on Thursday, Edward Fletcher, of 26, Denmark-street, Altrincham, cattle dealer, WAS charged with assaulting Urias Sindbach, at the horse fair on the previous day.— Prosecutor said he was standing in the fair in charge of a colt, when defendant came along and was running against the animal when he (witness) warned him not to get too near it. Defendant then struck the colt, and also struck witness a violent blow over the head with a stick. Prisoner followed this up by again striking the colt, and bitting witness on the back with the stick. Corrobora- tive evidence having been given, the Bench sentenced the prisoner to two months' imprisonment with bard labour. —Prisoner begged hard to be fined inst,ad of bein; sent to hard labour, but the Bench refused to listen to his appeal, and be was removed to ptison. .

INNOVATIONS AT A FUNERAL —The funeral of tbe late Mr. A. R. Haughey, M.D., who was killed in a street acci- dent at Crewe last week, took place on Tuesday, and was the occasion of a very large demonstration. From the de- cased's residence to Coppenhall parish church—distance more than a mile—the streets were lined with people, and all the shops were shut. The procession was half a mile in length, and was preceded through the streets by a surpliced choir, singing, and an acolyte bearing a huge cross on high. The usual hearse was dispensed with, the coffin being borne on a waggonette covered with a in agnincent pall-cloth. 01 arrival at the church the coffin was placA in the chancel, at its head being three candles, lighted, the centre one biisig about four feet long. On the altar were eight candles, two of which were lighted. There was a singular departure from the usual service by the celebration of communion, there being about 100 communicants. The service was carried ou by the Rev. W. C. iteid (rector), Canon Black- burne, and other clergy.

FODT AND MOUTH—bISEASE Cheshire, unhappily, after a considerable decrease in the statistics of the disease, Lieut.-Colonel Hamersley riveals, in his state- ment issued the other day, a somewhat alarming increase, which, coming as it does immediately upon the oprning of cub-hunting four days a week, will inevitably direct farmers' attention further to fox-hunting as a means by which the disease inpread. Last week there were only 303 animals remaining under treatment; since then 244 fresh animals have been attacked. 2 died, 170 recovered, and 375 remain under treatment, being an increase of 72 affected animals. The disease has appeared upon 17 farms in the townships of Tattenhall, Cholmlndelev, Stretton' Little Budworth, Wor- lestog, Acton, Brindley, Poole, Ledsham, Great Mollington, Bollington, Dunlan-&-the-Hill, Alton, and Caton. Swine fever has broken out at Hartford, Anderton, and Altrincham, three animals being attacked. One place is infected with ' sheep-sclb, and four animals remain under' treatment at Allastock The county is again, happily, free from pleuro- pneumonia,
ANOTHER GREAT WALKING FEAT
BY 808 CARLISLE.

Bob Carlisle, now known as the champion long distance walker, has announced his intention of attempting even a more extraordinary performance than that which he brought to such a satisfactory conclusion a few weeks ago. It may be briefly observed that among his previous feats have been his famous walk from the Land's End (Cornwall) to John O'Groat's (Scotland) and back again with a wheel- barrow, and his walk of 2,020 miles within 1.000 hours but the new undertaking will prove even a more difficult task than either of these two. A week or two ago it was reported over the country that E. P. Weston, a noted pedestrian, was about to commence a walk of 50 miles daily for 100 consecutive days, in addition to which he would deliver a lecture on '"Pea versus Beer' each evening. Bob Carlisle publicly asked if he couli ' accompany Weston on his " tour" ass means of testing the relative abilities of the two men. Westqr., however, evidently anxious about his own honour, did not notice the I challenge; or at any rate did not venture to reply to it. De- termined not to be thus cast aside, Carlisle announces that he will, of his own accord, make an s,tteinpt to accomplish the feat. He will commence at 0.15 a.m. on Monday next, starting from Mr. Melling's, New Market Inn, and his first journey will be to the Bridgewater Hotel, Leigh. His sub- sentient route will be between Leigh, Chowbent, Tyldeslev and Astley, repeating the journey each day until the 60 miles are completed. There will be no walk- ing on the .Sunday, and during the 17 weeks which the 100 week-nays will occupy, Carlisle intends to walk in a separate district each week: bo only y thatw will he means ns walkm a ksion gm ai tourmiles da itlbvr,o tblguht oeuat chLaenveaensihn ;guile Nwriiitl give a public address. The walk is not being undertaken for any bet or wager, and Carlisle states that he will not walk as a teetotaller, but fres to partake of stimulants. He adds that he will again finish his walk at Earlestown ; and if he is successful—as many Earlestown friends hay.) heartily wished him to be—there is not the least dou'a that the enthusiasm and excitement manifested at the conclusion i of his last performance will be repeated.

Ashton and Woods) for the defendent.—Mr. Davies Meted that on the 23h February, 1880, the plaintiff let the room to the defend tnt, the terms being that the room should be let to the defendant for 103. per week, the rent to be paid quarterly. From the 25th February, 1880, to the 27th March this year the rent had been paid regularly, at the rate of £6 103. per quarter. Acrzon, BY A WALTON STRAW DEALER, 7- In this Case Richard Wi:kinsos, hay and straw dealer. Leigh-villas, Lower Walton, sought to rectiver frorci the London and North-Western Railway Co. £4 7s. 4d.; the value of straw lost in transit from Warrington to Liverpool-road, :Alan- chester:l-The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Percy Davies, and the railway company by Mr. Preston, from'the solicitors' department, Liverpool.—Mr. Davies said the plaintiff was a hay and straw dealer,, and had for the last 15 years had many transaction with the railway company, by whom he was very well known, having paid them hundreds of pounds for carriage of hay and straw. A few yearsago he had to send to Manchester from Warrington some straw which he had bought from farmers, and at that time, as there was seme straw stolen, he gave information to the cmpany's servants, and in consequence a man was ant for a long term of imprisonment. He wished to bring this forward to show that this was a case where there must have been wholesale pilfering of straw, and that the defendant company must be made liable for this loss. The straw was taken to Manchester oilstrucks belonging-ix; the company between the 14th and 23d May this year. On • the 14th May, Mr. Wilkinson, the plaintiff, sold to Drhiseree Cozens, army contractors, Manchester, a certtin q.nanTrty of straw, and he himself, being a hard-working man, went and etw this straw de ivered at Bank Quay by A carter named Lunt. Os that day, and other days up to the 23rd May, straw weighing 17 tons 12 cwt. was &livered. The first consignment never reached its destination until the 23rd May, although it ought to have gone on the 14th of that menth. The plaintiff made enquiries as to the cause of the delay, the result of which was Mar, it being excursion time, all the servants of the company had received instructions that all straw, hay, and things of that sort, should be placed on the sidings. When the straw reached Manchester it only weighed 16 tons 0 cwt. 1 qr., which was 1 ton 11 cwt. 3 qrs. short; and he (Mr. Davies) submitted that for such gross negligence on the part of the company the plaintiff should not have to suffer.—Evidence was oiled to support of the action, but after the case had procseded for some time, his Honour amended the claim by adeing the nuns of Mr. Cozens as plaintiff, and adjourned the further hearing until the 25th inst.

div.head: IRISH fftSToRY. LECTURE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: IRISH fftSToRY. LECTURE AT EARLESTOWN.

The Rev. W. R. Byrne delivered a lecture in St. Mary's Catholic Hall, Newton-le-Willows, on Mondty evening, on "The early history of Ireland, as told. in her ballads." Theia was a very good attendance. The Rev. Father LENNON, who presided, in introducing the lecturer, said that the subject was an interesting one to all lovers of history, and especially to those of their parish who had a right to be interested in the history of Ireland. He thought there could be no subiect after religion that could interest so much the bulk of his parish as that, the opening subject of the winter night lectures. (Applause.) The Rev. Father &rime then delivered his lecture, which throughout bristled with wit and hunriur, and with im- personations of Pat, that kept the audience convulsed with laughter. During the course of his lecture be said that in looking through ancient history they would always find that wherever there was real hot blood in the veins ot men there they would not find the historians of the people who wrote down hard facts, but rather those who wrote down songs. Among several illustrations of this he mentioned Ancient Greece, of whose history we should know very little were it not for its Homer. So it was with Ireland. Thera they had their birds who wrote all the aspirations of the heart, all that the imagination bodied forth; the 'wee, sympathies, joys, and, in a word, everything that made up the pulse of the nation's heart. They found the bard in pride of place from the very com- mencement, in the very twilight, of his'.ory. They found him near the thrones of the many kings that held sway in the land, and they found him in the offices of the great ones. They could not go anywhere without fiading the son of song with the harp in his hand. The history of Ire- land is perhaps better known than the history cf most coun- tries. In referring to the invasions which Ireland suffered prior to the Christian era, each of which hid left its trace behind it, he dwelt more particularly on that by the Phoenicians, which took place about 3,000 B.C. He quoted verses marking the event, and said that the history of these invaders was simply the history of Ireland from that day to this. From what the bards had left they found that all the great traits of the Irish were inherited from these invaders. In those early times men were known and distinguished in cempanv by the number of colours they were allowed to wear. A serf, a man who was under a master, and whose body and limbs were at the command of his master, was allowed to wear a dress of one colour oQly. A freeman could wear two colours; and men of higher grade, officers who were in attendance mann royalty, could wear three colours; while the king could wear five colours only. The bard was allowed to wear four colours, and was considered next in dignity and place to the king of the land. The bards were divided into three sections. 'The duty of one section was to tell in verse the history of their wars; that of another was to commit to verse all the laws of the nation and make the people familiar with them by singing them; and the duty of the third section was to narrate to the people their genealogy, and they might be called the domestic bards. That trait of indefiniteness bound in the

Trish character was traceable to the bards, who put into rhyme everything, so that the people never troubled them- selves with dates or anything of that Bert. The lecturer went on to descriee the great power which the bards exer- cised, and of which they themselves were fully conscious. At the head of the army went the bards, and as soon as they struck their harps the soldiers were fired with enthusiasm and they rushed on either to death or victory. Or say that the spirit of anelancholy was upon a man, and David en- tered the apartment with his harp, whith under his skilful fingers was made to dart forth hope, and Saul was himself again, great and kingly. Then, attain, the harp was found In the festal hall. There was a bridal procession; the praise of the bride and bridegroom were sung by the bard, and another would take his place and tell the genealogy of the pair, urging them to imitate the virtues of their predecessors. The lecturer mentioned among other great traits in the Irish character, that of enthusiasm in battle, and also that of great reverence for the dead. Passing on, he sald that from time immemorial the land had been split up into fac- tions. Even to our own day that went on, as was witnessed in Belfast the other day. Unfortunately these sins die- graced the history of Ireland in every chapter, and almost in every page. But‘often they did not find specimens of true heroism. Another trait in the Irish character was the tenderness of passion that an Irishman had for his native country and the marvellous passion for the woman with whom he had plighted his troth at the altar; and thiklecterer here read "The lament of the Irish emigrant," and in closing.' his lecture sang " Tbe.belis of Shandon," 'which elicited Rmev".hF:Pt6elariZENNON moved a vote of thanks to the The lecturer. mr.EosTisn seconded the motion, which was carried, and the meeting then separated. • id I

THE Ammar ASSIZES.—The following dates have been fixed for kidding the ensuing autumn assizes on the Nor- thern circuit, before Justices Denman and Field :—Carlisle, Wednesday, October 24; Manchester, Monday, October ; and Liverpool, Monday, November 12. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—There is a continued want want of animation in the Manchester iron market, and the general expectation that trade will be quiet during the winter operates against any large bnying for for- ward requirements. Where business has to be sought orders of any i Portance can only be secured by some concession upon pre nt prices, and there is an easier tone in the mar- ket. On Tinsley, buyers of pig iron who had orders of any weight to 11103 were holding back for lower prices, and in some cases sellers were open to entertain offers. Local makers of pig iron, although they are firm at their full list for forge qualities, would give way a little to secure orders for foundry iron, whilst on the other hand in district brands some of the Lincolnshire makers are conceding about 6d., and sales have been made at is per ton under the full quoted rates for forge qualities. Delivered equal to Manchester prices average about 45s 3d, less 2, for forge and foundry Lancashire; 44s 4d for forge and scrap to 45s 10d for foundry Lincolnshire, less 2; and 47e Cd net cash for good foundry brands of Middlesborough. Forge proprietors in this district are kept fully employed on present orders, and although some of the merchants are underselling makers' prices for delivery into the Manchester district, prices are firm at £6 2s 6d to 5s for bars, VI 12s Od to £6 15s for hoops, and £8 to £8 5s for sheets:— Business generally in the coal trade of this district is quiet, and althmigh the present output of the pits is being dis- posed of without much difficulty there is no pressure for. Supplies. The exceptional mildness of the weather naturally tends to restrict the inquiry for house fire coals, and there is no great activity in the demand for thejswer qualities of round coals for iron making and general trade requirements. Slack is in some cases reported to be moving off rather more . freely than it has been of late, the chemical trade showing signs of improvement, which tends to increase the demand for this class 'of fuel; but at present supplies continue plentiful in the market, with common sorts of slack very low in price. For round coals prices generally are steady, but the full list rates are not in all cases firmly adhered to. At the pit mouth best coal averages 9s 6d to lOs ; seconds, 7s 6d to 8s; com- mon round coal for steam and ironmaking purposes, 5s 9d to 64 3d; burgy, 4s 6cl to ss; good slack, 3s 61 to 4s; and common qualities of slack about 3s per ton. For shipment there has been a tolerably good demand daring the week, and for Lancashire steam coal, delivered at the high level, Liverpool, or the Garston Docks, sellers have been able to realise about 8s per ton.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1883.,

PROMINENCE ought, we think, to ‘be to some of the fruits of Sir S. NoßTHcariS visit to Ireland. The Tory press has been careful to comment in laudatory terms on the political advantages likely to accrue from Sir STAFFORD'S campaign; but on the disorderly and violent behaviour of the Orange mobS attending the various gatherings he -haS addressed it has been discreetly silent. Let it not, however, be supposed that there ha., been nothing but peace and harmony attend' ing the visit; on the contrary, it has been accompanied by rioting and bloodshed, if 110 t by murder. The leader of the Tory Opposi- tion and his friends have been eminently successful in arousing the dormant religious antipathies of the people not only of Belfast, but of the population throughout the whole of the North of Ireland; and as is always the case when religious bigotry is obtruded into a discussion—and more especially into an Irish discussion—serious consequences have. been the result. For instance, on Friday Sir STAFFORD visited Carrickfergus, and in the evening a torch-light procession, headed by an Orange band, took place. In the course of their noisy peregrinations the processionistS made their way to Ballynaleigh, where, with- out any provocation, they partially wrecked a convent. One of the nuns, Madame IS CHANTAL, was lying ill in bed at the time, and she died the following morning, her death being accelerated by the attack on the building. After maliciously giving vent to their passion on the convent, the proceS- sionists returned to Belfast, and the offices of two newspapers were attacked, without an)/ show of reason, and considerable damage done. Other buildings suffered more or less from the violence of the fanatical crowd: Saturday was a great day for disturbances. An Orange demonstration on a large scale took place at the Botanical Gardens, Belfast, at which, we regret to say, speeches of an inflammatory character were delivered by the Duke of ABERCORN and the Marquis of WATERFORD. The leader of the Opposition, it should be stated, was more temperate in his remarks. On leaving the Gardens, the Orangemen, who 'were naturally much excited, processioned the streets, and it is said they were met by a Roman Catholic mob. A fierce conflict ensued. A strong force of police, mounted and on foot, endeavoured to avert a collision, but they were ordered by the leaders of the Orangemen to stand aside as the procession ists "were prepared to clear the street." A hand-to-hand fight followed, stones were freely used on both sides, and some terrible scalp wounds were inflicted with heavy sticks. The processionists, it is reported, did "murderous execution" with the halberts which they carried, and a number of the combatants had to be removed in an insen- sible state to their homes. But slight hopes are entertained for the recovery of one of the injured men. Three policemen had to be carried away from the scene of the melee, which was altogether of the most violent character. Perhaps the most genuine testi- mony, as it is the most unvarnished, that can be adduced of the evil consequences of Sir STAFFORD'S visit is contained in the follow' ing letter received by a London firm towards the close of last week, and published in the Daily News :—" Sir,—We have finish our work and all is satisfactory. Sir, itis very rough here now Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, M.P., has come. There was fighting and stoning going on as we were leaving work, and Ive had to be very sharp not to geta crack. I hey .ask them that they come acrost who they are for, and if you are not for the same side as them you get knocked about, and I hear that - Saturday will be a very bad day to be here, so I hope we shall be away before then. We are not safe here just now, and me and Bill are frightened to stop any longer." The Tory Press, we have said, has been discreetly silent with reference to these riots. We venture to think, however, that if Sir CHARLES DILKE, or any memiltr of the present Government, had visited Ireland and . similar disturbances had arisen' their con- duct would have been denounced in the verY strongest language. They would have been charged with encouraging, if not actuallY urging, the people to rebellion; it would, have been said that it was the intention 01 Sir CHARLES and other Radical members of the Cabinet to secure for Ireland by means of such a rebellion legislative independence ; it is not improbable they would have been, charged with treason, only thinly veiled; ano as a matter of course there would have been

loud demands for their meetings to be stir pressed. Nothing, indeed, would have been too hard for the Tory Press to have said, Yet now when the LEADER of the OPposiTlO is the cause of these riots we hear not a
_ whisper of wrong-doing. We notice that a 1 meeting in connection with the National
League convened to be held at Ennis the
other day was proclaimed by order of the LORD LIEUTENANT, who no doubt had suili-
cient reason for so doing, though there are grounds for believing that such a course was unnecessary, inasmuch as the watherin7 does
nct seem to have created any fervour or

enthusiasm. At the meetings in connection With the National League intemperate language is only what may be expected, and AIL HEALY'S violent utterances on Sunday cannot be too strongly condemned; but the sPeeches of the Duke of ABERCORN and the Marquis of WATERFORD on Saturday, can scarcely be regarded as models Worthy of imitation The Duke of ABERCORN says "it did not suit the Government of Mr. GLADSTONE to leave Ireland alone. It suited him better," the buke proceeded, " for party purposes to set Class against class, and to stamp out the Con- s.ervatives even at the risk of introducing in its place a reign of sedition and outrage." The Marquis of WATERFORD was even more immoderate, for he plainly charged the Go- vernment with being answerable for all the ?nurders which have been recently committed In Ireland. The Duke of ABERCORN has occupied the position of Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, and statements such as these coming from one who has held so exalted a position are not only calculated to inflame the pas- sions of the people and to stir up strife and discord where there is now peace and con- tentment, but we believe they are made with the object of bringing the Government into Contempt. It would be much more to the Purpose if these Conservative statesmen Would tell us how they would have the Go- yernrnent treat Ireland. If the policy which is now being followed does not suit them, , let them say what will. Are they pre- I Pared, if returned to power at the next election, to reverse the policy of the Govern- Merit ? Let them state boldly, as it has been Pointedly put :—" All this Gladstone legisla- tion is injustice and ruinous; give us a Majority and we shall reverse it; we shall re- I establish the minority church, repealing the I acts of 1828 and 1829, and repealing the acts ; of 1870 and 1873 ; restore Ireland to its ' nappy condition of 1828, when only Tory landlords exercised rule, and the people . had no rights beyond a Hamiltonian and fleresfordian will and pleasure." If they I Will do this then we will know what is reallyl Ineant. This they dare not do, for they know full well they would not be listened to; and therefore they content themselves with casting as much abuse as possible at the Government. we have very grave doubts whether any Political benefit will be the outcome of this campaign ; we know already that it has had a most damaging effect upon the tranquility of the north of Ireland, and for this Sir STAF- ?.ORD and his friends must be held respon- sible. It is only to be hoped that the corn- j rnotion which Sir STAFFORD has created may not permeate the whole of the country, and ' sO. give encouragement to the outrage and , crime of which we have already had too much experience.

GOOD TEMPLARY AT WIDNES. The members of the Star of Widnes Longe 1.0.Gr.T. held a public tea meeting in the Public Hall, Hutchinson-street, on Wednesday evening. Subscqumtly a well attended meeting was held, under the presidency 4.f Staff-Captain Dunes, of the Blue Ribbon Army. Addresses were delivered by the chairman, Messrs Morris Jones (of Liverpool), and D. Houghton and J. W. Hall (of Warrington). A programme of songs and recita- tions was gone through by members of the order.

• k.,HURCIT OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCR DEMONSTRATION, WIDNFS.—AbOId five hundred members of the Widnes Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society met at the National Schools, on Saturday afternoon, shortly aCter two o'clock, and after forming into processional order they paraded the principal thoroughfares in the locality. The procwsion was headed by the banner of the society and the Star of Temperance brass band. The Mersey Missinns Sunday school band also occupied a position in the ranks. On returning service was held in the Parish Church, and the Rev. R. Postance, incumbent of St. Burnabas,Livfrpool, preached an appropriate serm.n. In the evening a public entertainaunt was held in the schoolroom, under the preFi- dency of the Vicar. There was a large audience. A capital programme was gone through, the following taking part : Messrs. John Moors, T. Sanders, W. Shaw, Roscoe, Stride, N. Sherratt, Carter Price, F. Hartland, Jessop, J. Furniture, P. Shaw; Miss Jones, Miss Fairley, and Miss A. L. Wilkin- son. The Mersey Missions band played several selections during the evening. The proceedings concluded with the usual votes of thinks.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE RAILWAY AT FARNWORTH.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE RAILWAY AT FARNWORTH.

On Monday afternoon, at the Griffin Inn, Farnworth, Mr. T. W. Barker, the County Coroner, held an inquest en the body of William Jones, who died on Saturday morning from injuries received on the L. & N. W. Railway on Friday evening. Jones, who lived at 6, Derby-road, Farnworth, was a platelayer, and on finishing his work on Friday evening he rode flour Whines to Farnworth Bank on the step of a goods van, which was attached to a train going to St. Helens. He alighted into the six foot at Farnworth Bank. but as there were three other trains following close behind, he had to wait until they had passed in order to cross the line to go towards his house. At this time a passenger train from St. Helens was due, but the deceased was apparently not aware of the: fact, and whilst he was standing there it approached him unseen at a speed of about 30 miles an hour. Owing to his not being in the centre of the six foot, the outside cylinder of the engine struck him and sent him against the waggons of the train that was passing in the opposite direction. He was shortly after- wards picked up, suffering from a wound in the head which was bleeding profusely, four men curled him home, and he was attended by Dr. Booth, but after suffering great pain he died next morning at six o'clock. Richard Ashton, platelayer, Bold, Thomas Robinson, fireman of the goods train, John Hewitt, the driver, William Birchall, the driver, William Eligham, the guard, and Wihhiom Guest, the fireman of the pissenger train, having given evidence bearing out these facts, the jury returned a verdict of " accidental death." The deceased leaves a wife and nine children.
HARVEST FESTIVALS. HALTON PARISH CHURCH.

The'annual harvest festival in connection with the Halton Parish Church took place on Thursday evening. The decorations bad been carried out in the usual-artistic style, and on an extensive scale, and the sacred edifice was bright with flowers, green plants, and cereals. Mr. Yaop, of The Mount, had lent a quantity of stove plants, which included two fine specimens of palms; Mr. Wigg, contributed cut flowers, while the farmers in the neighbourhood gave cereals in abundance. The communion was decorated by Lady Brooke and the Misses Brooke; pulpit, Mrs. Acton and Miss Short; reading desk, Miss Fryer; windows, Miss Leach and Mr. Ackerley ; seats, Mrs. Woodier and Miss Chrimes; font, Mrs. Stokes and Mrs Wright; gas standards, Mr. Holmes. The male members of the congregation generally as-isted. The service was conducted by the Rev. J. Sheepshanks, of St. Margaret's, Aufleld, Liverpool, and the Rev. J. Lock- wood, the vicar. The former gentleman also preached an appropriate sermon. The anthem, 0 give thanks to the Lord" was sung by the choir with good effect. Mr. (lea- cock presided at the organ._ _

div.head: DITTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: DITTON PARISH CHURCH.

On rhcreday evening the annual thanksgiving service for the ingathering of the harvest took place at Ditton Parish Church, which had been charmingly decorated with fruits, flowers, and cereals, which had been furnished by the parish- ioners in great bundance. The following ladies and gentle- men must be credited with the labour of adorning the edifice :—Mrs. Brown, Mrr. Lewis, Mrs. Lucas, Miss Longton, Miss Payne. Messrs. J. Longton, R. Lewis, Dwetryhouse, and Hutchinson. Plants were lent by Miss Turton, Messrs. Roberts, Hallows, Lewis, Warne, and Hutchinson. There was a large congregation at the service, in which the follow- ing clergy took part:—Rev. T. Chambers, Rector of Wile- wood; R. R. P. Stewart, vicar of Hale; and the Rev. W. Wright, curate of Gateaere. The Very Rev., the Dean of Chester, preached an excellent sermon. The service was full choral, the choir singing with taste and harmony the anthem "Oh Lord how manifold are Thy works." The Rev. S. Cassells Brown, the vicar, presided at the harmo- nium.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

A special meeting of the Widnes School Board was held on Thursday afternoon, for the purpose of receiving and signing the annual financial etatement. Mr. T. S. Thnmis presided, and there were also present the Revs. Father Fennelly, Father Clarke, Messrs. Bradshaw and Shaw, and G. H. Denby (clerk). The statement showed that the re- csipts for the past year amount :d to £6,373 19s 10J, includ- e. in a balance in band on the 29th September, 1882, of £l9 16be id. The grants from the Committee of Council on Educaion, including grants from the Science and Art Do- partment amounted to £1,631 is Bd, whilst the rate at 6.72 d in the realised £3,450, but this included tbe sum of £1,150, which the overseers were in arrear on last year's precept. The school fees amounted to £1,234 is 3J. The total ex- penditure amounted to £6,373 19s 10d. This sum included £740 148 9d, being the expenses of administration—viz salaries of officers and legal expenses. The expenses of mainLenance of public elementary schools was: by salaries of teachers £3,128 19s 6(1; books, apparatus, and stationery, £251 10s 10d; fue4l, furniture, repairs to building. dm, £385 787 d ; rents, rates, taxes, and insurance, £l9 171 61 : other expenses of maintenance, £7l 6s 3d; total, £3.857 is 84. The repayment of principal of lo as amounted to £278 18s sd; interest on loans, £1,031 15s 2d. The out- standing liabilties of the Board at the end of the year were—loans from Public Loans Commis- sioners £29,260' other liabilities, including overdrawn £316 2s. 4d.—Mr. R. SHAW said they would notice that the amount paid to teachers was very large, £3,128 19s. 6d., whilst last year the amount was £2,654 is. 3d., making a difference of £474 12s. 3d. This arose from the difference in the scale of payment adopted. The teachers had already received their proportion of the grants: it was included in their salaries, so the larger proportion of the grant would go to the credit of the Board. The Finance Committee hoped that the Board would be gainers rather than losers by this arrange- mmt.—The CH&IRMAN observed that the expenses of the year by that arrangement were made to appear larger than they really were, but next year would put it right —Mr SHAw said the expenses appeared nearly £5OO worse than than they were. The Board had now received all that was due to them from the overseers—(hear, hear)— who were now perseetiv square with the Board.— The CHAIRMAN: That is very satisfactory. He felt sure that the overseers would now pay up regularly, and the Board could with safety issue precepts just to meet their requirements. The Board would receive a large sum from the grant which would put them right. The treasurer had not suffered from any overdrafts, and the account had worked satisfactorily for both the treasurer and the Board. He moved that the chairman sign the statement.—Father CLARKE seconded the motion. He thought the item received for beoke—X9 3s 61—was very small, and an im- provement ought to be effected.—Father FENNELLY wished the Board would give some directions on the matter.—The CHAIRMAN thought the best thing would be to call ti. attention of the head teachers to the subject.—Father FEN NELLY said the committee had done that repeatedly. Th, answer was that books were not used for home metica W3B passed, and the Saard rose.

Mr. Warden's career will probably lead to the clearing up of the law on a point where at present it is in a state of haze. The general principle as to the liability of a gratuit- ous bfilee is very well known, bat the law in its anxiety to do justice and to prevent fraud, has always been very ac- commodating in its view of how slight an obligation may convert a gratuitous into a paid bailee. Of course every- one will iee the justice of the proposition that if the Bank I kept the securities merely for the convenience of the customer it could only be liable for gross neglikence. Otherwise it would have all risk and no gain. But it will be put forward as an argument in favour of the owners that the bank undertook a duty and was to cal.h the coupons as they became due, and that it was for this purpose and not merely for safe custody that they were entrusted to its officers. The point is fine, and the legal argument will be very interesting. The matter will cer- tainly be taken to the courts. There is too much money at stake not to have the question fought out. Mr. Warden will have the satisfaction of knowing that he has helped to build up the common law of England. It is one of the distinctions that fall to the lot of eminent criminals.

One of the vacant garters has been conferred on the Duke of Argyle, which diposes of a rumour that the Marquis of Lorne was to be the recipient. It will scarcely ba said that the son is a stronger man than the father, and obviously his only claim was his royal alliance. It would have been very bad taste to pass over the father in order to decorate the son. The selection, as it is, causes some surprise and considerable disappointment. No distinction is so highly coveted.

Of all the Premier's duties, it is well known there is none that so worries him so much as his church patronage. The eternal fitness of things helps him in his other difficulties. Between rival candidates of equal merit be will naturally prefer the one who has belonged to his own party. But it is supposed there are no politics in the church, and it is known beyond all doubt that there area great many parties. It is well that all shades of legitimate opinion should be represented on the episcopal bench, and EY) the Premier con- scientiously trying to do his duty is very hard put. One appointment has lately lagged a considerable time. Dean Boyd is dead some months, and all sorts of candidates have been announced for the vacant deanery. There seemed almost some mysterious reason why it should not be filled up sooner. The latest candidate to whoin it has been said to be offered is the Dean of Durham. Its acceptance could scarcely be called preferment, as there would be a considerable sacrifice of in- come. But the Dean is raid to dislike Durham, or at least the north, and Exeter has residential attractions enjoyed by few other cities. Dean Lake was a liberal parson when clerical Oxonians of that party were rare, and be is con- nected with the Premier by marriage. Mrs. Lake was a Gladstone, and, more attractive than her attractive husband, is generally known in the diocese as Lake Superior.

They are more ornate but less comfortable than those at Hastings, St. Bernards, and Margate, and I hear, but can scarcely believe, cost £l5O each.

Mr. Tennyson is going to change his publishers, and abandonding Messrs. Kegan Paul to take up with the Mac- Millans. This habit of leasing art copyright and changing the lessee belongs peculiarly, if not exclusively, to the present generation. The Laureate,like all the poets of his time, began with Moxon. All the Lake school went to this most sympathetic and liberal of publishers, while Longman stuck to Tom Moore, and Byron to John Murray. Tenny- son left Moxon and took up with Strahan, but the results were not quite satisfactory. Ido not mean that the terms were not liberal and were not paid, but that the publishers work was not so, very well done. I believe that the editions are stereotyped, and that some arrangement can be nude by which they pass to the new publisher, but the Strahan editions of Tennyson are less pleasant reading than the Moxon octavo volume. The MacMillans are really the pioneers of the charming one volume editions of the poets, now common enough, on toned paper, and in decorative binding. Their Golden Treasury series eff•cted very much the same kind of revolution in the book trade that Scribner achieved for the magazine issuer. It will bo pleasant to see in what new form the most popular poet of the century will be presented to his admirers.

It will be curious to see what sort of a campaign the American Evangelists will conduct this season. The Irish provinces might not seem so favourable for a religious up- heavel as England and the Capital. But no doubt Messrs. Moody and Sankey are well advised. They will be in Lon- don next month, and we shall probably have both them and Btrnum with us simultaneously. The showman of the elephant will be encamped in the west. He has not yet made final arrangements where his exhibition will be opened. Messrs. Moody and Sankey go, of course, to the Agricul- tural Hall. They will find the Salvation Army and the Blue Ribbon squadron practically established since their last visit. I hear they expect a success quite unparalleled, and will be able to utilise the strong religious feeling that is moving a little out of control amongst this great middle class popu- lation of the capital. Messrs. Mo ody and Sankey have never come into opposition, through the ill-judged activity of their converts, with the police or the magistrates. They have neither assaulted nor needed protection. The existence of the Salvation Army must to some extent complicate their programme. Many of the clergy who supported them are opposed to General Booth and his regiment. There will be need for strategy, but Mr.:Vfoody is a good organiser as well as a good speaker.

I think we shall soon see a simplification of omnibus 1 fares, and that a penny will take the place of two pence as the recognisA unit of cost. Thus the new line started in North London, connecting Junetion-road aed Holloway- road, simplifies the trouble of its conductors by having a single charge of a penny for any distancJ. It is scircely fair to see how the London Omnibus Company are quietly taking all the hints which the Road Car Company give them, and, at the same time, are learning by the failures of the latter what they are to avoid. For years the old company stuck to its old pattern of vehicle, to its old scale of fares, and to its nigeiardly estimate of the amount of room which twelve Londoners seated in a row ought to occupy. Either they took a mistaken average of the human race and its bulk, or eke London omnibuses have a special attraction for abnormally corpulent women. Aa a matter of fact, there is rarely room enough for five of them. Then came the road car, with a possibility for women to go on the roof. The privilege was largely availed of by the younger women, and the seats all facing the same way made the new omnibuses look like that of a moving theatre. But the read car was hung on very eccentric wheels, and this part of the experiment was costly and a failure. The L. G. 0. Co. took the hint. They are now builsilng their omnibuses with what dramatic authors would call a practical ladder, and they are adding a few inches for the relief of the "big twelve" who happen to be inside. I hear the proposal of a new line to run from the Royal Oak to Victoria via Notting Hill Gate, Kensington, South Kens- , ington, and Chelsea. Additional omnibus communication between North and South is still much needed.

div.head: WOUNDING OF A WOMAN AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE WOUNDING OF A WOMAN AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., at Widnes Police Court, yesterday morning, Patrick Cannon, a labourer, was brought up on remand charged with having, on the let inst., unlawfully wounded Catherine Kilroy, an old Iriehwoman, living in Barn-street, Widnes.—lnspector Wood said about nine o'clock on the evening of the day named the prisoner went to the woman in Cromwell-street, and after making use of some offensive expressions charged her with being the cause of his wife's incarceration in gaol. At the same time he knocked her to the ground, and kicked her in a most brutal manner. For a week the woman's life was in danger.—Catherine Kilroy was then called, and although she was put through a thorough cross-questioning by the inspector and Mr. Lewin, the magistrates' clerk, she persisted in stating that she could not identify the man who attacked her.—The Inspector: Have you received any money to say this was not the man who did it? No, sir.—lnspector :* Didn't you swear Witness: No, sin—lnspector : Listen to me. Didn't you swear on the 2nd of this month that the prisoner was the man who knocked you down and kicked you ?—The witness, with great volubility, denied having done so, and Inspector Wood said he would proceed no further with the case.— The prisoner, who was represented by Mr. J. W. Knowles, was then discharged. WIDNES BAPTIST CHAPEL.

The Rev. R. Yeatman, who has taken charge of the Bap- tist Denomination in Widnes, preached two sermons in the above chapel on Sunday, when collections were made. The amount realised was £2. On Tuesday evening, a reception tea meeting was held in the same place, and about 70 per- sons were present. The tables were presided over by Miss Frances Pass.y, Mies Welling, Miss Bailey, Miss Ratcliffe, and Miss Harvey. At the public meeting afterwards held Mr. E. Carey presided, and in offering a hearty welcome to the Rev. R. Yeatman, observed that there was a wide sphere for Christian labour in Widnes. He believed Mr. Yeatman was determined to do his utmost for the neighbourhood in which he lived, but it was impossible for him to make any impression if he Worked alone. They would all have to work with him, and he was sure he saw before him the I nucleus of a powerful religious organisation. It was certain that the Baptist community in Widnes had had a cantinuons existence since 1871. They had had two ministers, but for the greater part of that period had been dependent upon Liverpool for supplies. They were now making another effort to have a stationed minister, and to make the church really prosperous, and it would afford him the utmost pleasure to assist in such a consummation.— Then Rev. R. Yeatman then delivered an earnest address, In which be urged thls members to renewed exertions in the chapel and Sunday school. He stated that it was intended to form a temperance association in connection with the chapel, and by and by a band of hope. There would also probably be commenced a tract district; and doubtless many other channels for labouring Cristians would be formed.— Addresses were also delivered by the Rev. R. Pilling, of Hill Cliffe, and Mr. Clarke, of Hough Green.
WIDNES SCHOA BOARD ELECTION.

The triennial election of 11 members of the -Niii—dWe's School Board is fixed to take place on Tuesday, the 23rd October, and yesterday was the last day on which nomina- tions could be received by the returning officer, Mr. S. H. Hartley, of Present. There is a general feeling amongst the ratepayers that a contest upon the present occasion is undesirable, and the representatives of the religious denomi- nations in the town seem to share the same view. Besides the expense which would thus be saved, it is admitted that the manner in which the Education Acts have been adminis- tered by the present Board leaves no room for complaint, and the interest of education in the town would be enhanced by the retiring members' re-election. At present the Board consists of four gentlemen who represent the Church of England section of the ratepayers, four representing the Roman Catholics, and three the Nonconformists, and these religious denominations are willing to accept the same ' share of representation in the future to avoid a contest. The Roman Catholics have, however, nominated, in addition to the four retiring members, the Revs. T. Finegan and J. ' Clarke, and Messrs. Bradshaw and Dr. O'Keeffe. Mr. J. E. Johnson, who will retire, if by so doing, a contest can be avoided. In the event of a struggle, there is no doubt the Roman Catholics are numerically strong enough to elect all their candidates, Toe Church of England section is desirious of re-electing their four retiring repre- sentatives, viz., Messrs. T. S. Timmis (chairman of the Board), J. Brock, J.P., H. Brunner, and H. Wade, Deacon. Mr. Brock and Mr. Brunner intimated a wish not to serve again, but the former gentleman, after an interview with a deputation consisting of Mr. J. B. Imisen and Mr. Crawford consented to allow his nomination. Mr. Brunner persisted in his first determination, but we understand that further efforts will be made to win his consent. The Nonconfor- mists have nominated Messrs. R. Shaw, R. H. Davies, and Peter Glover. The latter gentleman takes the place of Mr. W. Hartland, who, owing to old age, expressed a desire not to be nominated. It is stated that Mr. W. 'l'. Husband and Mr. J. W. Wareing have been nominated as independent , candidate., and in that case unless withdrawals take place, a contest is inevitable. A meeting of ratepayers for the pur- pose of arranging a settlement will be held in the Drill Hall this afternoon.

div.head: LECTURE BY MR. J. MORRISON
div.p: LECTURE BY MR. J. MORRISON
AT WIDNES.

The members of St. Bede's Young Men's Society, Apple- ton, held their first public entertainment and meeting of the season on Monday evening, when a crowded audience as- se.nbled in the schoolroom. The Rev. T. Finnegan pre- sided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Morrison (the president), A. Cawley, Hunt, Hurst, F. Heyes, It. Bradshaw, Leatherbarrow, Ire. Mr. J. Morrison was announced to de- liver a lecture, entitled "A little sketch of English and Irish poetry." In introducing the lecturer, the Chairman said his duty was both an easy and a pleasant one. Pleasant because he knew that Mr. Morrison was highly appreciated by everyone in that room, and well known for his many acts of kindness and generosity, not only to the Catholics of Appleton and Widnes, but to everyone residing in Widnes. (Applause.) The Lam:tuna, who was cordially received, said he pur- posed confining his remarks chiefly to ballad poetry, because he thought that this class of writing was best understood by most of them. In ballad poetry the inner life of a peo- ple was described; it was the reflection of their wants and aspirations, and the truest history of their feelings. The poets had most nndoubtedly assisted powerfully in bringing the wrongs 'of a people promi - neatly before the public. It was an admitted fact that Moore's poetry assisted materially in achieving Catlio- lie emancipation, an Act which English Catholics should *ever forget was for the relief of the Catholics in this country, as well as for their co-religionists across the channel. If they took the works of any of the great poets such as Moore, of Ireland, and Tennyson, of England, they found the beauties of neture, scenes in domestic life, and the history of their day depicted in the most soul-stirring language. The lecturer then read extracts from the Eng- lish poets—Teanyson, Arthur Matthieson, G. R. Sims, and Tom Hood. There were, he continued, few people more attached to poetry than the Irish. They were swayed by its influence as the tide by the moon. And why? Because it told them of the many great sacrifices made by their fore- fathers, and of their undying love and attachment to their faith and country. In the ballad poetry of Ireland was recorded the principal events in her history, and all who had taken the trouble to study Irish history:must know that centuries of oppression instead of crushing out the national spirit and faith of the people, had kindled in it higher resolves, and he trusted that he should not be considered as trespassing on the domain of politics, which is prohibited by the rule of the Young Men's Society, if he ventured to express a hope—a hope which he was sure was felt by every Englishman in the room—"that our legislature will in a time of peace, and not in a time of panic, remove all the grievances under under which Ireland suffers, and grant her people the same rights that we possess in this country, and I for one do not fear that granting to Irishmen the same rights as we enjoy will in the slightest degree jeopardise the integrity of the empire ; on the contrary, I firmly believe it will tend to consolidate it, and make Great Britain and Ireland in reality a United Kingdom." Ireland had indeed been rich in her poets dur- ing the present century. There was quite a galaxy of poe- tical writers, including,amougst others, the immortal Moore, Lover, Manyan, Thomas Davies, Dennis, Florence McCorthy, T. D. Sullivan, and Sir Charles Gavan Duffy, and they formed in their works the throbbing of Ireland's heart. The poets of Ireland had certtinlv done gre it petriotic work for their country because by their workings they had excited in the minds of the English a desire to know more about Ireland's wrongs. After reading a number of poems, the lecturer observed that while there was some dross in the writings of the poets there was a great deal of pure gold. Poetry, therefore, if properly selected would tend to sooth and cheer them in the struaglas of life, and if sometimes it pictured the dark side of nature its correcave power was still true to its mission by tea:Alin them that error was frequently the best warning. They must ever regard those poets, who, by their writings had elevated humanity as the true philai,thropiss. Such men had ad- ded new charm to life—a pleasure which charmed their childhood, animated their manhood, and in old age called back to memory the most beautiful recollections of the past. The entertainment commenced with Balfe's pretty duet "The sailor sighs," which was given with harmonious ex- pression and warmly apylauded. Mr. Hanlon followed with a capital rendering of The blue Alsatian mountains." Miss Johnson executed with skill the pianoforte solo " Reininis- causes of England," and later in the evening, "Reminiscences of Ireland " was performed by the same lady. The duet " Mother, can this glory be," was charmingly sung by Miss Wright and Miss Brown, while Miss Leatherbarrow gave a cultured interpretation of the song " The harp that once through Tara's halls," and she was heartily applauded. Miss Brown gave "The Arab's farewell to his steed " with much pathos, and Miss I eatherbtrrow was warmly applauded for her rendering of the " Shells of the ocean." The programme concluded with the National Anthem.

Olt the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. Cow- LET, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, and a similar compliment having been paid the ladies who had taken part in the entertainment and the chairman, the meeting concluded.
_ - A RUNCORN MAN INJURED AT WIDNES.

About twelve o'clock noon, yesterday, Mr. John Faulkner, of Cawdor-street, Runcorn, fell into a caustic pan whilst following his employment at Messrs. Mathieson'a works, Widnes. He was quickly rescued from his perilous posi- tion, and the usuAl remedies applied to the injured parts; his arm and body being scalded. He was conveyed home on a stretcher, and is being attended by Dr. Robinson.

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee contained the gas engineer's report, which stated that "The third new lwd of through renrts at gas woi ks was put on full work on the 24th September. I have weighed the coke produced from these retorts, and the results give 44 per cent, of coke for sale, or 22 per cent. more than the old system. This with our last year's c•msurnption of Mil trill make over 3,000 tons of c.,ke for sale per annum. The above system also reduces our cost of cart.onising about 20 pr cent. which will save in stcker's wages about £l5O per annum with our present make of gas. We have now a large stock of coke on hand and I beg to recommend that the price be reduced from to is. per ton." ILLEAFAL U5.1.E OF WATER.

PROPERTY OWNERS AND BAD TRADE—PERSONALITIES. _ _

The Highway Committee instructed the surveyor to the owner respecting the encroachment upon the passage between Water and Barn-streets, and have it removed. The surveyor was iestructed to relay footwalks at corner of Irwell-street, to remove the pillar lamp at junction of Pear-street and arrange for a bracket lamp. Messrs. D. Lea and Son asked permission to erect a wooded shed behind the Railway Hotel. The application was refused. The surveyor was instructed to cell npon Mr. Hughes to flag footpath adjoining the Post Office. Respecting the Leigh estate the surveyor was instructed to call upon Mr. Shel- merdine to fel ig the footpaths opposite the land leased or sold fronting Croft, Lacey and Alforde-streets, as per agree- ment. The chairman and surveyor were requested to see Mr. Shelmerdine respecting the boundary of the market land between Alforde and Market-streets, fronting Victoria- road; also about Appleton property. The surveyor was in- structed to take up and relay the curbs of Birchfield-road, Appleton-end, and form a proper footpath. R commended that Deacon-road be raised at a coat not exceeding £3O, as per arrangement with the property owners. It was recom- mended that the following streets be made, sewered, West-bank—Parsonage-road and J Imes and Hurst-streets. Waterloo-road—Wellington-street and part of Marsh-street Newtown—Charlotte, Elizabeth, Margaret and Victoria- streets. Sinem's Cress Thorpe and Gladstone- streets, parts of Dickson and Frederick - streets. Lugsdale Ellison, Lea and Fisher - streets. The surveyor was instructed to give netice that unless the noceeesary repairs are at once done to Old Beerhouse, Water- str..ot, applications be made to the magistrates for an order to have it pulled down. Instructions were given to I write to the Superintendent of Police respecting the destruc- tion of property, and to ask him to prosecute a few offen- ders as an example. Plan for additions and alterations to Simm's Cross Board School, and plan for shop, cottage, and outbuildings in Church-street, for Mr. S. Pursill, approved eubject to the approval of the Health Committee.—Mr. MIDWOOD moved, and Mr. SADLER secluded, the adepticn of the minutes.—Mr. WEBSTER, refeteing to recommenda- tion respecting the making of streets, slid ha should like to know whether any of the owners of property in these streets had applied for the streets to be made, and whether they re- quired to be made. Some of the streets were not in bad condition, and would not require to be made for 20 years to come. If these stree,s had to be made at the present time it might Ue the ruin of some of the small property owners, and he suggested that it would be better if the question was deferred for the preset:v.—Mr. ':',IARTLEY also thought the present an inopportune time to make these streets —The CHAIRMAN : I thiuk you ought to wait for an explanation before you condemn the action of the committee simply because youare uninformed. Mr. MARTLEY said there were other streets in the district that r(quired nicking, and he asked whether it was not competent for the Board to make all the streets by borrow- ing the money and spreading the repayments over a length of time. It seemed to him that tio,re was some sinister motive in the present recommen letion. lf they wanted to make Streets make all of them, and borrow the money and not pauperise the property owners. ',Hear, hear.)—Mr. goucrioroet disagreed with, the recommendation, and Mr. JOHNSON remarked that about a month ago Mr. Mi,iwood took the sense of the property owners in Irwell-street before flagging that street, while now he recommended about a dozen streets to be made without So much as consulting one owner. Gladstone-street was equal to any highway in Widnes, while the London and North-Western Railway was expected to take a number of the streets from them. He therefore thought it was foolishness to cripple the property owners by making these streets. Victoria and Nelson-streets were in a worse state than any of these recommended to be made.—Mr. MIDWOoD seid the committee had another bject in view than to improve the town.—Mr. MARTLEY : The chairman of the committee has.—Mr. MIDWOOD : I think, Mr. Chairman, he ought to withdraw that remark.— The CITAIRMAN replied that lie had not beard it, but Mr. :Warder or anyone else had no right to interrupt a member whilst speekinge—Mr. MinwooD then went on to explain that the streets it: question were in a very bid state, and lumbered with all manner of rubbish.

The hoard. however, hal no power to cleanse them in any way, and the committee thought it would be wise to make a fvw in various parts of the town. The committee pro- posed to have them made in a cheaper way than formerly, and allow the owners to rep ty the money in seven or ten years, with interest.—Mr. JonssoN asked Mr. Midwood if he had not more interest in other streets than he had in these ?—Tbe CHAIRMAN : I don't think you ought to become personal.—Mr. Mit:moon said Mr Johnson was present at the committee meeting, and he was agreeable to the streets being made, until they got to Gladstone-street, where be appeared to be the owner of a shop, aNd then he raised all manner of objections.—Mr. JOHNSON: objected to the whole lot without excepti‘n.—The CHAIRMA.N a,ked if :kir. Johnson wished it to be understood that the-members of the guard worked for their pA.sonal ends ?—Mr. JOHNSON: No, not at all.—The CHAIRMAN: You are really inferring that it is so.—Mr. B. DurroN sympathised very much with the chairman of the Highway Committee, and was prepared to stand by him in his endeavours to improve the town. The streets named, with the exception of one or two, wanted repairing, and as he was part owner of premises in one street, he might equally complain with Messrs. Martley, Houghton, and Johnsen. Ha believed that this was _ _ _

certainly a bad tune to have streets made in Widnes, as many owners of property were in in a very poor way. Rents were down from twenty to twenty-five per cant. all round; perhaps there wore a few exceptional business pre- mises. Ha stated advisedly that there was a great deal of property in Widnes being transferred to the mortgagees, and it was a very serious question with a good many people how they could retain their property until batter times. At the same time the easy terms of repayment proposed by Mr. Midwood would scarcely injure the weak-backed pro- perty owner. and he should certainly sustain Mr. Midwood in his endeavours to keep the town in good condition—Mr. MIDWOOD observed that a good deal had been sald'about him having some personal interest in this matter, and he should like to have a word on that subject.—The CHAIR- MAN: I should not if I were you.—To show that he had no feeling in it at all, he ought state that he Was the mort- gagee in possession of nine houses in these streets, and the owner in another instance, so that he would feel the hard- ship as much as anyone.—Mr. MARTLEY moved that the minute referring to the making of streets be expunged. He was very sorry to hear cue remark that came from the Chairman—that ha ha a personal interact. Well, he cer- tainly did not deny— —The CHAIRMAN: Who arc you speaking of ?—Mr. MARTLEY : I am speaking of a remark you made.—The Crum:awe (in astonishment) : I said ? —Mr. MARTLEY : Yes.-1 he CHAIRMAN: I never said word at all.—Mr. MARTLEY : I beg your pardon, you said I was interested in one strect.—The CH/mamma : I never said anything of the sort.—Mr. MARTLEY : lam no doubt in error. I beg your pardon.—Mr. DorroN It was ale I think, Mr. Martley.—The CHAIRMAN : I never made such a remark. The whole thing is irrevelant.—Mr. HOUGHTON seconded the amendment. Six or eight of the streets would do with repairing he said, and that be had no doubt the landlords would do if written to. They would then last for years.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that some of these streets were in a dirty condition, and the only way the committie could get control over them was by the method proposed by the committee.—Mr. HOUGHTON understood that, but in some of the streets he could not find a cabbage leaf.—Dr. O'KEEFFE supported the amendment. They had had a succession of unfortunate years in Widnes, from which they had not yet recovered, and he thought the pre- sent an inopportune time. He was glad to see, however. that the manufacturers were greatly recovered. (Laughter.) —Mr. CARET: I wish we were.—The amendment was then put to the vote and carried by a large majority.

ithe same time. The clerk wrote to Mr. Jeffreys, enclosing copy of foregoing letter, giving notice that he would be held responsible. Messrs. Jepson dis. div.head: TO 7SE ERECTED.
div.p: TO 7SE ERECTED.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported to the Health Committee that during the month of September there had ben births, or 39 36 per 1,000, and 46 deaths, or 22.0 S per 1,000. Zymotic diseases caused ten deaths. Thirty-seven of the deaths occurred amongst children. Inspector's Report for September stated that five small-pox were reported during the month. viz. : one ease at each of the following places, Ncs. 11, 12, and 13, John. street, Lagsdale, No. 99, Midwood-street and Widnes-road. opposite Derby Arms. One case of measles and two caseS of typhus fever were also reported. There had been one death from scarlet fever. The patient from No. 11, John— street, has been removed to the workhouse hospital, also a case of continued fever; but the relieving officer (Mr. Scannell) refused to send any of the others. Disinfection was strictly attended to. There was great trouble with the convalescent patients. Four of the late small-pox 'patients were now quite well, and the others were recovering. The medical otllcer and inspector were instructed to take imme- diate action in dealing with the cases in John-street and Mid wood-street, and render monetary assistance if necessary. Five tenders for temparary infectious hospital were opened, and consideration deferred. The chairman and surveyor were instructed to negotiate with Mr. Ireland for land for the erection of a permanent building, subject to the approval of the Board. The Local Government Board 'motioned the re-appointment of Mr. Cooper as medic al officer for a period of twelve months. Dr. O'KEEFE moved the confirmation of the minutes. He was sorry to say that small-pox seemed to be spreading, instead of decreaeing, as the first c ise occurred in Widnes- road and now there was another in the same road. The patient WAS keeping in his house. Of course the proper precautions possible for isolation and disinfection were being taken, but it was in a very public place. It was especially unfortunate that it was in the imintdiate neigh- bourhood, in fact directly opposite the house of one of the members of the Board. He (the doctor) hoped it would be the means of induclng that member to agree to the im- mediate erection of an Infectious Diseases Hospital. (Hear, hear.) He thought the disease was approaching the resi- dences of other members of the Board, also, who had op- posed the construction of such a hospital, and everybody knew that small-pox was a most loaths)me disease, so frightful in its nature, and to anybody going through a ward where there were four patients the smill would be enough to frighten any person for ever, and make him wish that the disease was eliminated from the face of the earth. He said this as a warning to the members of the Board, in order that they would not oppose the erection of an infec- tious diseases hospital again. He was thoroughly in earnest almut it. If they did not erect an hospital now, they would be forced to do so shortly. When the death from the disease was reported to the Local Government Board, the first mes- senger they would have from them would be an inspector, who would give the Board commanding orders. On the previous day they had the advice of Mr. Davies, for

whom he had a very profound respect. He con-idered that the site for a hospital which Mr. Higg:nson and himself (the doctor) had selected was one of the most suitable in Widnes. Mr. Bradshaw's academy at Appleton had been mentioned, and he had ascertained that the area of the
ground to.-sell was 10,643_equare yards, independent—of

, . . , , ..... the building, but he dared say that the owner expected more than the Board would be willing to expend. fie did not care which site the Board selected, provided it met the ordinary requirements of an infectious diseases hos-

_ pita!, namely, that it be centrally situated so as to be easily accessible from all parts of the township; that it have facil- ities for good drainage, that it be placed in an airy situation, and lastly that it be reasonably removed from any habitation, lie had no personal interest whatever in any site, but he thought it was absolutely necessary to procead immediately with the construction of the hospital. Of

course smallpox was not the only disease they had to fear. They had scarlatina, which was a fatal, although not to horrible a disease as smallpox—measles, typhus fever, ty- phoid fever, and now they had got orders to prepare for an invasion of cholera. If the Board rejected his proposal for a hospital he threw the responsibility from his own shoulders as chairman of the Health Committee on to theirs. The
probability of infection increased according to the squares of the distance, and the chances of infection would be 81 at the Appleton site, and 9 at Halton View.--51r. CAREY
second.o.d.—Mr. WEssrsn inquired whether the committee had discovered the cause of the outbreak. Scarlet fever
occurred in the same neighbourhood last year, and it had been mentioned to him that pig keeping was the cause. The
ground was saturated with lilth from _pigs—Dr. O'KEEFE

ridiculed the idea of such a czuse, and said wherever pigs were kept in a position injurious to health the inspector ordered their immediate removal. If Mr. Webster knew of •nber of the Board—i. - inform
any case it was his duty as a member of the Board—it ought - corn-
all events —to
mittee where there were any insanitary conditions, and they would be rectified.—The minutes were passed.—

Su os:quently the Board went into committee on the hospi- tal question. OPENING OF A PUBLIC PARE AT COVENTRY.—At Coven- try, on Thursday, a park presented to the city by Mr. David Spencer, and a recreation ground presented by the Trustees of 6ir Thomas White's sharities, were publicly opened, and a'statue of Sir Thomas White, who some centuries back was a great benefactor to Coventry and other midland towns, was unveiled amidst considerable rejoicings.

Tits OUTRAGE AT NANTwicn.—The scandalous outrage upon Mr. Bateman, Cherley, Nantwich, will shortly form the subject of a magisterial investigation, summonses hav- ing been issued at the instance of the Nantwich Board of Guardians, of which Mr. Bateman is senior vice-chairman. The attack was made in Nantwich. Mr. Bateman was cursed, a gun pointed at his breast, and warned to prepare for violent death. Numerous letters of sympathy have been sent to Mr. Bateman, who is 84 years of age, and was vice- president to the Primitive Methodist denominatioa. THE IRON TRADE QUARTERLY MEETING.—There was a very large attendance at the quarterly meeting of the iron trade, on Thursday afternoon, and ironmasters and buyers were present from all parts of the kingdom. A few Ameri- can buyers attended. Prices both for pig and finished iron were redecland without alteration upon last quarter, marked bars being £7 10s. to £8 2s. od, unmarked sorts £6 10s., an& all-mine pigs 625. 6d. to 655. Plate makers complained of the quietness of trade. Merchant sheets and sheets for gal- vanisers were most in demand. Export orders were re- ported as being very sati‘factory, and the home inquiries were also more numerous. There was a better demand for coal. but the market was said to be flooded with fuel of all claFses. A meeting of the trade will be held next week to consider the application of the men for an advance of 10 per cent. in wages. manatparrar,insetd.
