div.head: 7-fatter3 to the Vitor:
div.p: 7-fatter3 to the Vitor:

OUR NATIONAL CHURCH. " I conAdev the Cburch of England the puye,t National Church in the world. Is doctrires and its sacraments whtch cons itute the essence of a t hurch I hot I consciensiothdy. I reverence the Liturgy next to th,t Bibte."—ADAM C.LARKS. Sir,—lt seems to me that the subject under drscus.sion is not "Our National Church," but' the abuses of and in Our National Church." "Clifford Dix" and his colleagues have not advanced one single argument which has to do with the principle of a "National Church." There is no doubt that they want the Church disestablished, but let me ask them in the language of "F. M. S." to give us something tangible. Let them give us some reasons for the disestablishment, and also their proposals after it is disestablished. At all events before the work of demolition begins let us knew what is to be substituted that we may form a calm judgment on the whole case. I cannot find that the query of "Church- man " as to the Liberationists' intentions with regard to the new church at Walton has yet been answered. But allow me, sir, to put before your readers the real value and object of an Established Church, by asking the questions (1) Should religion be connected with the State; (2) What are the advantages arising from such connection; (3) Is the union of Church and State worth preserving? Firstly,—shaudd re- ligion be connected with the State? My own opinion is that it should. The State by this recognition of religion, to my mind, gives religion a special recommendation to all ins subjects. It also gives the State a tone and a backbone., so to spealle. And I should support the -connection were it only on the same grounds as the promoters of a cricket club take in their endeavours to establish it on. a firm basis. They endeavour to „get the weightiest and most influential gentleman as president, then a vice-president is appointed, dec., and so on. The main aim being to get a tone, a backbone to the club So in the connection of religion with the State. The State is its president, and from this religion receives a recognition and 1 recommendation such as no private body could obtain. Bishop Daniel Wilson says:—' An establishment is not essential to Christianity as the infidel would insinuate, for the three or four centuries of its history prove that the Church of Christ, as a Church, can exist independently of the State. But, though an establishment is not essential to Christianity itself, it is essential to every Christian Government which desires to discharge the highest obligations towards the people committed to its care. A connection between Christianity and the rulers of a Christian country is imperiously required to ful- fil the duty of the parent of the State to his vast family; this is not only expedient, but lawful, scriptural, and abso- lutely necessary to the very first principles of legislation. Human power must rest on the fear of God; laws without conscience and a reference to the Supreme Arbiter are im- potent. Every nation upon earth, both before and after the appearance of Christianity has therefore acknowledged the necessity of some religion as the support of civil authority. Even the heathen did this; so that we have universal con- sent and the voice of conscience speaking in all ages and nations in support of Establishment. The care of the souls of men is no mere to be left to the chances of a voluntary system than the care of their bodies or their property. As medical appointments and laws generally are formed in every state so much more should religious establishments. For, in the corruption of our nature, the supply here will not be created, es in matters of this world, by the necessity—the necessity being least felt where it is in truth the most deplorable. , A paternal government must therefore supply the demand beforehand; but still in so discreet a manner that ample room may be left for the salutary operation of individual effort, as it is, and no compulsion ever attempted or thought of. Taus the very weakness and corruption of our nature demand religious establishments." Dr. Samuel Warren (a learned lawyer) says—" It is the duty of each, ever and most solemnly to remember the true objects of the union, and so strengthen its hold upon the intellect and the heart of an enlightened people. No Christian statesman can fail to regard as the true and lasting object of society the promotion of man's present and future happiness, and in so doing the glory of his Maker. Our rulers should regard the State as religion regards an indi- vidual ; as having tempobal, subordinate to eternal interests, with corresponding duties, motives, and objects." "In a Christian commonwealth," says the illustrious Edmund Burke," the Church and State are one and the same thing, being different in integral parts of the same whole. Reli- gion is so far from being out of the province or duty of a Christian magistrate, that it is, and it ought to be, not only his care, but the principal thing in his care ; because it is one of the great bonds of human society and its object the supreme good,—the ultimate end and object of man him- self." The Bishop of Liverpool (then Rev. J. C. Ryle, M.A.,) in a paper read before the Nottingham Congress in October, 1871, says :—" I declare with all my love for the Church of England I had rather see her privileges and en- dowments taken away from her and transferred to Metho- dists, Independents, or Baptists, than see the rulers of old England refuse altogether to recognise religion." Those ringing wards, he goes on," which John Owen addressed to the House of Commons in Cromwell's time, are just as true now:as they were 200 years ago,"—" if you say that you have nothing to do with religion as rulers of this nation, God will quickly manifest that be has nothing to do with you as rulers." The late Dean Stanley in his "Essays on Church and State" says :—" The essential features of the connection of Church and State which are sufficient to secure the principle however inadequately or faintly it be represented may be stated thus :—The first is, that the Slats should recognise and support some religious expression of the community; the second is, that this religious expression sheuld be controlled and guided by the State." I may state here Dean Stanley's reply to the Liberationist cry, that "the State made the choice of a creed and set it up above the others." He says, "In point of fact the state has never, strictly speaking, made a choice at all. The Church of England—meaning thereby the ecclesiastical system of England—has grown up historically like all the other elements of the English Commonwealth. It is not a single institution, but a group of institutions; not a corpo- ration, but a group of corporations. The State can be said to have chosen these, only in the same way that it has chosen monarchy, and the House of Lords, and the univer- sities, and the House of Commons, and the three denomina- tions each in their several ways. Mr. Thomas Hughes, 31. P., who said he " came before the audienemas a Radical," said, in speaking at Birmingham in 1872, "The connection between Church and State forces on the Legislature, on Government, on statesmen, on all men engaged in public affairs—in short, upon the national conscience—the fact that the nation, in its corporate capacity has a spiritual as well as a material life, that it cannot confine itself to the _preservation of material things, of body and goods. The endeavour to separate things spiritual in individual, family, or national life, is, we hold, a grievous blunder, and certain to prove most mischievous and futile. The man, the family, the nation must live both lives. We desire that they may be pledged as deeply as possible to live them according to a Christian standard." So much on. my first point. Now to the second—" The advantages arising from the Church's Connection with the State." Lord Brougham, after dis- passionately weighing them, comes to the conclusion that, "on the whole, greater mischiefs resalt from baying ne Establishment at all, and that the balance is decidedly in favour of such an institution." It is hardly neceesary to ,repeat at length the arguments of Arnold' and "(Thal- -mere" as to the benefit of 'securing a clergy in those parts of the country where it is least likely that mach pro- vision would be made by the people themselves; something saved out of the scramble which no covetousness can appro- priate and no folly waste; a provision made for the public purposes in the most unattractive districts, no 1C39 than in the most inviting—a man of education placate in every part of the country in the most improving- of all situations, that is, a life of constant intercourse with men, of which the direct and acknowledged bnai- nem is to do them good; physically and morally." The late John James Teyler, an eminent Nonconformist, ' says :—"An. Established Church, if properly worked out, supplies an instrumentility for acting uniformly and con- stantly on the moral and spiritual condition of the whole ,esetintry which bermonises with ali our ideas of a perfect civilisation." The opinions of the into Dean Stanley on this point are too lengthy to be here quetal, but your readers may read these for themselves in his " Essays on Church and State," which is precurable at the Warrington Library. But the following anecdote taken from the rtb,)ve book is worth mentioning. It is a conversation overheard between a Free Churchman and an English Churchwomen. F. C. : D'ye ken wha's the head of your Chorch ? It's the Qdctell. E. C.: "Well, I'm glad to hear it, I believe that's she's a very decent body. But d'ye ken who's the head of your Church ?—ye think ye ken wha it is—it's no such thing. I'll tell you—irs Joseph Thompson, the tailor, that neither ye nor the minister dare peep or wag a linger if it dies not please him. He's the head of your Church, and for my part I am quite as well contend with the head of ours." "Strip this con- versation of its grotesque personalitiee," says Dean Stanley, "anti it exactly represents the true and only difference be- tween an Established and a so-called "Free Church." But 41:0 return. Sir Roundell Palmer (now Lord Selborne) in

1873 said "the erepanisation of the Chureh system gave more means and opportunities of overtaking the very poor who can do nothing for themselves, than any other system which yet has existed." The present Archbishop of Canterbury said in July lest—" The separation would deprive the State of her very sent" Then again, there is another advantage to be derived from the connection which must not be over- looked, awl that is this: an Established Church is bound to minister to all the subjects of the realm, no matter of what belief. But tbe moment it ceases to exist as a public, as a national body this obligation ceases. It becomes a private body, and is only expected to look after its own flock. And the fact would be that numbers of persons would be left wholly without that spiritual food which is always within the grasp and can always be demanded at the hands of an established clergy. "What's everybody's business is nobody's busioess." New to my third point : "is the union of Church and State worth preserving ?" Dr. Samuel Warren says :—" This alliance exists in fact and as a fact, and is interwcven with the whole tieeta of our national institutions. It cannot now be separated without imperilling the welfare and the very existence of the body politic, and doing irreparable injury to both Church and State. It is the duty of each ever and most solemnly to remember the true objects of that union, and so strengthen its hold upon the intellect and the heart of an enlightened people." In an article on Arthur Penhreen Stanley, in the January number of the Century Magazine, an American writer says :—" The political and philanthropical arguments , for a National Church are strong. It is, or may be made, the safest bulwark against sectarian bigotry, the most.effi- cient machinery for supplying the moral needs of the com- munity . , . . end the Church of England which is committed to so much less than the Church of Rome, and which, with her allied churches in both hemispheres, stands already second in importance to the Church of Rome alone—the Church of England, it may well be said, has a better chance than any other religious corporation of finding herself erect after the general re-construction, and constitut- ing in some sense or other the Church of the future." The Rev. Charles Marshall says :—How can nonconformity battle with fanaticism ?—with those who pretend to an ex- traordinary degree of sanctity, to a faith not found in the Gospel, to an especial call which supersedes the necessity of education, and of the setting apart to the ministry of the Word commanded and practised by the apostles themselves? —with those who seduce the people from their appointed, ministers, separate them from the communion of the Church gain a complete ascendancy over them, and instil into their minds the most dangerous opinions and the most active enthusiasm/ The precepts of the Gospel and the whole history of mankind declare the principles of these fanatics to be utterly inconsistent with true religion and the well-being of society. Brethren, our established and endowed Church ley the holy scriptures, can battle with infidelity. Our established and endowed Church, by the Protestant Articles, can distinguish the Christian re- ligion from its corruptions, and can battle with 'every. Our established and endowed Church, by the reformed liturgy, can battle with fanaticism. Our established and endowed Church, kept Protestant and put e by the providence, by the word, and by the spirit of God, will propagate and per- petuate the religion of the people ; and religion is the only sure basis of every government ; for you may as well attempt to build a city without a foundation as to preserve a State without religion. Brethren, it is atgreat privilege as well as a great duty to support an established and an en- dowed Church, in order to spread and to hand down re- ligion to future generations; but the greatest blessing of all is to have it in your hearts and guiding your lives, so that you fear God, honour the -Queen, love the brotherhood, and (wive your country !" Mr. Gladstone declares that "The Church of England has not only been a part of of the history of this country, but a part so vital, entering so profoundly into the entire life and action of the country, that the severing of the two wouhl leave nothing behind but a bleeding and lacerated mass. Take the Church of England out of the History of England, and the Hietoxy of England becomes a chaos without order, without life, and without meaning." Speech in the House of Commons, May 16, 1873.—Sir William Harcourt thus speaks of one probable result of such a catastrophe as dis- establiehnitnt ; "In my opinion, he isee purblind politician who does not perceive . that the residuary legatee of disestablishment will infallibly be the Church of Rome." Speech at Oxferd, Dec. 21, 1874.— Lord Selborne, speaking at Alton, on December 23rd, 1874, mader the following very earnest appeal:—"lf sacrilege was to coma upon this land, let the clergy, at least, have nothing to do with it. Let them not be persuaded to think that a better state of things would exist if the Church were free from State control than that under which they now lived. Let them not for one moment imagine that a better state of things would be arrived at by their helping the enemies of religion and of the Church, who were striving to take away from men their churches and their endownments. They might depend upon it that those who were discon- tented and wished to pull the Church down about their heads would find themselves no better off in any point of view if it were done. They would rather be very much the worse; while, with respect to the State, he trembled, as a citizen, to think of the consequences that might result from the breaking of those ties that entered so deeply into the whole national and social life of the country, and were so entwined around existing institutions." The Rev. Canon Hole says :—" What would become of the poor of England? At this moment there is hardly a vil- lage in the land in which there is not a man ready to answer the first sell of sickness and sorrow, to minister to the souls and bodies of the pewee., and minister as lovingly as to the noble, as to the rich, to advise in perplexity, to re- lieve in want." The Bishop of Petelborough in "The Voluntary System ' says:—" The Church establishment is of inestimable value as a national testimony to the value of religion throughout the length anl breadth of the land. Is it a slight advantage, moreover, which the establishment bestows upon the poor man, in that it gives him a right to come to the parish church for worship, and to the p Irish clergyman tor instruction and for counsel ? There is not a parishioner in any parish in England, be he high or low, tich or poor, who has not a right, as a citizen of England, to claim the service of the minister of the National Church, to call him to his bedside at any hour of the day or of the night to give him the ordinances of reli- gion, to censole and strengthen him in his sorrow or his suffering. The poor man has the same right to the services of the parish clergyman that he has to those of the parish doctor, and for the same reasons; tooth are appointed to minister to him gratuiteutly. For all these reasons then, both as regards the paster and the people, we hold that the territorial, fixed, parochial system of the English national Church is, of all Tilers, the best calculated to preduce a learned, efficient, independent, influential, and pious pastorate, and to promote and maintain the purity and power of religion in this country. Abuses it may have, not a few; defects in its working, arising from the imperfections and infirmities of those who work it, it must have, many and great. But, despite all these abuses and all these defects, it is the noblest ad the wisest system of national ' religious instruction and edification" that the wisdom and piety of a nati.n ever deqeised. Let us hope the English people will wait, before they destroy it, until its assailant produce any system calculated to work at least half so welt." I cannot go to greatelength on these three points, but I trust that I have adduced sufficient evidence in their support. As to who who would be the sufferer in case of Disestablishment, I think there can be no doubt. The poor man would feel it more than anyone. More attention in any private sect is shown—perhaps to some extent naturally—to the man of wealth and importance, and the peer man is left to shift for himself, and to "like it or lump it." He has no remedy. But in the case of an Established Church he can "demand attention." Again, would the "workingman " be any better off for the Disestablishment ? Mr. Thomas Hughes the Radical M.P. whom I quoted in an earlier part of my fetter, says not, and concludes by saying—" If, as I maintain, the existence of the Estee liehment (of the direct communication between this nation and Christianity, that is) forces nothing on you, and takes nothing away from yen; if you are just as free and as well off, whether ft continues or whether it ceases, just let me ask you to try to understand the case of those to whom it has a very deep and real meaning—my case for instance, and that of many others, who have always endeavoured to gain for you your Lir share of politieel power, and of all the good things of this world." Now to "Clifford Dix." He tells me that he has " more than once in this discussion pointed out that the Radical portion of the community will not accept any historical or traditional rights that Church- men claim to have in the phrase "State Church." This is not a political question, but allow me to say that my firm belief is that it is just this want of a knowledge of historical rights and facts which makes a man a Radical-. For does not my opponent know that Radicalism has always "been a synonym" for ignorance and stupidity. "Clifford Dix," it seems, does not accept my statement that "there never was a: Church of Rome in England." But I re- iterate it. I am quite aware, " Mr. Dix," of the mission which Pope Gregory sent over to England in the year 596-7. As regards doctrine, and what I may term its spiritual corporate shape, the Church of England is practically identical " with the Church founded in England, possibly even by one of the Apostles, at any rate not later than about the second or third century A.D." (See on this interesting gnestion the Rev. C. T. C. Trelawny's Perranzabuloe, the Lost Church Found ; or the Church of England not a new Church, p. 32, ed. of 1868.) It is worthy of note that in 314 A. D. three English bishops signed canons enacted at a council at Arles, in Gaul ; two of these were respectively Bishops of London and York. The see of the third has not been c',arly identified, but pro- bably it was Caerleon-on-Usk, in Monmouthsaire. (Haddan and Stable.. councils and Eccl. Decu. motto, vol. i., p. 7.) There can he no doubt, therefore, that a breech of the C :ristlan Church existed in Britain some time before this occurrence, and the know- ledge of this fact becomes important when we consider the claim sometimes advanced by Renee that it was to the Roman monk Augustine (597 A.D.) that England really owes it,s Christianity. The Englieh Church of the third centutv we both pure and independent. It suffered under the Diocle- tian persecution, and the name of one of its martyrs, St. Alban, has corns down to us (284-6 A se). Afterwards it be- -o.,nie bliolited by the falee teaching of Ar:tts (300 A se), who denied the Godhead of Christ ; and, subs, queotly, by that of pekgeoe (400 AD.), who denied the doctrine of original sin and asserted that man could be saved hy his own merits. When England, forty years after the departure of the Romans (about 400 AD). was overrun by the Saxons (450- 681 ann.), who were at that time pagans (Sh. Turner, History of the Anglo-Saxons, vol. i. book ii. c. iv.), the Epglish Church and its monuments and records were in great part swept away (Bede, Historia F:cclesi- a stica, bk. i. C. xiv.). There rcuniined, however, sufficient

div.head: EXAMINER, SA TURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA TURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1883.

to show that it was quite an independent Church, and was untainted by the later corruptions of Rome (compare Gil- das, Historia, § 26, Bohn's ed. p. 313). During the period comprised between 409 A.D. and 449 A.D. the clergy largely guided the nation, and Gibbon thinks there were as many as thirty or forty Bishops (Decline and Fall, ch. xxxi. vol. iv. p. 134, ed. of 1854). The year 597 marks an important epoch in the history of the Church of England. Tne arrival of Augustine, an agent of the Pope of Rome, then took place; but it is a gross distortion of the facts to allege that England then received Christianity for the first, time, and owes gratitude to Rome accordingly. On the contrary, Augustine on his arrival found British bishops here, who, though they welcomed Lim in a fraternal spirit, studiously refused to put themselves under either him or his master. May I ask " Clifford Dix," when he says that the Parish Church was, like the Grammar School, filched and diverted from her original purpose by those "saintly and pious reformers," what the original purposes of the above-men- church and school wee, and also explain by what means they have been filched and diverted from them? I should also like to know what he means after telling me that the "Radical portion of the community will not accept any historical rights of Churchmen in the phrase 'State Church, ' " by inviting me either to quote some "historical facts" or accept his arguments. These seem to be the only points in his letter. And now, in conclusson, let me say that I have endeavoured to prove that, in the first place, it is desirable to connect religion with the State; secondly, the advantages derived from such a connection; and thirdly, that the union is worth preserving. Let me ask your readers' attention to the foregoing statements, and also let me ask them to be on their guard during the coming winter, when so many liberationist lying spirits are abroad. Thanking you for your courtesy and forbearance, Mr. Editor, whilst this correspondence has been going on, I remain, , yours, &c., • H, J. WESTBROOK. Stockton Heath, October, 1883.

Sir,—Your correspondent "F. M. S." seems to have ' Eaten of the insane root That, takes the reason prisoner, confeqaently he cannot be in a desirable frame of mind and temper so necessary for the wise guidance of so important a subject as the one under consideration. He tells us "that there is little difficulty in supplying matter especially adapted for stricture." Does this mean that whatever argu- ments Libarationists urge, it is the easiest thing possible for supporters of the Establishment to confute them ; if so, why not at once set about the work? Our arguments may be fit for nothing but "ridicule and censure," but allow me to direct "F. M. S.'s" attention to this little fact—the day is gone by for ridicule. To laugh down your .opponent means h istening your own ruin. Having said this much, allow me to compliment " F. M. S." on the exactness of his quota- tions from my previous letters, and also te say, that had he only made an effort to answer half of them he would have done some service, not only to Mr. Westbrook, but to the "Grand Old Church." of which he seems to be so poor a defender. No wonder that he hails with delight the state- ment of the British Quarterly, that the Episcopal Church is showing signs of a quickening of spiritual life. The lash of public opinion has been brought to bear upon this inert mass of selfishness; it is merely rousing itself, and like the blood sucking octopus, seeking for something upon which to fix its suckers. Theists, Atheists. Materialists, Agnostics, &c., &c., are now forcing themselves to the front; they are growing fast, and will soon form the majority, and woe to the supporters of the Establishment if they decide to return evil for evil. Bat I have faith that the advancing tide will scek not to overwhelm, but rather to raise up. ' "F. M. S." asks ms to point out "all the other nations which have been or are more prosperous than our own," No need to do this. My imaginary trip supplied an argu- ment that is unanswerable. Other nations that allowed the grip of the Churce to tighten around the threat of progress, have fallen strangled. Esigland threw this old man of the sea off its back at the time when Dissent declared its existence. History tells us of the Church coercing Parlia- ment into passing Acts forcing all the people to. attend her services. All our towns and villages, bending to the tyran- nical will of the venerable squires, erected the stocks and the pillory, and the parson took care that— Wherever God erects a house of prayer, The devil a'ways bunch a chapel there. The radical and progressive spirit of Englishmen has cleared away stocks and pillory. Liberal education codes will thin the devil's chapels, and these revoluticnary doctrines, taken altogether, will frustrate the knavish tricks of Conservative Churchmen. lam sure that "F. M. S." must know that for a great number of years the Church pulpit and the political platform have resounded again and again with the dismal groans of the grand old Church's defenders bewail- ing the spread of doctrines that were leading to England's downfall; and yet he allows she stands erect, proud, amongst the nations of the earth. Be thankful, the Radicals will yet carry her on to something grander. Yes' Ahab must have the vineyard; that is, the exclusive lock must be wrenched off. " Dishing up isolated instances of abase," why, sir, your columns might be turned into a Newgate calendar; and if the wrong-doings of Church par- sons merely were recorded, your space would not nearly suffice. We are told that under the present system every village is guaranteed the presence of an educated gentle- man Yes, but it must be one who can have his own way; one to whom the hat must be doffed; one who can say, this Church is mina. Nay. one who can soy— am monarch of all I survey, My right there 's none to dispute. It is well known that the disgraceful manner in which ont of our leading clergymen, and his wife, conducted them- selves towards the poor in his parish, alienated the feelings of these people. They distinctly refused to have their doors opened unexpectedly. They refused to have the oven peered into and the pan lid taken off, and to be questioned as to what they had for dinner ; and because they did so refuse, they are never visited. Tell ma how often the poor living around the Parish Church are visited in a kindly, loving, and helping spirit by the Rector? • Show me the , good work he is doing in return for the wages he receives, I and I will hold my peace. CLIFFORD DIX.- IWarrington, Oct., 1833. [I his correspondence must cease at this point.—En. W. and M.-C. Ex.] THE SALVAIION ARMY. Sir.—" Lowly Ranger" seems to be in a most unhappy,' state of mind. Living, as he does, within hearing of live different churches no wonder the jangling and clanging of , the discordant belle has driven him distracted. Congreve I tells us
Music hath charms to sooih the savage breast; And I can assure my friend that I think no music so sweet as that of the
Silver bells. If " Lowly Ranger" will take my advice, he will at once remove from a district so much givert_over
Ti the rolling Oi the bells ; And take up his abode where the sweet Talkie, tinkle, tinkle. .the Icy air of night,

Will reach him; and if he does not C-onfess that from one peal of bells he receives a soothing benefit, why, then he must be like poor Jessica— I am never merry when I hear sweet music; And, like Lorenzo, I must say— Ti e man that hath no music in himsel, Nor is not movecl with concord of sweet sounds, Is fit for treasons, strAtagems, and spoils.

Having said so much in defence of campanology, allow me to express my great surprise that "Lowly Ranger" should, in his defence of the "poor and ignorant," find it necessary to urge extenuating circumstances. "Lowly Ranger" admires the Salvation band, accompanied, as he states, with voices singing pretty melodies. This is mere pathos. No musician in the world would use so dignified a term as band to the heterogeneous assortment of instruments that accompanies the "drum thumper." Music indeed ! The Salvation army, I confess, has not yet disturbed my Sunday morning's rest; bat I must say that if it has done so in the ridiculous sense in which "Lowly Ranger" thinks so very desireble, well, I think it probable the curses heard from those whom it.pas roused from "nature's sweet res- torer." must have been both loud and deep. That in itself would be a pity. No, a working man having done his duty during six days out of the seven may be allowed his own choice as to rising early or late on Sunday mornings, Salo- bath breaking nothwithstanding. If Publican Booth's armies wish to act as national knockers vp, let them go into the quiet and respectable streets, say down Bold-street, Museum-street, and the various cross streets in that district. I am much surprised at the poetic quotation. As a specimen of intolerance it is simply unique, but it is launched at one who like myself bPlieved not in the "endless fire "doctrine. Does not "Lowly Ranger" know that associations are being formed composed in the main of rev, gentlemen, whose ob- ject is to drive out this God-degrading doctrine. The Rev. W. Impey, 'Wesleyan missionary, has but just returned fr;,in Africa, and confessed that he cannot preach that "hell is a dark and bottomless pit, full of fire and brimstone, in which the wicked will be for ever and ever punished by having their bodies tormented by this fire, and their souls by a sense of the wrath of God." Now I ask if this doctrine is to be thrown over by the educated, are we to retain it for the consolation of the poor? In the same poem from which "Lowly Ranger " quotes occurs the following, and to those who desire the brimstone doctrine it specially applies : Puir culi preterrlin' light to scatter Truth's lovely face vti' dirt ye spatter. For me I trow I shanna flatter Bic impudence; A frog might croak, or pyet chatter,

lr sober sense. We are told that the doctrines and Ways of the Army are not "outrageous to the class .drho share in them." What an argument! Because the ways of the midnight brawlers are congenial to their tastes, there must be no interference. What are these men and women doing meeting night after tight in their barracks? Women ,neglecting their homes, the men wasting good time that might be devoted to self- improvement. -How many of them have ever bought a book or read one through? How many of them belong to the Public Library? I dare assert not one; and vet they, with children talre babies, perched up on chairs, presume to teach the people the way of salvation. Well may a writer in the Christian World term their meetino "revolting ex- hibitions," well may he say that their "appeals to heaven were disgusting and revolting," and hope the day will come when such hurleFque of religion will be impossible. In u,rnpiring the Salvation Army to the Prophets of Baal I think the writer most happy. I quite agree with "Lowly Ranger" in his remarks respecting the Rotnish Church and silver being expected at the doors; and. as for paid adver- tisements in religious magazines, this is not an unmixed evil. It is a well-koown fact that most of our cheap litera- ture is so only in consequence of the %large number of advertisements that are inserted ..and paid for.

And now, sir, allow me to have a word with "Fair Play." So fully persuaded am I that this gentle pleader for the one stale herring, viz: "The SaN'ation Army," has not arrived at the years of discretion, that I must say it did not need his infantine confession that he had been a "member of society for 14 years. As he grows older, learns more of the ways of men, and also tries to fathom that most complex piece of machinery, the human mind, he will come to the same conclusion that I bave,—that all religious or anti-re- ligious denominations must be prepared for criticism. Sects or combinations'of men are simply made up of units or in- dividuale, and each manor woman must be looked upon as a fallible being, and as inch open to all honest criticism. When "Fair Play" tells us that the people do not under- stand "paid ministers" on account of their "college gram- mar," I think he makes a great mistake. They are under- stood so far as grammar is concerned, but I very much_coes- tion whether either the minister or his congregation under- stand what may be termed their church theology. This has now become so intricate that it requires a special surgical operation before the average brain can receive it. Another reason is, I am quite sure of this, that the poor and ill-clad people won't have, nay, refuse to have, anything to do with the "gentle folks." With the incident quoted by "Fair Play," I have little to do, more than to say, that sobriety and a strict attention to home affairs would accomplish the same good results. I must say my friend abuses that most beautiful word "mercy." To say "that if a man struck him on the cheek he would not return the blow," and then claim to be merciful is a sheer misapplication of the word. The proper term to use would be coward; nay, a harder word would be more fitting, and I say it would be criminal and an encourage- ment to all law-breakers, for if you allow a man to st:ike you once, I see no reason why you should hinder him from repeating the dose, and where would that land us? Don't tell me of example, with the class of men under considera- tion it would have no deterring effect whatever. The fact is, all the brave defenders of the "Salvation Army" are in the same plight as the Army itself—they are groping in the dark, not haying any idea of the principle embodied in the little word "truth." They think to be satisfied with some- thing that is not even its shadow. With true Jesuitical instincts they think and act as if the end justifi,cl the means, not seeing that the movement is built on the sand, and, like scores of fanatical rivals, will be swept away by the waves of advancing thought. My friend pleads for the right to sell War Crus `. because no religious cause can be carried on without money." I grant this. It would be as difficult to turn the other cheek to the smiter as it would be to go out into all the world taking neither ssrip nor purse. In fact, you must take thought for to-morrow if you intend to live; but I thought War Crus were sold to benefit the purchaser and not to increase Publican Booth's income. Perhaps I was mistaken. HIGH RANGER.

BY JOHN SAUNDERS,
AtialOr Of " HiRELL ; OR, LOVE BORN OF STRIFE." "ABEL DR,..I{E'S WIFE." " ISRAEL MORT, OVERMAN," &C., &C.
CHAPTER XXIV.-STEPHEN TAKES TO POETRY AND IS
DULY REWARDED
The moment Lord Harlaxton appeared in the room, Miss Vandeleur put down the book as quickly as she had taken it op. and advanced with a smile to meet him, and said,
You have succeeded?"

"Yes," was the reply. "The locket was found on inquiry in the possession of one of the assistants, who was confuoed and agitated; and said that in the hurry of business she quite forgot to mention it. Unluckily, the mistress on learn- ing our names became so impressed with her duty to you that she would not give it up till satisfied that you had no desire to prosecute." "Oh, my dear lord, it is really too bad to trespass again on your goodness, but lam sure the poor girl meant no harm, and ought to be instantly put out of her misery." Lord Elarlaxton looked at her and at Stephen before he again spoke: "I will do that at once. A servant shall go directly." "The mission is too noble for such a messenger," said Miss Vandeleur. "But as you please! " There was was no mistaking the haughty tone of her voice, and Lord Har- laxton hastened to reassure her:

"Oh, I will go with pleasure, if you really wish it." "I do indeed, for the poor girl'u sake. And I shall be grateful—most grateful !" "Rally ? " asked the Earl in his tenderest tone. "Really ! " responded the lady in her most impressive manner.
" And I shall find you here on my return ?"
"Can you doubt ii?"

Lord Harlaxton waited for no more; but, kissing his fingers to her, and she similarly responding, be hu-ried away, intending also as hurriedly to return ; Mie!.! Van'l2:eur watching demonstratively his departure. That clever lady had accomplished her object. She was again alone with Stephen. And if she had been a little un- scrupulous as to the means, in her overmastering desire to prevent the Earl's interruption from stopping the natural progress and end of such a beginning, it must be said in her excuse that much of the attitude she had assumed with the Earl was habitual to her, and therefore thought lightly of 1 by herself, and consequently (so she chose to assume) by others. And as to Stephen's being a witness of her be- haviour, if she thought at all of the effect upon him, it was only to attribute to him the same strong motive for securing Lord Harlaxton's departure as she felt herself; and there- fore the same self-condonation, if any such were needed, of the lover-like artifice she had so skilfully but disingenuously used ; not merely to relieve the assistant, as to whom she had spoken with true feeling, but to give Lord Harlaxton no alternative but that of executing the mission himself. But these few words and the accompanying manner that so favourably influenced the Earl had a precisely opposite effect upon Stephen. He had watched with critical interest all that passed; and the resulting influence was decisive. , All that he had previously feared, returned to him with tea- fold intensity of conviction, jealousy pouring oil On tho In- ward fire; and was luTTed. lip in bit attyint,:m self :

Incorrigible! I was riett. Coquetry in her very Wood ! This decides me! " And so, at the very moment Miss Vandeleur and Lord Harlaxton were exchanging a last look befcre he would pass from her sight, Stephen was giving the ptomised signal to cientleman Jack, who notwithstanding the long delay had kept steadily on the watch. He opened the window, and then op:-ned his handkerchief slowly out, which Gentleman Jack duly saw, and exulted in accordingly. Then Stephen walked away, took a chair in a corner, sat down, and began to write in a notebook. Lord liarlaxOn

now quite gone, Miss Vandeleur turned towards Stephen, her face bright and joyous, her air and atitude full of cone flding loving expectancy. Seeing how Stephen was engaged, and his back being towards her, she said to herself : " Writing ! Poetry, perhaps! And to me !" With airy, noiseless, dainty steps she drew near, and suddenly snatched the book from him, crying aloud, "I've got it !" In alarm and anger that must have been unmistakeable to Miss Van- deleur in any other and less pre-occupied mood, Stephen exclaimed, " Miss Vandeleur !" "Oh, you may pretend to be vexed,' but I am not going to be Miss Vandeleured out of my peep !" Stephen at once changed his manner, and said softly and anxionslv, "Let me then, as a favour, request you to give me back that book uneead." - " Is it poetry ?" demanded Miss Vandeleur. "I don't call it so," was the answer. "To a lady ?" " No," said Stephen. " Ab, traitor, yea evade me !" exclaimed Miss Vande- leur, returning to the charge, just when she seemed about to give way. "Is it on a lady ?" Yes," replied Stephen, in something like the tones of a criminal, wile knows hie answer may bring hie speedy exe- cution, but feels toastrained to giv; 'it, as the only chance of escapee by mollifying his judge. But the judge in question was inexorable, believing, no doubt, the poetry concerned her, and would be something very sweet and precious; and which Stkpben's caution as to committing himself after having had time for reflection made him so unwilling to consent to surrender ; so she promptly asked, " What lady ?" "I won't tell you!" was Stephen's evilly prompt reply. " And I'll answer no more questions tit, you have given me back my book." Determined not to be baffled, and beginning now to sus- pect there was more in the matter than she had been sup- posing, Miss Vandeleur said— " The Countess is close by. May I show it to her ?" " Cert vilely not!" "Now then for my ultimatum," said Miss Vandeleur. " I will give it beck if you will assure me on your honour as a genneman that what is written on that page—and she held it up for him to look at—has nothing whatever to do with me ? " " What I could answer is one thing, but whetter I ought to answer a qu3stien so forced on me is quite another thing." Moving swiftly and suddenly so-as to 7eave a table betwc en her and Stephen, she said— " Then I will read! " He moved threateningly towards her, still veiling his true feelings under a half-humourous manner, but she stopped him by saying— " One step nearer, and I scream for the Countess ! She's close by ! " Abondouin all further effort, Stephen turned away, saying—

may have cause to regret this; Miss Vandeleur! " Oh, I know," said that young lady recovering her f)y- ousness, as she recovered her c mtidenc4 that all was right, through Stephen yielding at last. "Oh, I know," she said again to .him. " Poets always make such a fuss when they think they have written any- thing particularly good. The world even must not know except on its knees, and prepared for worship. I tell you beforehand, I know I have a treat in store." Aed so slying, Miss Vandeleur began to read— " Fair Olwen bath such wondrous charms, 'Tis heaven to be within her arms; And she's--"

The sudden stop that then took place was a critical mo- ment for both parties. Stephen felt his eves irresistibly drawn to Miss Vandeleur's, though prepared to receive a dreadful shock in so doing. _ _

What hc had feared, however, and tried so earnestly to prevent—too late—were as nothing to the reality. Miss Vandeleur's face flushed to a theper, darker red than he had ever seen before in a human countenance and then changed to so deadly a white as filled Stephen with fear and remorse.

But it required only a few moments for her to recover her courage and self-possession, and deal with the insult which had pierced her to the very quick, in a manner Stephen was even yet little prepared for. rurnigg her eyes, which literally blazed with anger, full on Stephen, but speaking in low measured accents, that in- dicated the strength of leer self-command, in spite of the occasional tremor that would find way to Stephen's ear and heart ; while a forced smile, almost a laugh, broke over her face, she said,
"You think I have not the courage to finish as I began— and read your verses aloud. Listen:
"And she's -'' But stay! The poet-creator likes no doubt to study his creation as a whole.

And Stephen did listen; rapt in wonder, admiration, and bitter keen remorse for tho cruel anguish he had inflicted, while meaning only to satiate, and so relieve, his own resent- ment at her behavioar to Lord Harlaxton •, and at the same time satisfy himself by a burning record of the incident that he was justified in the immediate event to follow his de•P parture. In this state did he listen to the verges of his note book, every line thrilling from the voice of the speaker still more &eply through his heart and mind,

"Fair Olwen bath such wondrous charms, 'Tis heaven to be within her arms; And she's so charitably given, She wishes all mankind in heaven. "You have underlined the last few words. If I have failed to do them justice pardon me. Awl now there only remains to say, 'The fair Olwen thanks. yew " " clelieve me=---," murmured Stephen, in a voice of deep agitation. " What ! That you did not *mean me? I do! I will believe it if you say so. I may have been rash and foolish, and fearfully mistaken." o spake the unhappy girl—her hope ani love in an instant once more dominating her. Stephen half shut his eyes for a few 4ec9nds, as if to take the safer counsel with himself, but at last was constrained to ray— "l would lie if I could. I cannot."

What might have followed, had they both been left alone, neither was destined to know; for Lord Harlaxton now returned, and saw in both their faces, but more especially in Miss Vandeleues, signs of some deep offence. having
been given, which he naturally supposed Stephen alone could have given. _
"What does this mean ?" he demanded of Stephen, in fierce accents.
"I have nothing to say to you," retorted Stephen, calmly confronting him.

Miss Vandeleur now interposed, and addressing the Earl, said in tones of icy severity, "And as to me, these verses, called forth by my flagrant behaviour with you, may suffi- ciently speak." And therewith she gave him the notebook, still open at the page. He read them hurriedly, in a lo Ar voice, but distinct enough for both the hearers again to hear, what was now a kind of terrible punishment to both. When be had done, their effect upon him was shown in the epithet he launched at Stephen— " Scoundrel !"

"Brother !" answered Stephen, simply; but the tone and manner were such as to indicate a meaning for the word worse even than the one that had been applied to him. "But take comfort. You are both of a mind. My presence may be inconvenient. I withdraw !"
fie bowed low to Miss Vandeleui, who had turned away, and immediately left the saloon, and then the home of his ancestry, perhaps for ever.
"I hear the Countess's step!" said Miss Vandeleur. "Spare her! oh, spare her the knowledge of what has passed." "By all means. Let us withdraw for a minute or two to consider how to meet her.."

They had scarcely left the place before the Countess entered ; her face, step, and gestures all betokening the joy- ful expectation that possessed her, and which her eager thoughts shaped in some such fashion as this "Allis ready. He has won her. They love me—will sympathise with the story I must now tell—will be foremost in proposing of themselves the sacrifice necessary. I shall lie down to-night freed from the past—seciire for the future! And how grateful, heaven alone will know !" At one and the same moment Lord Harlaxton returned with Miss Vandeleur, and Richards, the steward, came in from the hall to say,— "This card, my lady, has just been left at the door for you by a shabby, strange-looking man, in a dress suit." As the Countess received the card her face showed that she was conscious she was about to read what she felt must be for her a sentence of death. The card ran "Dearest mother,— _

• "All is settled against me as regards the lady. Igo now to begin a new career. Give me in thought the blessing I could not ask for is words. I will deserve it if I can. Farewell. May heaven preserve, and tenderly regard you.

The Countess would have fallen prostrate on the floor, as she reached the last words, but that Miss Vandeleur and the Earl ha el been carefully watching, and so caught and placed her in a chair, senseless; while Miss Vandeleur, who knelt at her feet, in bitterest distress, alternately chafed and kissed her hands—and Lord Harlaxton leaned over both with looks of the deepest sympathy. CHAPTER XXY.—THE DEPARTURE. Stilling,as well as he could the emotion he felt at:quitting his home to go forth into the world, penniless or nearly so, to seek his fortune, while resigning every advantage that birth, friends, inatrnce ha q given him as aide, Stephen ot'.'t,ile so swiftly—fiercely along through one back street after another, that Gentleman Jack with the portmanteau could scarcely keep up with him. He looked indeed not merely as though he were seeking his fortune' but meant to take her by the throat when found, and compel her to come to terms. The route chosen enabled him to escape notice of any acquaintance, and 80 he reached an inn in the snburbs, where he obtained a private room. _ _

"Thanks Jack for this service," he said, the moment the portmanteau was deposited on the table. "I can't ask you to sit down and refresh yourself, but there's half-a-crown to get what you want elsewhere. Here we part. I know not yet what I shall do, but a speedy decision is forced on me. And that requires careful thinking out. So good bye !"
Ife bekiout his band to Gentleman Jack, who did not, however, take it, though he took the money from it, say- ing-7_

You want, I see, to keep your movements unknown !" "From my family, yes ; for a time." "Well, then, won't it be better to let ins stay till you have decided on your course, so that I may again be your luggage bearer instead of a stranger ?" Stephen hesitated for a single moment, then said, with sharp decision— "No, we part hers!" " When to meet again ?" _ _

" Ah, who shall say! Since I cannot foresee my own course, how am I likely to guess at yours ?" " Well, I was in bops that—" began Gentleman Jack, but Stephen interrupted him hastily. "All I can say that you will care to hear is to repeat my promise to aid you in some decent say of life, if fortune ever gives me the means. My prospects, however, at pre- sent are so blank, that it is at once ludicrous and painful my talking of anything of the kind." 'Seeing Gentleman Jack still hesitated, while looking at him with a pleading face, he added, " Now. Jack, let us part in good feeling. Minutes even are precious. I cannot and will not be delayed—there Again he held out his hand, and this time it was Wien and very warmly pressed. Then, with something like a tear, which gentleman Jack managed to squeeze into his cye, they geparatEd—to that w9rtily'fs great disgust.
CHAPTER XXVI. - GENTLEMAN JACK ACHIEVES A GREAT STROKE, IN WHICH MANY WOULD LIKE TO IMI- TATE HIM.

Some little time before Stephen's departure. CiettaVnan Jack had nude much use of his opportunities in hovering about Harlaxton House as to get familiar with two or three of the servant& and hangers-on. He thus picked up bit by- bit gossip about the fatnily, which meant nothing in par- ticular to the retailers, but a great deal to Gentleman Jack. • For it mast must now be tld that his incessant attempts to revive the old friendship with Stephen were not solely owing to his poverty And deep rate plight, but to a belief that had long been growing in his mind, that there was a secret atTectlng the family which possibly might have some special relation to Stephen, and at all events might be worth finding out.

Stephen himself, in unguarded mocds of companionship, had sill things which first inspired the ides; while, like the gossipers afo-esaid, be had evidently drawn no such conclu,ion in his own thoughts. The difference in character between the two brothers— their unbrothet ly attitude towards each other; the Countess's long solitude, and something mysterious in her reserve— these, and similar facts, were caught up and treasured by Gentleman Jack, as matters to be borne in mind, and looked info if the chance came.
Had not the time come, he asked himself, when Sfephen gave him the first intjmation that he was,t!!!nlcing of leav- ing home?
Such a departure, othPrwiss unmeaning and idiotic, might be only one step of Stephen's progress towards a solution of the secret.
If he could then stick to him, he would soon find it out, or find he was mi2talten.

But if Stephen drove him away! How then could he keep open any channel of communicition—any means fora future meeting. Hence arose once more the idea of a confederate inside the walls of Harlaxton House; and who could that possibly be but his wife? Surely, one would think, the most unlikely person in the world, after their previous meet- ing, and agreement to treat each other as strangers; an arrangement which circumstances had not yet given Gentleman Jack an opportunity to break, much to his annoyance.

But having no sort of respect for the sex, and it may be said for him in excuse that he had known only too many individual examples of its worse members, and accustomed to think only of what he wanted from women, and bow easiest to get it, be put aside all her previous demonstra- tions of intense adverse feeling, and determined—what? Why to make love for the second time to his wife—even under the most hostile and one would think depressing of condiiions.
But Gentleman Jack was delighted with the fun and con- flict of the idea—and resolved to lose no time in carrying it out, if he could.

He already bad observ2d signs that told him Mrs. Davis was in high favour with the Countess. What then more natural than that the latter in unguarded moments would dr(--p occasionally a few words, which, collected and put to- gether, and then read by so skilful an expounder of social hier•glyphics as be was, would tell him all he ?ranted to know: or at least indicate the path through which to go in search for the final truth.

Not daring to venture upon any attempt to see and speak to her in Harlaxton House, bow was he to make the pro- posed experiment? He could discover but one chance—to watch her going out, and whither she went, and then act as he should see best.
He then found that when she did leave the house it was always to call on her former landlady, who had been very kind to her.

This was annoying. His experiences in society as an un- welcome caller warned him that Mrs. Davis after their for- mer meeting would in all probability have taken precau- tions against any further visits from him there. So he determined to waylay her, and the opportunity came at last.

He had chosen a spot that might well be called a lover's seat—a bench under a spreading tree beside Park Lane. There he had once seen her stop to rest and muse; and there should be the scene of his triumph! It was the dull London season for the fashionable world; lo%t trees, grass, and flowers were in thuir fullest glory, as if suggesting they were only the happler to be left alone. Consequently few were the passers by, to hear or interrupt the meditated interview.

There she met him, ac he emerged from behind a tree. He took off his hat, and immediately addressing her said, " Permit me to ask, since we have so accidentally met, if you are satisfied with my part sf the compact " Yes," :,he said simply—end said no more, determined notao be drawn into prolonged talk. "That at least is a comfort—l wish Mary you knew how great a one ! and how hard I have found it, for quite other reasons than you may attribute to me, to be silent while I hear everybody speaking so well of you, and I can't but think to myself,—'Ab, if they would and could so speak of me to her!' 'I hen when I do once now and then calch a glimpse of you, I have to say to myself how content and happy she looks, while I am.so solitary and miserable; and all the time I can but see how she is recovering all lizr

former good looks—beanty I ought to say, but I wish ri express myself mildly, and then my hopes, which I not help Mary for the life of me, would die out in doll and regret that I didn't manage matters differently' would if I had another chance, but which I.know#All/*" will dot give me!" 51 To say that Mrs. Davis could not listen to this, without some touch of inner feeling, carrying her hack to the corr. happy but very brief period of courtship, is merely to iDdr cate she was like most women tender-hearted at the And, therefore, somewhat impressed, not alone by his but by the look, gesture, and demeanour that accomPael harmonised with, and supported the words. But she knew him too well to relax her caution, 6d while she lingered, perhaps unconsciously, to hear if he he anything more to say; then rose, and wished him, "Good morning." a 1° He saw and seized his advantage, and endeayoure press it home, while managing to make her continue " walk, and let him move by her side. "I did not intend, Mary, to have said what I have °lb; nor to have let you seen my true feeling and self-reproseo but I forgot myself while gazing on you. But thereLBiitig end of that matter. And now I want to tell you some"' el that if you are a true woman mu2t interest you. Threu're a number of little things, I have been led to suspect thipej is some great secret in the Harlaxton family in vihiohlros friend Stephen is interested, which is kept from him. will ask, what does that matter to me? In a selfish sel, does not matter • but Stephen has been very kirLd r the new clothes I wear could net have been bought Dote' him, and bad as I may be, and as I begin to fear / li been to you, I do want to show him the worth of the saying, One good turn +deserves another.' div.head: POLITICAL GAMBLING.
div.p: POLITICAL GAMBLING.

Sir,—Under the above heading I wish to say a few words respecting the machinery that now moves the whole political world—Parliamentary and municipal. Unless great care is taken this ponderous Juggernaut is likely to crash us all to deg beneath its unrelentless wheels. Time was when the ordinary householder had little or nothing to do with politics. To-day, the whole of the duties comprehended in the word " citizenship " fall equally on the shoulders of the poor as on those of the rich. The most important question we can ask ourselves is, "Are we all alike carrying out our political duties honestly ?" He would be a bold man who answered this question in the affirmative. Forty years ago men banded themselves together and formed leagues for the purpose of gaining their political rights. To-day it is necessary t peopie eheuld be taught how- to use thoso ;:o; rights. Education and organisatioft ire terms representing means to success. By the Liberal party, are they really so? Not by any means, if by success we mean one more step towards national comfort and happi- ness. A victory gained by imposing upon ignorance is nO victory. We may organize and reduce ourselves mentally to be mere puppets in the hands of those skilful enough to know how to use us. But we may also so harmonise organization with education that no Centurian amongst us would be'able to say to one, " Go, and he goeth ;" and to another, "Come and he cometh." In the local councils of the party, wise advice based upon lengthy experience may I be given, nay, is given and received by that sturdy indepen- dence of spirit and utterance that always betokens a healthy body. More than this, we look to our representatives in the imperial and local parliaments to assert and practice that independence of action which is BO peculiar a feature in the Liberal politician. Bur, sir, I wish this to be understood: Broadly speaking, the people are divided into two parties—Liberals and Tories —and in each party (more especially is this the case with the latter) only a very few can claim to be politicians. Yet when the day of election comes every one must go to the poll. It !netters not however limited his knowledge may be, what amount of good the country has derived from Liberal or Conservative Governments, or in municipal matters which is• the best administrative townsman, the voter must go and vote with his party. Now, what is this state of things tending to? This: our so-called politicians are losing political honesty. Would-be M.P.'s would-be town councillors, are looked upon as so many sponges to be sacked thoroughly dry ere they get tired of representing a selfish people. The member of Parliament Is expected to preside at every church ani chapel meeting, and above all things to centribute largely; attend every bazaar, and in- vest his money in things he does not want. In fact, he must be all things to all men; and if he be a Tory, every sottish and scheming hos'elry, every court and alley, pours forth all eorts of femiliar, creeping, seedy things in seeeo'a of opportunities. " They Who trust to principle at() newhere at an election corr pared with those who trust to prejudice." When once the gentleman is elected he goes to Parliament, saying he represents a free and enlightened constituency," knowing at the same time that their only freedom is to lig'aen his pockets. In municipal matters this detestable and corroding want of principle is eating out all honour and all manliness. Nay, the more ignorant a man is, the more despotic does he become. To be able to judge as to the qualities of two candidates is something gained. With this man argument may gain something; but with the man who holds his hands out, waiting to have the palm tickled, what can you do? He will take your money, and hold him- self open for the next bid. No worse, mind you, than the handsome lady or gentleman who 'does the fleecing in the bazaar. Take the latest election that Warrington has been disgraced by. I should think that fully one-half of the voters expected to receive, and did receive, beer, pies, or cigars after voting. Nearly every man doing work on that day expected to be paid. Nearly every ward committee man looked upon the work done as a personal favour to the candidate, and as such ought to receive his share of the spoil. Nay, the candidates themselves, by their actions, lent serengtka to this view. Cabs and 'buses were engaged and placed at the service of the "free and independent voter," and off he was hurried to the polling booth. Every man is on the look-out for someone with in- fluence, seeking to make his vote a means of bettering his worldly position. Each and everyone is making politics subservient to his ambitious designs. At the time when Mr. Disraeli was last returned with a triumphant majority "ladies of quality" were brought down and peradectround the city of Norwich like show-women. Mr. Huddlestone won his seat by these arts. Mr. H. K. Spark, of Darlington, went to the poll without canvassing, and he lost the seat. From this it appears that the people are willing to be gulled, and unwilling to in ike the smallest sacrifice; and so long as this state of things exists we cannot hope for a high political tone he permeate the people. There is scarcely a friendly society that does not seek to I swell its funds by appeals to the sitting member. In the lodge room bitter personal feeling, engendered by political differences, are now making "friendship, love, and truth" mere bye-words and things of the past. Chaos reigns. I have said that in the pest leagues were formed for certain objects. No need to form them now. Clubs in sufficient numbers exist for every purpose. Can these clubs be used for political educational purposes? To meet night after night to play cards and billiards will leave us in the chaotic state I have described. If the people are to be roused to a full sense of the duties, our leaders must refuse to engage vehicles. lam speaking now to Whig and Tory alike. To the Liberal, reform in our municipal elections means the attainment of great possibilities. To the Tory it means loss of privilege, loss of caste; it means, in short, equality, and that they never liked. The Tory claims to be the patriot, par excellence; if tkis be so, let him join hand with the Liberal and refuse te countenance the spending of money, and devise means whereby every election in the town shall be carried out by joint committees, these only te be required for legal purposes. Let the clubs I have referred to arrange for political lectures free, and make strenuous endeavours to get the people there to listen. If the Tories think that the ballot is not required at all elections, that canvassing outr,ht not to be done away with, or that the Corrupt Practices Bill is not required in municipal matters, let them bring lectuiers out to prove their argumeet, and I have no doubt the Liberals will not be behindliand. Keep this in mind. An educated youth is growing up to manhood, and his require- ments will be of a higher order than those that obtain amongst us to-day. H. W. Warringtou, October, 1883.

div.p: A COLUtEu LION.

Sir,—l write to correct a statement which appeared in your paper of Saturday, the oth inst., giving an account of the Lymm Local Board meeting of the 4th inst. Under the headino•b-of " Looking up a gas meter," my name is given as having locked up my meter, and thereby having given the gas manager occasion tm pay five futile visits to take a regis- ter of the index. 'foie statement is alto_zether incorrect. I have never locked up my gavmeter, and your reportir has made a mistake in the name. As a member of the Gas Committee of the Lynam Local Board, I therefore ask you to give due prominence to this letter in your next issue, as this statement, as gone forth, is liable to render my position both false and ridiculous.—l am, sir, yours faithfully. ARTHUR W. CALLINDER. liaslemere, Lymtr,Oct. 10, 1883. •

Sir,—! shall be glad if soma of your numerous readers can inform me why the Water compiny are still charging on the #ros-s rental instead of the assessed value? Some time ago I understood that the legality of charging on the former had been decided against them. Yesterday, however, I received my account for the current half -year and it still bears the red clause, "Pending a final decision in the courts, &c., &c. say from 24t,hJitne, 1881." div.head: BOWLERS TEA PARTY AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: BOWLERS TEA PARTY AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

The bowling season at tke Warrington Liberal Club was brought to a conclusion on Saturday by a tea party which took place in the reading-room of the club. It was presided over by the member for the borough, J. G. McMinnies, Esq., and the vice-chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Morris, F.G.S. Between 30 and 40 gentlemen were present, amongst them being Mr. Councillor Monks, J.P., Dr. Gornall, Mr. H. Roberts (Liberal agent), and Messrs. S. Kenyon, S. Barlow, T. Fairclongh, &c. After tea the Chairman proposed "The health of Her Majesty," and subsequently "The health of the Prince and Princess of Wales and the rest of the Royal Family," accompanying each toast with a few felicitous and appropriate observations. The toasts were Tery cordially re:ponded to. "The health of the Prize-winners, and success to them," was next given by the Chairman, who announced that the chief prize-winners were Messrs. Thomas Critchley, Thomas Bridge, and S. Kenyon, whom he warmly congratulated on their success. I Musical nours greeted this toast, which was responded to by M-ssrs. Bridge, Critchley, and Kenyon respectively. Mr. S. Barlow subsequently addressed the company, and spoke hopefully of the success of the club and the position ,of the Liberal party in Warrington. During the course of the , evening Mr. J. Shaw Green and Mr. Thomas Hall put in an appea,ance, and were warmly received. "The health of the former gentleman " was proposed by the Chairman in very complimentary language. The toast was drunk with great enthusiasm, and Mr. Green feelingly acknowledged the compliment. He concluded his r.nnarks by proposing the "health of Mr. Hall," to which the latter gentleman suitably responded. The conviviality of the gathering was well sustained by songs either hurnourous or sentimental from Messrs. Thomas Fairciongh, C. C.ssidy, H. Roberts, and T. Bridge. The prizes were awarded as follows :—lst prize, handssme tea service, Mr. Bridge; 2ad, half-a-dozen table knives and forks, carving knife, &a., Mr. Critchley ; 3rd, ; a copper kettle, Mr. Kenyon; and 4th, a plaster bust of Mr. Gladst.ne, Mr. Gilbert. Six other prizes were dis- tributed to successful bowlers.

The DEPUTY CLERK read the following letter which had been received from the Clerk of the Peace in reference to the proposed bridge over Cogshall Brook : Clerk of the Peace's Office. Chester, 30`41 August, 1883.— Dear Sir,—Referring to your letter of the 19th ultimo. on the subject of a proposed bridge across Cogshall Brook, I beg to refer you to the Highway and Loemnotives (Amerriment) Act, 1878, by the 22nd section of which it is provided that the county authority (i e • the justices in quarter sessions) may make such contribution as it sees fit out of the coon .y rates towards the cost of any bridge to be thereafter erected after the same has been certified in accordance with the provisions ' of section 5 of the statute 43, George 111., c. 5, as a proper bridge to be maintained by the inhabitants of the county, so ; always that such contribution shall not exceed one-half the ; cos:, of erecting such bridge. The provisions of the Act of 43 Ge rge 111 , to which the above section of the Act of 1878 reft ;s, provide that bridges erected by individuals, or private pc-8 ens, or bodies corporate. must, if they are to besorne county bridges, be built in a substantial and corn. m; dions manner unoer the direction, or to the satisfaction of the eiunty surveyor or other person appointed by the justices in quarter sessions assembled. No applicati al has been made to the county authority under the 22nd section of the Act of 1878 fur a contribution towards the cost of Ziec,ing a new bridge, and it appears to me to be very doubtful whether the county authority can entertain an application for a con- tribution until a bridge has been erected and certified by the county surveyor, and the a-rt ual cost ascerta'ned. The matter could be brought before the con-t by some of the ex-efficio members of your Highway Board, giving notice of motion at the quarter sessions for a grant of a contribution. A motion for a grant fox more than one half the met of building the bridge could not be entertained. and I think it very doubtful whether a motion for the grant of a contribution is not premature. If I can give you any further information I shall be happy to do so.—l am, yours faith ully, THOMAS ROBERTS, ceputy clerk of the peace for Oheshlre.—ffenry Linaker, Esq., clerk to the Daresbury Highway Board, Frodsham. After some consideration of the above letter it was decided to defer the matter to the neat meeting.—There was no other business of public interest.

ENTERTAINMENT AT EARLESTOWN.—The first of a series of public entertainments under the auspices of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Lodge Room, Bridge-street, Earlestown, on Saturday evening last. There was a very good attendance, and Bro. A. Allison pre- sided. An enjoyable selection of songs, recitations, and readings were excellently given, a very pleasant evening being spent. An addition was made in 1867, and by doing something of the kind now the proposed large expenditure might be saved. —Mr. GILLESPIE was of opinion that the Local Government Board would not approve of the extension of a burial ground in the centre of a town, even if Mr. Legh would let them have the land.—Mr. EMMETT said the question raised by Mr. Glover was well worth considering. He was in favour of the suggestion of Mr. Glover, and did not see why the ratepayers should be saddled with the extra rate if they tuld stave it off by the extension of St. Peter's church- yard.—Mr. PARDEY asked why St. Peter's should be com- pelled to provide burial accommodation for everyone in the district, irrespective of sect or class.—Mr. EmetErr said he did not say or mean that.—Mr. PARDEY thought that was the meaning to be attached to his words. As one of the trustees of Newton Congregational Chapel, was Mr. Glover prepared to throw open their yard and burial ground to all the par- iehioners irrespective of sect P—Mr. GLOVER said he was not one of the trustees, and he could not therefore say anything a'rout it.—Mr. PARDEY: We have had the Rev. It would be no hardship for St Peter's to provide their own ground, and he believed with Mr. Emmett it would p tv them to do SI —Mr. PARDEY: The Congregationalists having provided their own ground can do whet they like with it, and now they want St. Peter's to provide and say it shall not be their own.—Mr. Eareterre said he did not say anything of the kind. —The CHAIRMAN said they, as Commissioners, had to provide a public burial ground where everybody •uld be buried.—Mr. FORSTER must be a hardsh7p to saddle the whole of the ratepayers with a rate when most of the bodies are provided with a burial ground.—Mr. PARDEY : They are net. Look at the Wesleyans, the Baptists, and others—they have not a yard of ground.—Mr. GILLESPIE was sorry to see it Was being mide a sectarian question, which it was not.
