Ile would be glad to see his way to meet the views which had been expressed, but there was a difficulty in the way. They were only wasting time; and before long, if they did not mind the question would become a very serious one. Supposing St. Peter's churchyard was extended so as to last. 10 or 12 years longer, what about the Wargrave ground, which, according to Dr. Hoffman, would be full in two or three years ? He believed it was only proper and right for the township generally that the Commissioners should look to a public cemetery being provided.—Mr. PARDEY said he would again move that application be made for sanction to borrow £7,000 for cemetery purposes, and that Mianeittee be appointed to consider the proposed items of expenditure. —Mr. GILLESPIE had great pleasure in seconding the motion. —The resolution was carried, and Messrs. Gooch, Gillespie, Glover, Pardey, and Emmett were appointed a sub-commit- tee to examine the details. Tliis was the only business of interest.
EARLESTOWN NEWS.

AN EARLESTOWN MAN IN TROUBLE AT SALFORD.—At the Salford Boroueh Court, on Monday, before the stipen- diary (Mr. J. Makinson), Patrick Cain, labourer, Collins Green, Earlestown, was brought up, in custody, charged with being drunk and travelling on the London and North- Western Railway from Liverpool to Ordsal-lane station without a ticket.—A ticket-collector at Ordsal-lane said that on the arrival of the seven o'clock train from Lime-street at Ordsal-lane. on Saturday night, he found the prisoner in a third-class compartment drunk. On being roused it was found that he had neither ticket nor money, and was so drunk that he could give no account of himself.—Prisoner now said he came from Burtonwood, Collins Green, near Earlestown, and did not know why he got into the train.— He was fined 20s_., or 14 days' imprisonment. A RUNAWAY HORSE AT NEWTON: SCATTERING LOAVES OF BREAD ALONG THE STREET.—A singular and alarming accident occurred in High-street, Newton, about three o'clock on Monday afternoon. A young man in the employ of Mr. P. Thompson, grocer, ikc., Bridge-street, Earlestown, Was in charge of a horse and trap, the latter filled with new- baked loaves of bread, which were being delivered at the houses of customers of Mr. Thompson. The horse was stopped in the narrow road leading to Colonel McCorquo- ' dale's residence, near St. Peter's Church, and while the per- son in charge was at a house near, the animal took fright and dashed down the road at a great speed. The trap came in contact with one of the iron guards of the trees planted along the footpaths, and created some commotion. The iron guard was much twisted, bent, and otherwise damaged, and but for the tree would have been knocked over. The force of the collision nearly upset the trap, and 30 or 40 loaves of bread, with a pair of scales, weights, ekd , were in- discrisinately scattered and thrown about the street in a:I directions for a distance of nearly 100 yards. The anima was brought to a standstill in High-street, fortunately, befere I any person had been injured. THE EARLESTOWN GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION--Tbe removal of Mr. E. J. Weaver, town missionary, from Earle-s. town by the committee of the Manchester City Missicn (in! connection with which Mr. Weaver has laboured with con- siderable success for some years past) has given rise to many expressions of regret on the part of the temperance community. One of Mr. Weaver's numerous works was the . management of the Earlestown Blue Ribbon and Gospel Temperance Movement, and his departure caused a cempul- , sory closing of the familiar wooden structure in Leigh-street, known as the Mission Tent. The friends of the temperance cause, however, were not willing to allow the Gospel Temperance Movement to ' die out, an! accordingly arrangements were made by which the Co-operative Hall was secured for services on the Sunday, and for an entertainment daring the week. The opening services were held on Sunday last, when there was a large attendance at each of the meetings. Excellent sermons were preached by Mr. Morris Jones, of Liverpool. On the following Tuesday evening the first public meeting and entertainment was held, under the presidency of Mr. John Clarke. The attendance was large, and such as to I encourage those who have taken in hand so good and com- mendable a move Went. Several songs and recitations were effectively given; Mr. Birks and Master Tripp rendering good service with their stringed instruments. At the close , of the meeting a temporary committee was appointed to see ' about the continuance of the services and meetings. RUPTURING A BLOOD VESSEL: PAINFUL DEATH AT ; Nesyroer.—A sad and painfully sudden death eceurred at I Newton, on Monday evening last. It seems that Miss Mary Winstanley. 29 years of age, residing at the house of her brother in High-street, has been suffering from consumption for the last two years; and for two months-she was attended by Dr. Watlein. About six o'clock on Monday night she was put to bed by her eldest sisters at which time she ap- peared in her usual state of health, and did not complain of anything wrong. At half-past seven the sister left the house. Miss Mary being the only occupant at that time. When she returned about nine o'clock, she entered the lobby and saw some object I lying at the foot of the stairs' which she imagined was .a white dog. She thereupon called the attention of Miss Mary Jane Johnson, of Newton, who was passing, and said that a white dog was in the lobby which she wanted putting out. Miss Johnson procared a light, and proceeding along the lobby discovered the body of Miss Mary Winstanley lying at the bottom of the stairs. Without acquainting the de- ceased's sister she ran for her father, named .John Johnson, who went to the house. When Mr. Johnson saw it was the body of Miss Mary Winstanley Dr. Watkins was immedi- ately sent for, but the boly was quite cold, and the young woman had evicjently been dead about .14 hour. tier mouth was full of blood, and a pool of blood was at the bottom of the stairs, while there was also a quantity of blood on the stairs, on the bedroom floor, and on the bed itself. It is supposed that the poor woman ruptured a blood vessel, and on finding that she had thus mortally in- jured herself she came downstairs to look for her sister or secure other held. On re whiner the bottom she appears to have fallen to the floor and gradually expired from the loss of blood On examlning the body Dr. Welkin gave a cer- tificate that the probable cause of death was sud:en and tg acute hemorrhage from the lungs.—An quest on the body was held at the Blue Lon Inn, Newton, on Wednesday afternoon, before Mr. Rewbottorra, deputy-coroner, and the jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical certificate.

div.head: FXAMINPT, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1883.
div.p: THE FXAMINPT, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 13, 1883.

MR. McMINNIES, MP., ON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETIES. The inaugural sleeting of the resuscitated Wycliffe Mutual Improvement Society took place on Monday even- ing, when a conversazione was held in Wycliffe school. There was a very good attendance, and amongst those pre- sent were Mr. J. G. McMinnies, 51. P., the Rev. J. Yonge, Mr. W. Wallington, Mr. John Harrison, and others. During the evening Mr. N. Greening and Mr. F. W. Monks exhibi- ted several powerful binocular and other microscopes, Mr. 11. Bond exhibited a "compound pendulum," and there- with traced upon paper some remarked figures resulting from two vibrations and and a rotating table. Mr. Rnddock perfcrmed a series of interesting and striking chemical ex- periments, which wers,watched with great attention. Mucn merriment was caused amongst the company by the galvanic coil and battery in charge of Mr. Rathbone. Refreshments were also provided, and with inspecting the above-mentioned objects, en eaging in pleasant conversation, anti listening to a well-arranged and capitally executed programme, an enjoy- •able evening was spent. After a pianoforte duet by Meesrs. T. R. Ferl and F. Gleave, „ The Rev. J. Thema said he was sure they were all glad to see Mr. McMinnies present, and he was sure they would not only give him a patient listening but a very hearty reception. (Applause). The enemies then rose and said: Ladies and gentle- men, in reference to what Mr. Yonge has said just now I can Assure you that your patience at all events will not be very much exhausted in giving me a patient listening, for I only intend to say a very few words. I suppose I need not tell you that in inaugurating this mutual improvement society we Are re Illy revie-ing something that existed some years age—(hear, hear)—and I believe it existed with tolerable SLICCZ3. It gave way, however, to what was called the Paliaenentary Debating Society,", which had greater attrac'ione:than were offered in connection with this society as it then existed. But the Parliamentary Society itself died troll cams internal disorder which I cannot quite ex- plain to.you. (laughter.) However, it was quite fatal to it, and we have what is really a resurrection to-night of a former society, and considering that it has no competitor in the town I suppose we may with very considerable hope expect that it will have a long and prosperous life. (Hear, hear.) My experience of muthial improvement societies, and discussion classes, and debating clebs, is that they have a very short life but that they are always coming to life again. (Laughter.) And that seems to be the case with our mutual improvement society to-night—(laughter); and I dare say that you will not expect me to-night to be quite and altogether original in any remarks I may have to make. I remember opening a mutual improvement society like this, or discussion club, I think it was called, some time ago, and I commenced by a quotation from Lord Bacon to the effect that "reading maketh a full man, writing an exact man, and conference," or discussion as we should call it now, `ta ready man." Now it appears to me that these mutual improvement societies do all that Lord Bacon expresses. Ido not see how you can prepare yourselves for taking part in a mutual im- provement society without reading up the subjects that you may have to discuss, and very likely speak about; and if you believe that you have to discuss and speak about them afterwards the probability is that you will read with a great deal more care than you otherwise would do. (Hear, hear.) My opinion is that the fault of our class—the fault of the middle class—the great besetting evil of the middle class, is careless reading. (Hear, hear.) We have our time and our minds so much occupied by things and by studies that are not of them- selves educational that we really have to read books in a way that perhaps does not do those books and our own in- tellect justice. We are almost compelled to reed cursorily, and not in a way that is likely to impress the subjects ahaut which we read upon our minds. Well now the ad- vantage of these mutual imptevement societies is that we ehall read, I think, with some care; and what we call care- less reading will be in some degree remedied. By reading we shall be fuller men. Then I have a strong opinion myself that it is always a good thing to write down as soon as you can—as soon as may be—the thoughts that pass through your minds. In reference to this matter what I said about reading also applies. I think there is a great deal of thought that is de- sultory—our minds are disorganised—we don't really think carefully; and my own opinion is that if we think more with a pen in our hands we shall think with very much greater effect. (Hear, hear.) So that in reference to that also writing might nnke us exact men. The conference, or what we should call discus- sion, that takes place in these mutual improvement socie- ties is, I think, very likely to make us ready men. It is a good thing that a man should be able to express himself with tolerable freedom and fluency. I do net see what is the use of a man having a great deal of information in his head if he cart only get it out in a stuttering manner that is very irritating and tantalising to his hearers, (Hear, hear.) It is a good thing that we should be able to express ourselves at any rate with tolerable fluency, and give out to others what we have in ourselves. I have known men who have failed in life entirely because they could net speak good English, and did not know how tteconduct themselves well in company. I think it is a very good thing indeed that young people should be able to express all that they know, and express it in a manner that is likely to be acceptable to those that they bad prepared to speak to. So that con- ference or discussion may make us ready men, and so may make us better men of the world. T:.ere is another advan- tage in these discussion classes; it is that they stimulate men to industry. My own opinion is, that the great fault of in inkind—one great fault of mankind—is intellectual idleness. There is hardly any kno.ving what can be accom- plished, by a man of even ordinary ability, by intellectual industry and energy. I daresay, if time would allow, I could show you, by many examples, that a great deal of what has been done by eminent men in this world has been done not in consequence of what we call the possession of genius, but in consequence of ordinary endowments indus- triously and perseveringly employed in a direction con- stantly aimed at. (Hear, hear.) Now, there have been great men in the world who have been endowed with what we call genius, but, in 99 eases out of 100, my idea is, that what has been effected by eminent and superior men has been effected in consequence of the culti- vation of their intellects by industryaenergy, and perse- verance.. (Applause.) There is another consideration that affects men very much, and may perh tits hereafter affect ether people. I think there is one modern circumstance 'Which is likely to make these mutual improvement classes gf great advantage, and it is the establishment of elementary Sclucation to the extent that we have establishea it in this sountry. (Hear, hear.) I suppose that nobody will gain- say that up to 1870 W•e, the British people, were perhaps the worst educated people in Europe. But a great change has taken place. Since the passing of that most beneficent ' Act in 1870, elementary education •in this country has in- creased wonderfully. I lave not the statistics but I think I should not be stating anything that is inaccurate if I were to say that there is sometbjnc like twice as much elementary education now as there was -13 years ago at any rate. do know this that the cost of the elementary education in this countrr at the present time .amounts to something like £e1,000,000 a year. I think it is not at all unlikely that befehe very long we shall find people saying that the reaction from entire neglect of educa- tion prior to 1870 is too great—eteat the pendulum ha 3 swung backwards too far, and tt let we really are now giving education to the children under 13 or 14 which is perhaps more than .they can ree, in after they leave school. Every boy and girl has now ti e opportunity of re- ceiving an education better in every eway than 99 out of 100 of the people who have made Lancasa hire and Yorkshire what they are received when we were yonn, For my own part I am not ashamed to say that when I a, ttead the annual examination at my schools at Farrington I am. n wonderfully surprised at the amount of information that the children have received, and I have been bound to adult 't to myself that I should certainly be plucked in the 4th a standard— (laughter)—as for presenting myself in the ath or oth it would be utterly impossible. jaaughter and applause. nc w, the question I am seriously consis er—F° and which I think is worth while considering by everys is whether the amount of education and information nei\ to young people up to the time they are 13 or 14 is retain 14 afterwards. My own experience is that it is not. (Hea't hear.) I believe in my own village of Farrington the young ' men of 20 years of age know less than they did when they- were 13. If that is so every instrumentality that has a ten- dency to foster and increase the educ Won that young people receive at 13 and 14 is of the utmost importance—(hear, hear)—and it strikes use that these mutual improvement classes are likely to have that effect. Now there is just one other thought I should like to mention. One reason at tits present time why young men—l wish I could say young women, but the fact of the matter is I do not know what young women have to say on any matter except " yes " or "no" (laughter)—but what I should like to say is this, there is one reason at the present time why yonng men should endeavour to ascertain for themselves what is true in reference to various ques- tions that affect us in this world moral, intellectual, and religious—and it is this : I think that every day the authority of newspapers, to which we have been in the habit of looking as our best possible public in- structors, is less than it was. (Hear, bear.) Ido not mean to say that there is any deterioration in the leading articles up to the present time, but I do say this that there is a great deterioration in newspapers in reference to what tiler assert and publish as facts every day. (Hear, hear.) My experience of newspapers is this, that whereas years ago no respectable editor or manager of a newspaper would pevelish a fact or make a statement without -verifying it, in the present day such is the eagerness to give news to the public that they publish anything which comes to their knowledge whether it is true or not. I supoose it will be in the know- ledge of readers of newspapers that a large portion of the columns of the newspapers you see every day are taken up with contradictions of something that they have meld one or two days before. (Laughter.) Well, in reference to matters of fact perhaps that is not of Very great importance, but whenever this disregard of truth comes into the leading articles of the newspapers, then as public instructors their glory is gone and their authority is entirely worthless. (Applause.) Well. now, ladies and gentlemen, coming to the meeting to-night we

have a vo.ry admirable programme w'iich we shall go through, and I hope that we shall all believe when we leave here that it has been good for us to be here, and that we have spent a very pleasant evening. I have before me the Frogramme of the first part of t'le season, and I find that you will have various papers and lectures read. You will have, including to-night, three social gatherings, and up to the end of December it seems to me that they have provided for you—those who had had the arrangement of these matters—a programme that for three months will be exceedingly interesting and exeedinoly instructive. As regards to-night I hope that we shall enjoy ourselves very much. There is no doubt at all that we shall do so, and I think that we may with reasonable expectation hope that the meeting to-night, of itself a great success, will be the forerunner of a prosperous career of our revived mutual im- provement society. (Applause.) The Rev. J. YONGE read a letter from Mr. Z. Armitage expressing his regret at being kept away,from theNgathering and his good wishes for the successful career of the resus- citated society. (Applause.) The rev, gentleman also apologised for the absence of Mr. Dignum, who was attend- ing the Congregational Union meetings at Sheffield. An interesting musical programme W 29 then performed, and attentively listened ho. Mrs. Pearson sang sweetly and with feeling M. Welling's sweet song, "Golden love." Later on another fair aspirant to musical la,mours—Miss Nellie Roberts—favoured the audience with "Derby and Joan," which suffered chiefly, or rather only, from a little nervousness on the part cf the singer. Mr. Pearson played a violin solo with dash and spirit. The son", "When stormy winds do blow," by Mr. W. Wallington, won a well- merited encore. To this he responded with the "Vicar of Bray," in which, however. he would have done well to have confined himself to a couple of the verses of this somewhat monotonous song. Mr. Furness's recitation, "Marian Grey and Christopher Stirling," was a graphically drawn word- , . ptcture well presented, and at its conclusion Mr. Furness was heartily applauded. The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. which were very pleasaut throughout, and it is to be hoped the meeting was an augury of the future success of the society so auspiciously revived.
SALVATIONISTS CHARGED WITH ASSAULT.

There was a large attendance of the public at Wallington Borough Court, yesterday, during the hearing of charges of assault against local Salvationists, in which great in- terest was manifested. Four members of the Warrington corps of the Salvation Army name James Jenkins, Watson Atkinson, Henry Jones, and William Crighton, were sum- moned for having on the 7th inst. unlawfully assaulted aud beaten Joseph tt bailey. There was a counter charge of the same date against Joseph Whalley of having assaulted Thomas Jenkies, and another charge against Martin Lane of assaulting Henry Jones.—Mr. Percy Davies, solicitor, appeared for the prosecutor Whalley and Mr. Cottingham, barrister, Manchester, appeared for the defendants in the first case, who appeared in dock in full uniform.—Mr. P. Davies, in opening the case, said it seamed the four defend- ants, along with a lot of others, were in the habit of patrolling—he supposed that was the proper word—the streets of Warrington, as their Worships (Captain Rey- nolds and Mr. Ziba Armitage) and every other inhabitant of the borough were well aware; and they had been in the habit of doing so for the last five or six months. They bad what they called a barracks, and that barracks was situate in Academy-street. Of course, every man in Warrington had a perfect right to walk the streets so long as he behaved himself, but be sub- mitted that the salvation Army did not behave itself, and therefore could not be tolerated.—Mr. Cotting- ham: I object, sir, to any statement whatsoever as to the conduct of this body called the Salvation Army. We are here upon a summons for assaulting certain individuals. Whatever is said as to the Salvation Army is wholly irreve- lent, and it is referred to simply for tbe purpose of attempt- ing to prejudice the Bench. I object to anything said about the conduct of the Salvation Army. We must come to the point of assault.—Mr. Davies submitted that Mr. Cotting- ham was entirely wrong as to what he said to the Bench, because he was leading on to the assault. He referred to the time when Warrington was a quiet, well-conducted town on Sunday afternoon before the Salvation Army came into the town.—Mr. Cottingham again objected, and asked the opinion of the Bench as to whether the conduct of the Salvation Army in general was to be made the subject of trial here.—The Bench : Certainly not.—Mr. Davies said the Army was walking down Horsemarket-street on the day named and Whalley and several friends were walking towards Academy-street through Scotland-road, when they noticed the Salvation Army sweeping down Buttermarket-street—(laughter)—with the loud noise of cymbals, a trumpet (he thought they had lately added a cornet), several banjos, and tambourines, some of the members waving handkerchiefs and walking backwards, and little boys—he dld not think he WAS going too far in stating—uttering blasphenay.—Mr. Cottingham said this was the third time he had had to object, and he was sure the Bench would have t essert its authority upon Mr. Davies before he would keep in proper restraint, He had no right to make such statements.—Mr. Armitage: I shall certainly obj,ct to sit here and hear the Salvation Army disrespectfully treated.—Mr. Davies proceeded to state that on arrival at the Barracks the men opened ranks to allow the female Salvationists to pass through to the Barracks, and in opening ranks the men caused the crowd that fol- lowed them to push the people back. That in itself was nat right. No man ought to be pushed in the streets. It was perfectly right that the female Salvationists should he pre- tected, but at the same time the S ilvatiouists had no right to push people in the streets. On this particular occasion the four defendants committed a ;nest unjustifiable assault upon Whittaker. He would call before the magistrates to prove his case James Fee, Joseph Whalley, John Riley, Dr. Cennell, Mr. Birchen, Mr. Beiuee, P.C. Smith, and Martin Lane.—At tee request of Mr. Cottingham the wit- nesses were ordered out of court. —Mr. Davies, continuing, said while the members of the army were filing hats the Barracks the crowd,which was attracted by the cornet,banjo, and other Instruments, pushed Whalley against the defen- dant Jenkins. Jenkins, "like a warrior bold," turned round and immediately struck Whalley a very heavy blow upon the shoulder, and then the other warriors joined in the melee. Atkinson seized Whalley by the collar, and in "throttling" him destroyed his handker- chief. Henry Jonee and Wm. Crighton seized him by the legs, threw him down on the floor, and dragged him about the street. The row was so great that it attrected the at- tention of Dr. Cannel!, who unfortunately lived in Academy- street. Soon P.C. 33 (Smith) came upon the scene and his client Whalley informed him but for the interference of this policeman, who took him out of this Salvation Army riot, he believed he would never have come out of it alive.— Joseph Whalley, the complainant, a box maker (out of em- ployment), residing at 47. Win wick-road, in confirming the above statement, said someone behind pushed him against Jenkins, Jenkins turned round and deliberately struck him a heavy blow on the left shoulder. They pushed him back, and they had so sooner done that than Atkinson seized him by the throat and ripped off his handkerchief. Jones then seized him by the legs, an dragged him on the floor. While down Crighton struck him several times. He was after- wards given in charge of the policeman by Atkinson, and the constable took him out of the crowd.—ln cross-examina- tion by Mr. Cottingham, witness said he belonged to the Catholics. He did not strike anybody, did not make any complaint to the police of any assault. He did not complain as he WAS so excited. He was a good Catholic, and so fond of his own religion he did not like any others. (Laughter.) His clothes did not get soiled.—James Fee also gave evidence, and said he did not interfere when the police came up, as they would have taken him. (Laughter.)—A number of other witnesses were called on behalf of Whalley, and then the Salvationists were individually sworn and gave evidence. It was to the effect that on opening ranks to protect the female soldiers from the violence of the crowd, Whalley, who was the aggressor, hit Jenkins a blow under the right ear, and he was seized by Atkinson and detained until the police came. Lane then came up to take Whalley's part, and struck Jones. Lane was then seized and %ken to the Barracks, where he was kept until Inspector Berry came, when he was released.— Jenkins, Atkinson, Jones, and Crighton all denied having struck Whalley, and Thos. Burrows, a Salvationist, deposed to seeing Lane kick Jones when being conveyed to the Bar- racks.—On the conclusion of the evidence, Mr. Cottingham addressed the Bench on behalf of the Salvationists. He stated that the Case had been brought into court simply to bring ridicule on the institution called the Salvation Army; but lie was glad to find that the Roinan Catholics had not disgraced themselves in any way. He at first thought that perhaps the row bad been caused by the low Irish popula- tion of the town, but he was glad to find that it was other- wise. He referred to the number of men going about the country disseminating Atheistical literature, and com- mended the efforts of bodies of people such , the Salvation Army, who since the days Wesley had been going about trying to do good. of eviewing the evidence, Mr. Cottinghain dwelt upon the In t fact that Whalley came out of this desperate attack without a Is mark of violeuce upon him, and with his clothes notsi,eve ng n torn. All the witnesses spoke under the de-pest ossibie r p ejudice, and he asked the Bench to discount that p •in the use it in inner. But for the feeling that Prejudict imported into the case against the Sal vationists, h had been . have thought it one of the most ordinary e should he asked the Bench to take into consideratiqn the cases ; and . prevailed in the matter. In conclusion, he araimUS tuat trusted that t his WAS a case in which the magistrates would . not to th The Sconclusion that the Salvation Army bad been to come v were a body entitled to protection rather than bl nue. animadversion. They were a body called into existence for a meritorious ut pose, and wrilese the c ise was proved up to p the hilt in all the particulars he thought the Bench ought not to convict —A fter a short censaltatien in private, Cap- tain Revnelde said they quite agrehd that Jenkins sheuld be bound over to ke sp the peace for six months, himself in £lO, and two suretie, of £5 each ; Atkinson was orcle,.ed to be similarly bound ON 'er for the same perioa ; and Martin o he bound over in like sums for the Lane was also ordered \ same period for the as, sault on Henry cones. The c tses against Henry Jones, W ihat Crighton, and Joseph Wh 41- I ley, complainants in the tare case were diemissed.—The dee;sion WAS rc,CciVed With cheers by tee assembled crowd t. in the street below the coat

Pit. SENTATION TO TfIE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON. On Monday afternoon a numerous company assembled in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, for the purpose of witnessing the presentation to the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. W. Quekett, M.A.) of a marble bust of himself, which has been most faithfully executed by our townsman, Ms. J. Warrington Wood. Amongst the company we noticed the Mayor of Warrington (J. Crosfield, Esq.), the Rev. W. and Mrs. Quekett, Rey. Canon and Mrs. Dodd (Stretton), Rey. Canon and Mrs. Whitley (Newton), Rev. S. Mrs., and Miss Wilkinson, Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. Carleton, Rev. W. Wilson (Burtonwood), Rev. G. F. and Mrs. Roberts, Rev. J. Harrison (curate of Holy Trinity), Alderman and Mrs. Harrison, Aldermen Pickmere, Thewlis, and Kean ; Councillor and Mrs. Brown ; Councillor and Mrs. Barker, Councillor and Mrs. R. W. Francomb, Councillor and Mrs. Hutchinson, Councillor R. W. and Mrs. Marsh, Councillor and Mrs Taylor, Councillor J. E. and Mrs. Wright, Councillors Ash- ton, Broadbent, Caldwell, and Woolfall, Captain teicholson, Dr. Mackie and Miss Gray, Dr. and Mrs. McFall, Mr. R. and the Misses Pickinere, Mr. N. 8., Mrs., and Miss Perci- val, Mr. Thomas, Mrs. and the Misses Robinson, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Jolley, Messrs. A. Crosfield, E. Aukland, S. Davies' J. Smethurst, H. Thornton, A. Woods, ate. The Council Chamber, as well as the entrance thereto, was adorned with a number of plants from the Park gardens tastefully arranged by Mr. Green, awl the bust occupied the ceaspicuoue piece in the room. The proc ;clings were opened by The MAYOR expressing the pleasure it had afforded him to give his consent to the presentation being made in the Council Chamber. His We ship also explained that he was not able to perform the presentation ceremony himself, because he nad to receive the bust from the Rector aft-r it was presented to him; and he (the Mayor) should be in a very curious posit on if he first presented it and then received it. Mr. ROBINSON then read letters of apology for absence which he had received from Lord 'Winmarleigh, Sir R. Cross, M.P., Islr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., Bishep Kelly,- Canon Hopwood, and others. Mr. Alderman PICKMERE then made the presenta- tion, remarking that it showed their appreciation of the good work the Rector had done for the glory of God and the welfare and future happiness of their fellow townsmen. After a reference to the fact that the late Charles Dickens had described Mr. Quekett as a " model curate," whilst labouring in the parish of St. George's-in- the-East, London, the worthy alderman said they all knew that when the Rector came amongst them he brought his knowledge and experience to bear on his work, and in a very few years he contrived by some means or other to raise sufficient funds to enlarge, to beautify, and to restore their grand old parish church with its noble spire; a church they were all proud of, and a church in which the poorest could wor- ship in simplicity and truth. (Applause.) The Rector had always studied to avoid anything which might tend to annoy the feelings of his parishioners in his conduct of the ser- vices ; they had been plain and unvarnished, simple and truthful. All knew the Rector as well as he did. The rev, gentleman deserved the tribute about to be paid him; and Me heartily hoped he would be spared for many years to see it. At all events the Rector now had the satisfaction of knowing that after his death, and when his friends and relatives looked upon the linaments of the bust they would be able to say," 'There was a man who di I his duty as Rector of Warrington." (Applause.) He was very proud to have the pleasure of presenting his old friend, if he might be so allowed to call him—for he worked with the Rector as treasurer of the National Schools for 12 or 14 years—witk the bust as a tribute from the people of Warrington. (Ap- plause.) The bust was here unveiled by Mr. R)binson amid ap- plause. The Rev. S. WILKINSON, in the course of a few cod- gratulatory observations, said they were preserving that day the memory of the Rector of Warrington in stone, but that was unnecessary, because he felt sure that for a long time the inhabitants of Warrington would remember the Rev. Wm. Quekett. (Applause) The rector had done a great deal of good work since he came to Warrington. They had only to go to the Parish Church and look at that noble building with its tower and spire—which might be called one of the finest built in modern times—to see a monument of:the Rector's work, and a proof that the inhabi- tants of the borough appreciated the rector by seconding him in raising the necessary funds. (Applause.) But he was not present that afternoon to praise the Rector. They knew him, they loved him, they respected him; and they had met to pay a deserved compliment to a good and holy man (Applause.) The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON also offered a few words of congratulation to the Rector upon the honour which had been done him; and Dr. MA.CKIR spoke in complimentary terms of the Rector on behalf of those outside the Parish Church. The BECTOK, on corning forward to acknowledge the presentation, was very warmly received. Tnis, he said, was the fourth time in his clerical life that he had been called upon by his parishioners to come forward and receive at their hands a tribute of their regard and affection. Other testimonials had been given to him coder peculiar circum- stances. The present one was doubly interesting to him, and be could hardly find words in which to express his tlgenks to all his friends for their great kindness to him. Proceeding to relate the circumstances under which Ihe wone to Warrington, the Rector said he laboured twenty-five years in London, and he there endeavoured to do many things. There was there a class of people who were called needlewomen, who worked very hard, and hal to make shirts at 21 I. each. He took up their cause, and he hit upon the expedient of writing to the Times from time to time, calling upon the public to come forward and assist in a great emigration scheme, the object being to send some of these poor distressed women to other countries, where they would be loved and respected. The appeal was responded to by a large number of nobility and gentry, and he was pleased to tell them that no less a sum than £40,000 was collected. A committee was formed and set to work, and he was deputed to provide ships to take these emigrants to other countries. No fewer than 36 ships I were obtained, and five thousand women sent away. (Ap- plause.) Lord Herbert and he were great friends, and when the work had been accomplished it was decided that some- thing; should he done for him. Lord Herbert spoke to Lord Aberdeen on his behalf, and asked that the next living that became vacant should he given to him. The appointment of the Bishop of Sodor and Man took place at this time, and whatever Church preferment he held was forfeited to the Crown. Se the great living of War- rington fell to the presentation of the Premier. A great exertion was made en behalf of the Lifford family to , possess it, and to give to the C. own another living. The family appealed to the Queen. who sent for Lord Aberdeen, and he told Her Majesty that he had promised Lord Herbert that his friend Mr. Quekett should have the living. He (the Rector) did not then know anything of this; all was done without his knowledge. Otte day, a very !rainy day, a poor man in the parish who was ill wished to see him before he died, and the poor fellow had sent an in- timation to him to his house that he had been reduced in circumstances and was in the workhouse. Reining as it was, he sent a message to the effect that he would see the man. He set off, and on his way thither he went under an arch- way to shelter from the storm. While he remained there in ran a gentleman without an umbrella, and he (the Rector) said to him, "Well, sir, you have come without a great coat or umbrella this wet day "I have," was the reply, "I am on a foolish errand. I have a letter to deliver to a clergyman in this neighbourhood, but I missed my way and having been sent in the wrong direction, I don't know where to go." "What is his name; because I live in this part of the world, and I may perhaps know the ad- dress ?" he asked. The gentleman then showed him the name and address, and he (the Rector), looking at the en- velope and seeing his own mime Upon it, said, "I am that gentleman." (Laughter and applause.) The gentleman then said he required an answer as soon as possible, because he had to meet Lord Aberdeen before three o'clock, as he was going to Windsor by comm and of the Queen; but he (the Rector) did not open the letter till he got to his study, when jee found that it was a very flattering one from Lord Aberdeen, offering him the living of War- rington. He at once went to the Clergy List to see what the living was worth—(laughter)—but the amount was not stated. However, he wrote to Lord Aberdeen accepting the living, and telling him that he would call upon him the next day and thank him personally for his kindoess. In I that way he became the Rector of Warrington. He came to the town a perfect stranger, and he brought with him a tin box containing a great seal. He should never forget it, because it was signed on behalf of the Government. He was inducted to Warrington under the Great Seal, and it cost him £B7. (Laughter.) He looked upon that as a large suns to pay before getting a penny from Warrington. (Re- newed laughter.) However, he came to Warrington with his credentials, which were read in the presence of the churchwardens and others. The door of the church was first opened, then he was told to lock everyone out and walk round the whole of the church, and next go up into the belfry and ring the bell—(laughter)L-to let the public know he had taken possession. He should never forget that. The stairs had been worn for 200 years, and the bell-ringers with their clogs had worn holes into them six inches deep. He could not step exactly in the same way the ringers had been in the habit of do- ing, and when he got about half way up the staircase he fell, damaged his hat, hurt his arm, and tore his trousers. (Laughter.) When he came down he showed himself to Mr. Lowe and the churchwardens. (Renewed laughter.) These gentlemen had been wondering where he had got to, and had begun to regard him is lost. He told them what had be- fallen him, and said, jokingly, "Now, Mr.-Churchwardens, I appeal to you to pay for a new pair of trousers out of the church rate," but they said they were sorry, and that there was no church rate. He then went away, and he had to walk in the condition described from the church to the Lion Hotel, where he was slaying. (Laughter.) Sunday came, and he went to the church. Large numbers came to one the new parson. •He bad to read the Thirty-nine Articles, and when he was! conducted by the clerk to his place he had to stand upon an old box, the lid of which was very shaky, and before blon was nothing but a smell pillar with a hoard on it to serve as a reading desk. (Laughter.) There was a gentleman then outing in the gallery, occupying the at now used by Alder man Webster, who was sorry to see that sate of things, and when after the service he (the Rector) went into the vestry, the clerk presented him with a chc,cpze sent by the gentleman signed but not filled in. He was to fill in any amount he liked and to have a e. w reading desk made at once for use in the church. His name was Norris. No doubt some present would remember

the name. That was the first gift he received. So he thanked God and took courage. Pee Rector afterwards related his efforts to restore the church, and mentioned the names of several gentlemen who had generously assisted him in his work. Turning to the future, Mr. Quekett said the inhabitants. of the town had presented him with his bust. An artist once told him that he always looked better on one side than he did on the other; and if any man ever took an interest in his work it was Mr. Wood in executing the bust. He (the Rector) should never forget the time. He had to sit to him for three weeks for four hours a day; in fact he should imagine that Mr. Wood knew how many 1 hairs he bad on his head. He also measured his eyes, nose, and mouth; and was made out of the same clay as the bust of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. (Laughter.) He travelled from Rome with the Chancellor of the Exchequer and in the same box, and they came to London together. (Laughter.) He was very proud of the bust, and he was happy to receive it. (Applause.) The Rector concluded by for- mally presenting the bust to the Mayor on behalf of the in- habitants of the town. The MAYOR, in accepting the bust, thanked the Rector for the gift presented to him as representing the Corperation of Warrington. He could only tell the Recter that it would be valued as being an everlasting record of one who had done a good work in his day, and of one who had been spared to live a long life. They would also appreciate the bust as a splendid piece of work on the part of the artist. (Applause.) It was one of those things that would make the people of Warrington proud that they had produced such a scalptor as Mr. John Warrington Wood. (Applause.) He 'ventured to say there was not a man living either in this or in any foreign country who could make a likeness in marble equal to Mr. John Warrington Wood, and be thought that was a great deal for Warrington to boast of. The bust would be placed in the Museum, add he hoped that those of many other Warrington worthies would be placed around it. He had long wished they had more works of art in thelluseum, both in sculpture and in painting. If there were any gentle- men present who were disposed to be liberal, or who were filled with local patriotism, they would be proud to receive any works of art they would present to the Corporation, which would be duly placed in the Museum and Lilerary. It was a means of educating their working classes that, in his opinion, was very valuable. (Applause.) Mr. ROBINSON having intimated that the presentation committee were under a liability of £l5, and that the members would be pleased to received additional subscrip- tions,

Councillor BROLDEENT moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding over the meeting, and the resolution was seconded by Alderman HARRISON and carried. The MAYOR, in acknowledging the compliment, said it was always a pleasure to him to assist in anything that united them and promoted a good feeling; and be must sly this for the Rector, that as far as he knew—and he had lived in Warrington all the time the Rector had been in it— he had never done anythise• that was calculated to cause separation or ill-feeling. (Applause.) Above all things he (the Mayor) loved to see a pure, simple, Christian fellow- ship exist among the people, no matter what their particu- lar religious belief might be. That was what they all bad to aim for. Ha thanked tl•em very much for their vote of thanks. (Applause.) A vote of thanks having been accorded Mr. Robinson, the secreta-y of the movement, and the same hiving been re- sponded to by him, the proceedings terminated.

THE CZAR AND CONSTITUTIONAL GOVERNMENT.—A Central Nevis telegram, dated St. Petersburg Thursday, , says :—lt is stated that the Czar's stay in Denmark has greatly modified his prejudices against constitutional government. It is understood that arrangements are being made by the authorities for a practical test at Deal during the pre- sent month of the merits of the life-saving apparatus ex- hibited at the Fisheries Exhibition. To enable the judges to make the awards the experiments will probably take place between the 15th and 20th inst. MISSING GENTLEMEN.—An advertisement appears in the Dublin papers of yesterday offering a handsome reward for information of the whereabouts or death of Lord Cecil Fair- ford, late of Cheltenham and Abergavenny ; of Mr. Henry Lynch Bloase, eldest son of Sir Robert Lynch Blosse ; Mr. Francis Blackburn eldest son of Mr. Edward Blackburn, of Rathfarnham Castle, Dublin ; and Mr. Edwin Curzin, eldest son of the late Hon. Sydney Curzon, of Kingston-on-Thames and Blackpool. THE GOVERNOR-ELECT OF CANADA. Yesterday after- noon the Marquis of Lansdowne arrived in Londonderry, accompanied by the Duke of Abercorn and a distinguished party. He was received by the Mayor, and an address was presented by the Corporation of Londonderry. The Marquis replied, dwelling on the fact that the Irish largely made Up the population of the Dominion. He eulogised Lord Dufferin and the Marquis of Lorne's administration. A luncheon was subsequently given at the palace of Dr. Alexander, Pro- testant bishop. Mr. Starkey, of Birmingham, who had been steviteeat Criccieth for some time past went out in a canoe about six p.m. on the 4th inst., and has not since been heard of. The canoe, which was found near Portmadoc Bar on Wednesday evening last, did not appear to have been upset, as the cushion was in its place, and there were only two inches of water inside the craft. A paddle was found near Morfabychan, and a hat which is supposed to have belonged to the missing gentleman was found yesterday morning near Criccieth Castle. AFFAIRS OF ALEXANDER BROTHERS: LIABILITIES £s2,ooo.—Yesterday morning, at the London Bankruptcy Court, an application was made to Mr. Registrar Brougham, sitting as Thief Judge, to appoint a receiver of the estate of Messrs. Alexander Brothers, whose failure for £62,000 was announced on Thursday. Mr. H. Montague, in making the application, stated that the debtors were merchants carry- ing on business at 7, Drapet's Gardens, E.C. The liabilities were stated at £52,000, but of that amount £52,000 was fully secured, and there were other assets of the value of £4,1500. He applied for the appointment of Mr. H. E. Broad, accountant, Walbrook, as receiver of the estate, and for an injunction against three suing- creditors, His HON- our granted the applications

div.head: SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE AND THE IRISH PARTY.
div.p: SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE AND THE IRISH PARTY.

_ The Dublin Nation says that when Parliament re- assembles it will be the imperative duty of the Irish national representatives to bring an indictment of the most serious character against Sir Stafford Northcote. It will be necessary to accuse jaim of acting the part of leader in the work of stirring up The embers of sectarian strife; of being a fomentor of public disturbances, and of being accessory to all the outrages which have disgraced Belfast during his visit. ilici Sir Stafford Northcote remained but another week in Belfast, it is not improbable that the whole town would by this time have been a scene of riot, plr.nder, and carnage.

THE ELECTION OF ASSISTANT OVERSEER FOR WA.RRINGTON. The counting of the votes in the matter of the election of an assistant overseer for Warrington was commenced at the Overseers' Office, at the Town Hall, on Saturday ni)rning last, at nine o'clock, and—excluding Sunday, of course— was continued without interruption until half-past four o'clock yesterday afternoon, when it practically cencluded. The proceedings were of a purely private nature, represen- tatives of the Press being excluded. The chairman of the overseers (Mr. Aldernean Kean) superintended the counting daily, being relieved only an hour each day for dinner by either Mr. Harrison or Mr. Blackhurst, brother over- seers. He was assisted by an equal number of scrutineers appointed on behalf of the candidates—f6ur each by the two political parties, and two each by the candidates. Mr. Green's scrutineers were Mr. Ridgway (solicitor), and Mr. Thornton, and for Mr. Turistall, the Conservative agent, Mr. Harnpson, did duty. The candidates themselves were present from time to time. The work, we may say, was ex- ceedingly tedious. every vote having to be to be tested; and the fact that 12 hours were spent at it each day . wi,l con- vey some idea of how carefully the whole matter must have been gone into. From the figures which we give below— and whicn we have the Chhirman's authority for stating were yesterday published without his knowledge or consent —it will be seen that Mr. Tunstall has a majority of nearly 500. It, will also he noticed that the number of bad and doubtfel votes put aside are about the same in number for each candidete. Counsel's opinion is, we believe, being taken on these votes. end after that is known there will ha an affiri,l declaration or the poll—probably on Wednesday. We may add that the scrutiny of the voting discloses the fact that some Conser- vatives have voted for Mr. Green, and on the other hand that a large number of Lileirals elected to vote for Mr. Tunstall. THE REV. G. S._REANEY'S WORK IN
LONDON.

The following from the pen of the London correspondent of a Manchester contemporary will be read with interest by many of our readers :—" A .new political and social move- ment which is going on at the East End of London Is deserving of notice as being promoted by a Nonconformist minister who was some time back very popular at War- rington. The Rev. G. S. Reaney having epent several years at Reading eince leaving Warrington, was list year appointed to be minister at Stepney Meeting House, one of the most prominent positions in the Congregationalist Church here or elsewhere. Mr. Reaney is an ardent Liberal. In former days be was not undistinguished in this respect, and it was he, I think, who made the famous declaration which electrified a Liberationist elnference at Manchester during the reign of the last Govern- ment, that "gratitude in politics is immoral." I fancy the declaration was afterwards modified or withdrawn; but Mr. Reaney has lost none of his enthusiasm for the prin- ciples of rogress. To-day, living among the great toiling million which has residence east of Landon Bridge, he has found political questions actively discussed beneath the sur- face and much grumbling and discontent with the condition of affairs. Believing that it were better we should, all hear what is to be said by the working thousands in their own behalf, he has organise,d a seriei of monthly meetings for the open discussion of What he calls "Poor Man's Politics." The idea at once attracted the working men of the district, and a couple of meetings have been held with a full attend- ance on each occasion. A month ago the gathering pro- nounced in the most emphatic fashion against emigration. Last night (Thursday) " work and wages " were under notice, or, as it was more pointedly put by one of the speakers, "Why are we so hard up ?" The wage-system was roundly denounced, and it shows the drift of feeling among the great massei of our town populations when we find it declared that "workmen should have a voice in how the work is to be produced, and how exchanged," and again that "the necessary change in this matter need not be violent." I see it stated that the programme of the Democratic Federation, which was repre- sented on the platform, found the widest accpptance in the meeting. Vence it is not surprising to' obsz-rve further that a resolution was passed calling on Government to establish relief works (with a reduction of the hours of work for those engaged on them), and also to start the business of "colonising" home lands. I don't know whether Mr. Reaney is satisfied with the direction which the debate has taken on either of these occasions, but it has been said that great influencs has been used with him to stop the meet- ings, from which it would appear that it he is satisfied cer- tain of his friends are not. It is indeed probable that habing begun the movement be finds it difficult to withdraw from it, and evidently he is much in the position of the unfortc- nate student who created the Frankenstein, as described so admirably by Mrs. Shelley,

GOOD TEMPLARS' EETINQ.— be members of the Hope of Eariestown Ltdge of Good Tetnplars held their weekly session on Monday evening in the Lodge-room, Bridge- street, Earlestown. The attendance was larger than on any previous occasion during the present year, about 60 mem- bers being present. After the opening ceremonies, six new members were initiated and several candidates proposed. Reports of the Visiting and Sick Committees were ten.lered, after which one or two items of business were considered. At the previous session a number of questions were handed in and discussed, and some of the members promised to read papers in reply to others at the succeeding meeting. In accordance with this promise, Brother E. Newman read a paper on "Are Juvenile Templara a Benefit to the Adult Order P"—to which qnestion he replied in the affirmative, maintaining they were useful in training the young in the principles of abstinence, which would be all the more stronger upon them in after years. Another question was, "Are British Home-made Wines and Cordials Intoxicating in their Character P"—an el Brother George Clarke read a number of extracts from pamphlets, Jrc., upon the point. An interesting discussion afterwards took place, the meeting throughout being of an instructive character.

"As INNOCENT AS A CLERGYMAN."—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Patrick Fox was charged with haying stolen 9s 6d, the property of Peter B!adburn, on the 6th inst. Bradburn, who lives at Ashton-le-Willows, had been in St. Helens on Saturday last, and intended to go home that evening, but missed his train. About 11 o'clock he fell in with prisoner in the streets, and p-isoner took him to some lodgings in Atlas-street, Parr. They went to bed together, but early the next morning, before complainant awoke, the prisoner got up and left the house, ancl after- wardi it was found that the money in question was missing from Bradburn's pockets.—On being asked if he were guilty prisoner said he was as "innocent as a clergyman." —Notwithstanding this assertion he was sent to gaol for one month's bard labour.

LARCENIES BY FEMALES AT ST. HELENS.—A young girl, 12 years of age, named Catherine Gilligan, was on Thurs- day, charged, at the St. Helens Police Court, with having stolen a shirt, valued at 2s. 61.„ the property of John Board- man. Mrs. Boardman, of 133, Hall-street, it seemed, had washed the shirt on Tuesday and afterwards bung it out along with other articles to dry. On assorting them for the mangle she missed the shirt, and it was afterwards ascer- tained that the prisoner, who had been seen hanging about where the clothes were drying, bad sold it for 31. to a girl named Waing, who goes about gathering rags.—A fine of 10s. was imposed,, or, in default, a week's impritooment.-- Alice Riley, a married woman, with. a child in "her arms, was also charged with having stolen a vest, valued at 83., the property of Francis Reed, of 19, Rimmer-street,Parr.— It appeared that about 10 o'clock, on Sunday night, Reed placed the vest in a box, which was afterwards locked. On Tuesday afternoon something which be was told caused him to examine the box, and he then found that the vest was gone. —A young woman, named Clara Fox, said that an Monday afternoon the prisoner called her into her house and asked her to take the vest to a pawnshop and pawn it. This she did do, and afterwards gave prisoner the money and the pawnticket.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to taking the vest and pawning it, but said she had been in the habit of taking Reed's clothes and pawning them without his authority.—Reed, on being recalled, said he was the priso- ner's father, and she had previously pawned his clothing, because she thought it was no crime pawning his, clothes, being her father. He had, however, warned her not to do it. and he brought this forward as a "test case."—A fine of 10s. was imposed, or, in default, seven days' imprison- ment.

div.head: CLERICAL BEHAVIOUR.
div.p: CLERICAL BEHAVIOUR.

An instance which has come under our notice of the somewhat erratic behaviour of a clergyman who enjoys a "fat livint" within 100 miles of Warrington is worth re- cording. The Church and parish, in which he is the central figure, are very ancient, but during the last few years both have in some respects bean modernised. Within a corn paratively short period the bells connected with the sacred edifice have been hung on an improved system, and they are now eminently suitable for what is known as "change- ringing." This fact has become widely known among change-ringers, and not many montha ago a team of these ringers journeyed from Tyldesley to this ancient building—a considerable distance, by the way—in the hope of having a pull at the bells. They were doomed to disappointment. On presenting themselves at the church, an interview was, of course, sought with the clergyman, when be bluntly refused to allow the strangers to enter the belfry, his excuse being that his own ringers were not present. It is said that subse- quently the clergyman intimated to his leading rioger that if at any time he wished to invite friends from other churches to use the bells, he could do s-e This intimation was made tome six month eince, but the leading ringer never acted upon it till the other day, when he invited four of his friends from War- rington, and two from Daresbury; to visit the parish and to ring a few changes on the bells. He thought he possessed a sort of carte blanche to act as suited him in the matter, and therefore he did not acquaint the clergyman of what he had done. The ringers paid their appointed visit on Satur- day week, the 29th nit.; and on arriving at the church found the regular ringers awaiting them, and straightway they took possession of the belfry. Before a single rope had been pulled, the clerk of the parish appeared upon the scene and interrogated the strangers as to their presence; and as he did not receive a satisfactory answer to his inquiries he communicated with the clergyman. The latter, tottering with age and evi- dently much excited, next turned up, and demanded to know who had given the strangers permission to use the bells. He was told that he had himself done so, but this he altogether repudiated in anything but elegant language, and then is peremptory and insulting tones ordered the belfry to be cleared. It was app trent from the clergymen's excited condition that it would be useless remonstrating or even apologising to him, consequently each and all the ringers took their departure. Oa getting beyond the precincts of the church they shook the dust from off their feet, and one of them indignantly exclaimed in accents loud enough to be heard by the clergyman, Well may people say the Church of England principles are good, but its foundation rotten, when there is such as you (pointing to the incumbent) at its head." The following Sunday the bells of that parish church were not tolled as usual; the ringers had struck work. They afterwards sent in a month's notice to determine their connection with the bells, and that notic!: they are now serving. Torus bell-ringers are now wanted for the parish.
ROBBING THE CORPORATION.
MR. PERCY DAVIES THROWS UP HIS BRIEF.

John Raftery, teamsman in the employ of Mr. James Warburton, farmer, was charged cm remand, at Warrington Borough Court, yesterday, with having on the Bth Septem- ber, stolen a quantity of vetches and grass, the property of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of War- rington.—Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk) prosecuted on behalf of the Corporation, and Mr. Percy Davies defen- ded the prisoder.—The facts of the case, which have already been published, are that on the date named the prisoner went with a load of vetches and grass to the Town Hall, and he was observed before entering the yard to throw off three bundles of grass which he afterwards look away with him. —During the hearing of the case, William Barlow, junior, who weighed the grass on his father's maciaine in Winwick- street. produced the svegh book, and said he altered a ticket at the request of prisoner when Mr. Davies said he had asked to see the book but the police would not allow him to see it. —Mr. Hunt (chief constable) took exception to this remark, and observed that Mr. Davies had seen everything in the book.—Mr. Davies asserted that the police would not let him see the book, and said that Mr. Hunt insulted him in an impudent manner; he never was insulted more by a policeman in his life before.—Mr. Hunt :. You saw it at Bar- low's shop.—Mr. Davies: I beg your pardon; I have not. I went there and Mr. Barlow said it was down here.—Mr. Hunt: You saw all that was in it. While this conversation was taking place, Alderman Burgess took his seat upon the bench, and Mr. Davies, on observing the Alderman, said he should give up his defence if he attempted to hear the case. —Alderman Burgess: You can please yourself; I shall not be put down.—Mr. Davies: I little thought you would have thought it was the thing.—Alderman Burgess : I want to know what the ticket shows in reference to the altered number.—Mr. D wise: I hope the reporters will take notics of what I say. The Mayor said ha would not appear in this case, but would leave it to be heard on Friday —Alderman Burgess: I was here.—Mr. Davies: I say it is most unfair that the Corporation should sit upon that bench.—Alder- man Burgess: I was here on Monday, and I did not hear the observation that you have stated fell from the Mayor and Major Pickmere.—Mr. Davies: You did not hear P—Aider- man Burgess: No.—Mr. Davies: The Mayor said this, and I leave it to you if he d'd not say that or not here —Alder- man Burgess, Allow me, please.—Mr. Davies: I shall refuse to go on with the case if you sit upon the bench, and there- fore you will be robbing the man of his defence.—Ald.rman Burgess: Will you let me see that book ?—Mr. Percy Davies: It is monstrous, monstrous.—Captain Raynolds : There are magistrates on tha bench who are not con- nected with the Corporation, Mr. Davies Mr. Burgess: You proposed an adjournment that you might , have an opportunity of preparing your defence, not to I put me off the bench.—Mr. Davies said the Corporation I were not ready with their case.—Captain Reynolds: I see there are two magistrates sitting on the b3nch whose opinion will not be in any way warped. I think you are leaving the man in peril —Mr. Davies: It is no trouble for Alder- man Burgess to retire from the Bench.—Alderman Bargess : Why should I retire p—Mr. Davies: It is not forms to dic- tate to you, and t3II you why you should retire. I should not be doing my duty to my client unless I took exception to your being on the bench.—Mr. Davies then took his seat. —Alde,man Burgess: Did you ever alter any other tickets for this man F—Witness: No, sir.—Mr. Davies: Don't cross- examine the witness; you cannot do it; yon'are the prose- cutor.—Mr. Davies, who again took up the case, then ad- dressed the Bench on behalf of the prisoner, and submitted that there was no evidence that the prisoner, who was a man of good character, took the grass.—Cantain Reynolds (to the prisoner) : We are sorry that a man with a long good character should lose it, as it is quite clear you kave lost yours this morning. We shall give you a month's im- prisonment. As regards the delibeeation of the Bench it has only been by ourselves.' Alderman Burgess has been here to watch the case for the Corporation, having some idea that their servants hal tint been qnite so vigilant as they might have been.—allerman Burgess: That is the tact. It is only that that brought me here.
